This is a digital copy of a book that was preserved for generations on library shelves before it was carefully scanned by Google as part of a project to make the world’s books discoverable online.

It has survived long enough for the copyright to expire and the book to enter the public domain <note>The "public domain" refers to creative works to which no exclusive intellectual property rights apply; they belong to the public.</note>. A public domain book is one that was never subject to copyright or whose legal copyright term has expired. Whether a book is in the public domain may vary country to country. Public domain books are our gateways to the past, representing a wealth of history, culture and knowledge that’s often difficult to discover.

Marks, notations and other marginalia <note>original: "marginalia"; handwritten notes or scribbles made in the margins of a book.</note> present in the original volume will appear in this file—a reminder of this book’s long journey from the publisher to a library and finally to you.

## **Usage guidelines**

Google is proud to partner with libraries to digitize public domain materials and make them widely accessible. Public domain books belong to the public and we are merely their custodians. Nevertheless, this work is expensive, so in order to keep providing this resource, we have taken steps to prevent abuse by commercial parties, including placing technical restrictions on automated querying.

We also ask that you:

+ *Make non-commercial use of the files* We designed Google Book Search for use by individuals, and we request that you use these files for personal, non-commercial purposes.

+ *Refrain from automated querying* Do not send automated queries of any sort to Google’s system: If you are conducting research on machine translation, optical character recognition <note>OCR; the electronic conversion of images of typed, handwritten or printed text into machine-encoded text.</note> or other areas where access to a large amount of text is helpful, please contact us. We encourage the use of public domain materials for these purposes and may be able to help.

+ *Maintain attribution* The Google “watermark” you see on each file is essential for informing people about this project and helping them find additional materials through Google Book Search. Please do not remove it.

+ *Keep it legal* Whatever your use, remember that you are responsible for ensuring that what you are doing is legal. Do not assume that just because we believe a book is in the public domain for users in the United States, that the work is also in the public domain for users in other countries. Whether a book is still in copyright varies from country to country, and we can’t offer guidance on whether any specific use of any specific book is allowed. Please do not assume that a book’s appearance in Google Book Search means it can be used in any manner anywhere in the world. Copyright infringement liability can be quite severe.

## **About Google Book Search**

Google’s mission is to organize the world’s information and to make it universally accessible and useful. Google Book Search helps readers discover the world’s books while helping authors and publishers reach new audiences. You can search through the full text of this book on the web at <insert>http://books.google.com/</insert>

Of the three writings by Bruno contained in this third
part of the second volume, ***On the Composition of Images*** <note>original: *De imaginum compositione*</note> has
not had any reprint since the original edition of 1591,
and among his mnemonic works <note>Mnemonic works are those concerning the "Art of Memory," a Renaissance system of using mental imagery and spatial architecture to organize and recall vast amounts of information.</note> it is one of the most obscure and most dif-
ficult to correct. It is for this reason that we have left
even the punctuation intact, whenever it either
did not seem that we understood with full certainty, or we could not
see a way to correct a phrase (even with high probability)
without being subsequently obliged to correct many
others in a completely improbable manner. Let
pages 287 and following serve as an example; where, if we had wanted to transform
the punctuation and the typographical composition of the original
edition, in order to keep the reader informed of the changes made
by us, it would have been necessary to print the same
text a second time entirely!

***The Hunting Torch*** <note>original: *Lampas venatoria*</note> instead, besides appearing in the reprint
by Gfrörer <note>August Friedrich Gfrörer (1803–1861), an editor who published a collection of Bruno's Latin works in the 19th century.</note> (=*G*), is found reproduced in three editions of the works
of Lull <note>Ramon Llull (c. 1232–1315), a philosopher and mystic whose logical "Art" of combining concepts was a primary influence on Bruno's thought.</note>, all three of which came from the Zetzner printing house of
Strasbourg, in the years 1598 (=*A*), 1609 (=*A*²), and 1651 (=*A*³).
In the apparatus <note>A "critical apparatus" is a series of notes in a scholarly edition that records different readings or variations found in different manuscripts or earlier editions of the text.</note> of our edition, we have only taken
into account *A*, nor can we say that having used it was of
notable utility. To use the other two as well

...seem such as to compel a different hypothesis.¹ It is certain, however, that he does not follow the original edition;² and the places in which, in contrast with *AB*, he agrees with it, are either emended by conjecture, or it must be admitted that the original edition was consulted exclusively for these instances and for the title page. These places, moreover, are not many:

p. 38, 5 to them <note>original: *illis*</note> *PG* : to others <note>original: *aliis*</note> *AB* || 39, 3 and thick <note>original: *spissisque*</note> *PG*: and ears of grain <note>original: *spicisque*</note> *AB* || 41, 4 because <note>original: *quia*</note> *PG*; where <note>original: *qua*</note> *AB* || 60, 5 because <note>original: *quia*</note> *PG*: [omitted] *AB* || 73, 28 between <note>original: *inter*</note> (after "than") *PG*: [omitted] *AB* || 77, 21 not <note>original: *non*</note> *PG*: [omitted] *AB*.

And so it will not even be surprising that in places of easy emendation, even *A'* returns to *P*, in contrast with *AA²*: for example p. 59, 13 'creative' <note>original: *creative*</note> *AA²*: 'crearive' <note>a likely typo in the original</note> *PA³G*; p. 20, 18 'are contained, and' *AA'G*: 'are contained and' *PA³* etc.

Very incorrect in the original edition, and often corrected with little method in the Gfrörer edition, is *The Art of Oratory* <note>original: *Artificium perorandi*, a treatise on rhetoric and persuasion</note>. The last pages especially are full of errors of every kind, depending in largest part on a false interpretation of Bruno's intricate and tiny handwriting; probably due to the inexperience of Alsted <note>Johann Heinrich Alsted (1588–1638), a German professor who edited some of Bruno's works</note> himself, as we are inclined to believe that Bruno's own autograph <note>The manuscript written in the author's own hand</note> had fallen into his hands. Some flaws we have removed ourselves, others Gfrörer had successfully corrected, and many others can be corrected by whoever believes it a useful task to set themselves to it on purpose. Meanwhile, we have followed our usual system, and in the text we have only introduced emendations that are absolutely obvious; for the rest, we have—

Now *G* corrects 'mixed' <note>original: *mistus*</note> into 'mixed' <note>original: *mixtus*</note> and the like at other times; and therefore it is not understood why he does not follow the edition here which, according to our hypothesis, he had before him. Concerning the proposed field of the hunt, most excellent Lord, I look around and see countless people laboring in vain. Some of them—following the futile instructions of bombastic grammarians (who, under <margin>10</margin> titles of the "art of invention," of "judgment," and of all other things—if it please the gods!—never cease to soil endless pages with filth)—consult those misguided farmers who would be better suited to cultivating other fields alongside ox-drivers. Others, hunting for monstrous birds by some literary method or other, lean on the fragile branches of a sapless tree; when these branches fail and are snatched away (as <margin>15</margin> is especially necessary), they fall "methodically" into a stony field. There, they become the miserable prey of those very birds they were trying to catch—namely, those empty thoughts which brood over the chicks of a perversely disposed ignorance in its nest. Some, with a certain servile and flattering compliance, <margin>20</margin> boast of having those men as their leaders who blow the hunting horn not so well in the games of children as in the open and [august...] <note>The word "augu-" is broken across the page; it likely completes as *augusto*, meaning noble or venerable.</note> of philoso- <sig>a 2v P</sig>

<header>GIORDANO BRUNO ON PROGRESS, ETC.</header>

...in a narrower field, thundering poorly, they entangle the dogs, scatter the wild beasts, and confound and defraud the more eager hunters. Nor are there lacking those more fortunate individuals who do not suffer from such a weakness of intellect that they are unaware that—beyond the mere titles of **judgment** and **invention** <note>In Renaissance logic, "invention" refers to the discovery of arguments, and "judgment" to the assessment of their validity.</note>—arts of this kind contain absolutely no <margin>5</margin> true invention and no judgment. Furthermore, because of the author’s <note>Referring to Aristotle.</note> obscurity and the fact that the meanings of his commentators are impassable to them, they cannot fruitfully take up the journey through the **Aristotelian paths**. Relying instead on the strength of their own intellect, they seem to say with the <margin>10</margin> tragic Oedipus: *I shall go this way, stripped of every guide. Alone, I will better find the path I seek.* <note>original: "huc omni duce spoliatus ibo. Melius inveniam viam, quam quaero, solus." A quote from Seneca's play *Oedipus*.</note> Pitying the deserted and unhappy condition of these men, I thought I would be doing something worthwhile if I labored in the ordering, exposition, cultivation, completion, and elucidation of this art, so that I might be a supporter to the best of my ability for those <margin>15</margin> whom heaven has destined to participate in these fruits.

As to what and how much I have achieved here, let it be the judgment of you and others (to whom it will be given to understand this). I preferred to dedicate these things to you and to offer, submit, and commend them to your examination, <margin>20</margin> judgment, and patronage—as one who, seeing with your own eyes, is not forced to commit things to be judged by the blind or the bleary-eyed. I mean those who, because they are ignorant, either pluck at things more fervently with feigned contempt, or—so that they might seem to know somewhat more—press their <margin>25</margin> lips together a little and almost wrinkle their noses, commending the same things rather coldly. Farewell, and receive as friends the **Muses**, who have decorated you with no common distinctions.

Indeed, we do not think it is sufficient to have caught the fleeing beast in the woody and brambly field if the hunter remains ignorant of how he should handle it and <margin>5</margin> turn it to his use. ### SECTION III.

Just as every inquiry or problem consists of two parts joined together by a substantive verb <note>original: "verbo substantivo" — the verb "to be," which links the subject and predicate.</note>, the first of which is that about which something is affirmed or denied, and the second is that which is affirmed or denied of the other; so too it is necessary that every syllogistic <margin>10</margin> <margin>708 G edition</margin> and enthymematic <term>An "enthymeme" is a logical argument where one of the premises is implied rather than stated directly.</term> argument consists of three terms: the major extreme **A**, the minor extreme **C**, and the middle **B**. ### SECTION V.

# GIORDANO BRUNO

Of these, the most difficult of all to establish is the universal affirmative <note>original: "problema universale affirmativum"; a statement asserting that all members of a group share a quality, such as "All humans are mortal."</note> and it is the most easily overturned; for a universal is refuted whether it applies to no one, or if it does not apply to someone. Moreover, the fact that it does not apply to someone is proven in all [logical figures], but that it applies to **5** none is shown in two. Next to this in the difficulty of its construction is the universal negative <note>A statement like "No humans are stones."</note>, which is destroyed by the fact that it applies to either all or some. Particulars <note>Statements about "some" members of a group.</note>, however, are refuted in only one way: the former <note>The particular affirmative, "Some A is B."</note> by "to all," and the latter <note>The particular negative, "Some A is not B."</note> by "to none." But because they are **10** found in more figures and modes, they are far more easily confirmed than universals.

### ON THE PROGRESS OF LOGICAL HUNTING.

First, [one looks] toward the <term>predicate</term> <note>The part of a statement that asserts something about the subject; for example, in "all humans are mortal," "mortal" is the predicate.</note> A; second, toward those things which are said of A or contain A, which are called **consequents** by Aristotle, and are signified by B; <margin>712 G</margin> third, | toward those things of which A is said, or which are <margin>a 7r P</margin> contained | by A, and are called **antecedents** by Aristotle, and are signified by C; fourth, toward those things which are contrary to A itself, or remote and alien, of which A is not said and which are not said of A, and which A does not contain and by which A could not be contained, and are called **contraries** by Aristotle, and are signified by D. In a similar order, one should look toward E, the <term>subject</term> <note>The main topic of a proposition; for example, in "all humans are mortal," "humans" is the subject.</note> of the inquiry or problem; toward those things which are said of the subject, signified by F; toward those things of which the subject is said, signified by G; and toward those things opposite and alien to the subject, signified by H.

[If the question is whether] some pleasure might not be good, "good" is the <term>predicate</term> of the problem, and "pleasure" is the <term>subject</term>.

A therefore signifies **GOOD**.
B [signifies] the useful, the things to be pursued, the desirable, the favoring, the preserving.
<margin>5</margin> C [signifies] happiness, health, integrity, beauty, virtue.
D [signifies] things to be avoided, the harmful, the alien, the destroying, the corrupting.
<margin>713 G</margin> E signifies **PLEASURE**.
F [signifies] the pleasing, the naturally desirable, the easy, the secure, <margin>10</margin> the tranquil.
G [signifies] pleasant company, riches, honor, a good marriage, vengeance upon enemies.
H [signifies] labor, pain, poverty, disgrace, boredom.

For those wishing, therefore, to universally conclude A of E <note>That is, to prove the statement "All pleasure is good."</note>, <margin>15</margin> one must look to the <term>antecedents</term> <note>Terms that imply the predicate; if C is true, then A (good) is true.</note> of the predicate and to the <term>consequents</term> <note>Terms implied by the subject; if E (pleasure) is true, then F is true.</note> of the subject; for if any of these are identical to the other, you will have what you intend according to the first <term>mood</term> of the first <term>figure</term> <note>A standard form of Aristotelian syllogism (e.g., Barbara: All M is P, All S is M, therefore All S is P).</note>. He who desires a <term>particular affirmative</term> <note>A statement such as "Some pleasure is good."</note> should look whether some of the antecedents of both are the same <margin>20</margin> <margin>a 8r P</margin> (for thus he will conclude in the first, third, and fourth [moods] of the third figure), or he should look to see if the <term>contraries</term> of the predicate and the antecedents of the subject agree; for he will be able to conclude in the first and third [moods] of the first figure by means of <term>conversion</term> <note>The logical process of switching the subject and predicate of a proposition.</note> of the conclusion. Likewise in the third [figure]. He who seeks a <term>universal negative</term> <note>A statement such as "No pleasure is good."</note> should see if there <margin>25</margin> is agreement between the consequents of the subject and the <term>repugnants</term> <note>Things that are logically incompatible with or opposite to a term.</note> of the predicate (for it will be concluded in the second [mood] of the first and the first [mood] of the second figure); or whether the repugnants of the subject and the consequents of the predicate agree, so that he may conclude in the second figure.

For one wishing, however, to conclude a <term>particular negative</term> <note>A statement in the form "Some S is not P," such as "Some pleasure is not good."</note>, one must look to the <term>antecedents</term> <note>Concepts that naturally precede or imply the subject.</note> of the subject and the <term>repugnants</term> <note>original: "repugnantia"; these are concepts that are incompatible with or contradict the predicate.</note> of the predicate; for in this way (except in the fourth <term>mood</term> of the second <term>figure</term> <note>Referring to the syllogistic form "Baroco," which traditionally requires a specific method of proof called *reductio ad absurdum*.</note>), it will be possible to conclude in all figures.

### VIII. Section.

In all of these (regarding other particular moods which might seem to have been omitted), the <term>rules of conversion</term> <note>The logical process of swapping the subject and predicate of a proposition while maintaining its truth value.</note> should be kept in mind. For where "Every E is A," then "some E is A" and "some A is E"; where "No E is A," then <margin>10</margin> "no A is E," "some E is not A," and "some A is not E"; where "A certain E is A," <note>original: "E quoddam est A"</note> there "a certain A is E"; where "A certain E is not A," there "a certain A is not E." <note>Bruno here lists the rules of logical conversion. Note that in standard Aristotelian logic, the particular negative ("Some S is not P") does not validly convert to "Some P is not S," though Bruno includes it here in his summary of rules.</note>

## ON THE HUNTING-LAMP OF LOGICIANS. <note>original: "De Lampade Venatoria Logicorum"; Bruno uses the metaphor of a "hunting-lamp" to describe the logical method used to "track down" the middle term of a syllogism.</note>

### THE LADDER.

---

#### SECTION I. <note>original: "I. Membrum"</note>

<margin>5</margin> Possession, which is near-divine, must be preceded by acquisition; laborious acquisition by discovery; diligent discovery by searching; skillful searching by light; the vivid fire of light by the preparation of a contriving intention; that intention by a watchful drive of the will; and finally, this will must be preceded by the <margin>10</margin> apprehension of the goal and the attainable good.

#### SECTION II.

The possible and attainable good—which the Prince of the Peripatetics <note>Aristotle (384–322 BCE). His followers were called "Peripatetics" (those who walk about) because of his habit of teaching while walking in the Lyceum.</note> proposed at the outset of this art—is that we might possess that path, once found and acquired, which has been correctly intended and sought out. This is the path by which we may offer propositions on any problem by arguing from <term>universals</term> <note>General principles or categories that apply to many individual instances.</note>; through these propositions, we may argue; <margin>15</margin> <margin>2 P</margin> in providing answers, we may reach a determination; and by reaching a determination, we may provide a response.

<summary>Bruno introduces a philosophical "ladder" of discovery, linking the human will and intention to the light of reason and final possession of knowledge. He aligns his method with Aristotle’s goal of being able to argue from universal principles on any given problem.</summary>

## SECTION III.

But who does not judge that we should strive toward that goal—perhaps not so violently or loftily, but in a more humble and sober manner—so that we may finally be seen to have attained these three things: namely, an exercise that is not in vain, conversations that are less idle, and, most important of all, a philosophical <margin>5</margin> contemplation that must not be overlooked? For first, this method provides a system by which we can argue about any proposed topic; second, it suggests an examination by which—once the opinions of many have been counted—we can raise objections against those who do not discourse well, drawing not from foreign ideas but from the internal character of each specific doctrine; and third, it applies a <term>balance</term> <note>original: "trutina"; a set of scales used for weighing arguments.</note> by which <margin>10</margin> we, being capable of doubting <margin>715 G</margin> either side of a contradiction, | may all the more easily discern and define what should be judged as true or false in individual cases. For just as a goldsmith—after gold has been separated from a mixture of other minerals by a kind of purifying art—takes the most precious of metals itself, now cleansed, <margin>15</margin> refined, and tested, and then beats it out, expands it, and uses it for specific shapes through casting to decorate his workshop; so too, after a problem has been placed under discussion and <margin>20</margin> <margin>3 P</margin> debate, | it follows that the <term>storehouse</term> <note>original: "apotheca"; while it can mean a shop or warehouse, Bruno uses it here as a metaphor for the mind's repository of knowledge.</note> of human reason is decorated with the character of an <term>apodictic</term> <note>original: "apodicticae"; a logical term for a proposition that is necessarily true or demonstrable, leaving no room for doubt.</note> conclusion, free from the stain of any uncertainty, derived from what has been posited, granted, proven, and made evident. Thus, first we are directed onto the path; second, we are strengthened for the encounter; and third, we wipe away the mist, as it were, from our eyes. <margin>25</margin> For first, this knowledge of the tracks renders the pursuit of that goal at which we aim accessible and easy; second, [it strengthens us...]

# THE FIELD
---
## THE FIRST MEMBER

<margin>5</margin>The **Field** is a universal space, encompassing many retreats and courtyards, in which one must attempt to hunt and to find. The first, middle, and last parts of this field relate, in their own orders, to those "places" <note>Aristotelian "topoi" or seats of arguments.</note> of argumentation, just as the letters of writing are held to be the bases and <margin>10</margin> elements of the writing itself. In these clearly **5 P** <note>Page 5 of the Prague manuscript.</note> lies the power of introducing and making known particular conclusions. Indeed, certain pre-ordered universal premises ought to stand first and be held beforehand in the soul; under these, the specific principles of each art are understood to be contained, as if in a <margin>15</margin> faculty ready for action. These are the very same things which the <term>demonstrator</term> <note>original: "demonstrator"; one who uses logic to prove certain, scientific truths.</note> uses for the one side which concludes only what is true, whereas the <term>topician</term> <note>original: "topicus"; a dialectician who argues from probability or common opinion on either side of a debate.</note> uses them indefinitely for drawing out either side of a contradiction. In this way, the former destines and adapts the same <term>sword</term> <note>original: "gladium"; logic as a weapon for defense or attack.</note> <margin>20</margin> only for defending and protecting the truth, while the latter uses it for pursuing whatever he wishes, according to the occasion and his own judgment.

## THE SECOND MEMBER

Here I greatly desire to examine the weight of the opinion of those <term>moles</term> <note>original: "talparum"; Bruno’s frequent term for those "blind" to his philosophical light.</note>, who perceive the end and importance of this art rising so high...

<margin>5</margin> the faculty of demonstration <note>original: "demonstrativa facultas"; the ability to prove something with absolute scientific certainty.</note> seems to show itself apart from the topical art <note>original: "topicam"; dialectic, or the art of reasoning from probable or generally accepted opinions.</note>, so that the demonstrator himself ought to believe he is all the more poor, the more he happens to be deeply saddened by the sense of his own lack. Indeed, I do not consider it a great enough virtue if someone following Socrates has attained that sense of lack, while they still wait | for better things to be <margin>718 G</margin> gained in another theater <note>likely referring to the afterlife or a higher plane of existence.</note>. Let him know, there|<margin>7 P</margin>fore, examining not with eyes but with ears, and discerning as if by divination—and the common crowd of the learned is no less ignorant of the use of this than of that—that <margin>10</margin> the demonstrator does not excel the topical logic simply by reason of a firmer argument (which may indicate and designate something remote and difficult). Rather, from another side, the topical art—with its ready-to-hand frugality, greater use, and more abundant possession—is able to equal the demonstrative <note>original: "apodictica"; absolute, necessary proof.</note> judgment. In this regard, perhaps the divine, <margin>15</margin> but certainly mute, judgment of Socrates did not turn the Athenian people away from the poisonous drink; yet the most skillful dialectic of the foreign and "barbarian" Gorgias <note>Gorgias of Leontini was a famous Greek sophist and rhetorician known for his persuasive power.</note> (hated by the local philosophers, who were not so much good critics as they were unlucky) was able to persuade them to erect a golden statue to him.

### I. PART.

In the middle of the Field is a tower, to which all returns collected from every part seem to belong. The tower itself denotes the **subject**, around which and about which every consideration revolves, and toward the <margin>25</margin> formation of which every **syllogistic apparatus** <note>original: "syllogisticus apparatus"; the collection of logical tools and formulas used to construct a formal argument or "syllogism."</note> looks; it aims for something to be [concluded] about this subject, or from this subject itself, in the conclusion...

<meta>This page continues the logical investigation into the nature of subjects and predicates. While the previous page contrasted the "topical" art (dialectic) with absolute "demonstration," this page categorizes the types of subjects one can study, identifying "Species" as the true focus of scientific inquiry and introducing a spatial mnemonic involving a "Field" and a "Tower."</meta>

<page-num>22</page-num>
<header>THE WORKS OF GIORDANO BRUNO</header>

...what results from it being affirmed or denied. By this term, for our present purpose, we wish to signify the manifold difference of subjects <note>original: "subiectorum"; in logic, the "subject" is the part of a proposition about which something is stated.</note>; for some beings are the most "subject" of all, others the least of all, while many are held to be more of a subject in one respect and less in another. 

The **first** are the **particulars** <note>individual, specific things or people.</note>, which stand under and are subjected to all else, and which are said to receive only **accidental** predication <note>original: "accidentalem... praedicationem"; describing qualities that are not essential to a thing's nature, such as its color or its current location.</note>; | <margin>**8 P**</margin> the **second** are those which are placed under no predicate, and about which it is permissible to affirm something according to the word, but not in a univocal sense <note>original: "univoce"; meaning the term doesn't have the exact same definition when applied to these highest categories. These are the most general concepts like "Being" itself.</note>; the **third**, however, holding a **middle station**, are those things about which other things are predicated, and which are themselves predicated of others. 

Of these, the first <note>the particulars</note> never enter the domain of "knowable" reason, but are instead confined within the limits of the sensible <note>things perceived by the senses</note>, of fable, of opinion, and of history. The second <note>the most general categories</note>, falling away into the other extreme of this region—such as those things which are first, highest, supreme, and most general—although they encounter a certain portion of "non-knowledge" <note>because they are so broad they cannot be defined by higher terms</note>, | <margin>**719 G**</margin> nevertheless no **essential** predication can be made concerning them. For this reason, they cannot be the subject of science or of a demonstrative conclusion, even though it is established that many things can be said of them under a certain logical or mathematical reasoning once they have become subjects of "intentions" <note>mental concepts or logical abstractions</note>. 

There remain, therefore, those enumerated in the **third place**, which are most frequently referred to in questioning and contemplative speculation. Wherefore, whatever is accepted as a subject of argumentation, of demonstrative conclusion, and of science, that very thing is a **species** <note>a specific class or type of thing that sharing essential characteristics.</note>, and it cannot be anything other than a species. It is this species about which we inquire whether something may be affirmed or denied, and in which we ask whether something is present or absent, searching through the surrounding **genera** <note>the broader families or categories to which a species belongs</note> and those things which exist around the genera. Let the universal members of these be designated through those partitions which are in the **Field around the Tower** <note>Bruno is referring to a mnemonic or symbolic diagram used in his art of memory and logic.</note>.

The left field contains "Genus" and "Difference." The right field is labeled "Property." The bottom field contains "Accident" and "Description."</image-desc>

<margin>10 P 720 G</margin>
# ON THE FOUR FIELDS IN THE PLAIN
# SURROUNDING THE TOWER.

---

### SECTION I.

<margin>5</margin> The fields, therefore, which lie around the tower in the Plain <note>original: "Campo"; Bruno often uses the "Field" or "Plain" as a mnemonic space where concepts are physically located to help the student remember them.</note>, designate the four primary things that can be stated about a species <note>original: "praedicabilia"; in logic, these are the 'predicables,' or categories of relationship between a subject and what is said about it.</note>. These are the field of **ACCIDENT**, the field of **GENUS**, the field of **PROPERTY**, and the field of **DEFINITION**. These would be handed down as six distinct fields in number, were it not for the fact that the field of Genus includes the field of Difference, and the field <margin>10</margin> of Property includes the field of Description. <note>Bruno is condensing the traditional "Five Predicables" of Porphyry (Genus, Difference, Species, Property, Accident) plus "Description" into four spatial areas. He argues that "Definition" is composed of "Genus" and "Difference," so they can be grouped together.</note>

Bruno explains that while there are six traditional categories of description, they can be grouped into these four spatial areas for easier study.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the logical exposition from page 23, where Bruno introduced the "Fields" surrounding the "Tower of Species." Having established the visual mnemonic, he now provides the theoretical justification for why there are exactly four (or six) ways to describe a subject.</meta>

<page-num>24</page-num>
<header>GIORDANO BRUNO</header>

## SECTION II.

In absolutely every inquiry, problem, or statement, it is necessary for two things to be found: one which is said about something <note>The predicate: what we are asserting about the subject.</note>, and the other about which something is said <note>The subject: the thing we are talking about.</note>. The latter is the **species**, while the former cannot be anything other than the four things already listed, or the six that can be enumerated.

## SECTION III.

Let the first reason for a sufficient distribution of the "fields" <note>Bruno refers to the mnemonic "Fields" (Definition, Genus, Property, Accident) used to categorize logical statements.</note> be this: that all things which can come into consideration or be brought into controversy are ultimately reduced to that specific number. For every question concerning a subject either asks what can be said **essentially** about it—and this will be, first, the **definition** <margin>11 P</margin> or a part of the definition (such as the **constitutive difference** of the subject species, or its **genus**); or, second, it will be a **description** or part of a description (such as a unique **property** or a common **accident**).

## SECTION IV.

The second reason is that every predication <note>original: "praedicatio"; the act of asserting that a quality belongs to a subject.</note> in some way declares the thing affirmed to be one with the subject, or makes it the very thing it affirms; likewise, it testifies that what is denied is in some way different or alien from that which it is denied of. Now, if all the modes of "the one" and (by the opposite reasoning) "the different" are brought together, then very easily every predicative...

<vocab>Giordano Bruno, logic, definition, genus, species, predication, critical apparatus</vocab>

<summary>Bruno explains that every statement consists of a subject (the species) and a predicate, and he argues that all predicates fall into specific categories (the "Fields") such as definition, genus, property, or accident. He justifies this structure by claiming these categories cover everything that can be essentially or descriptively said about a thing.</summary>

<page-num>25</page-num>
<header>ON THE HUNTER’S LAMP.</header>

...it will appear that any addition concerning the subject <term>species<note>The specific thing being discussed, such as "Human" or "Socrates."</note></term> is contained within the boundaries of these four fields. <margin>721 G</margin> | Therefore, "the one" is understood according to a threefold <term>genus<note>A general category.</note></term> (each of which is subsequently subdivided into several other species). I say that a thing is "one" either by **number**, or by **predication**, or by **analogy**.

First, that which is one by **number** is sevenfold:
1. By name alone, such as this "dog" which is an animal, and that "dog" which is a star <note>original: "canis... astrum"; refers to the constellation Canis Major and its star Sirius.</note>.
<margin>5</margin> 2. By definition alone, without the name, such as "this garment" and "this clothing."
3. By both name and definition, as when "Socrates" is the same person you might conversely call "the rational mortal animal, son of Sophroniscus" <note>Sophroniscus was the historical father of the philosopher Socrates.</note>.
<margin>10</margin> 4. Where two properties signify one and the same thing, such as "that which is capable of laughter" <note>original: "risibile"</note> and "that which is capable of philosophizing."
5. Where the meaning of a name concurs with the meaning of an <term>accident<note>A non-essential quality, like sitting down or being in a certain place.</note></term>, <margin>12 P</margin> | which is why Socrates is called "that one sitting," and that one sitting is called "Socrates."
<margin>15</margin> 6. Where the name and a unique descriptor <note>original: "proprium"</note> refer to the same thing, such as "capable of laughter" and "human," or "Socrates" and "that snub-nosed teacher of Plato."
7. Where a definition and a unique property are interchangeable, such as "capable of laughter" and "rational animal."

Second, that which is one by **predication** <note>The act of asserting a quality about a subject.</note> is fourfold:
1. By **genus**, such as "human" and "horse" are both "animal," or are the same under the concept of "animal."
<margin>20</margin> 2. By **species**, such as Socrates and Plato are the same in their "humanity" (for they are both "human," and are one under and within the essence of humanity).
3. By **subjection**, such as marble and milk are one under the quality of "whiteness."
4. By **inhesion** <note>The way qualities exist within a subject.</note>, such as "sweet" and "saffron-colored" are the same in "honey."

<margin>25</margin> Third, that which is one by **analogy** is fourfold:
1. Under the same name and the same concept, but participated in unequally, as when "healthy" is said of an animal, of a limb, of a medical sign, and of nourishment.
2. Under one and the same proportion of power, such as the relationship of a general to his army is the same as that of a king to his kingdom.
<margin>30</margin> 3. Under something that behaves in the same way...

Since "oneness" is spoken of in so many ways, | to each of which a different term responds with an opposite meaning, <margin>13 P</margin> | it will not be difficult to guess how they encompass all expressible things. It is established that all these things are reducible to the four aforementioned species <note>These are Definition, Genus, Property, and Accident.</note>. If "one in number" is reduced to the definition and the parts of a definition, then "one in genus," "one by proportion," and "one by accident" can similarly recognize their own classes without difficulty.

### IV. PART.

Thirdly, it can be made manifest that these categories do not exceed the **number four**. When we investigate any proposition or problem—which receive their validity through <term>syllogism<note>A logical argument where a conclusion is reached from two related premises.</note></term> and division—we certainly proceed by no other reasoning than by predicating something of a given subject.

Now, everything that is <term>predicated<note>Something said or asserted about a subject.</note></term> is either said **convertibly** with the subject or **by excess**. If it happens in the first way <note>That is, the subject and predicate are interchangeable.</note>, it will be either the **definition** or a **property** that is predicated. But if it happens in the second way <note>That is, the predicate is broader than the specific subject.</note>, then it will either be something taken from those parts which constitute the subject’s definition, and it will be the **genus** itself; or it will be something foreign to the subject’s definition, while nonetheless being more common than it, and that will be a **circumscriptive accident**.

<header>ON THE HUNTING LAMP</header>

### V. PART

<margin>14 P</margin> Fourthly, the enumeration of these categories is judged to be sufficient because the universe, and everything that exists or is named, is explained within the orders of the ten <term>predicaments<note>Also known as the Categories of Aristotle, these are the ten fundamental ways of describing any object: substance, quantity, quality, relation, place, time, position, state, action, and passion.</note></term>. Everything can be reduced to these same ten, <margin>5</margin> or is signified according to them, or is understood as being attached to them. Indeed, all propositions derived from these <term>categories<note>original: "cathegorijs"</note></term> express either "what" (substance), "what kind" (quality), "how much" (quantity), "toward what" (relation), or something else from the remaining famous classes. The parts, orders, and rationales of the attributes of each and every one of these <margin>10</margin> are indicated, identified, examined, and judged through genera, definitions, properties, and accidents.

## THE HUNTER <margin>723 G</margin>

### I. PART

Across this same vast field of hunting, a hunter may range with equal profit, not in one way, but certainly in many ways. <margin>15</margin> For whether a theologian is piously active through the law, or more argumentatively contemplative through faith, they have a subject to test through inquiry in order to find what they seek. Whether a philosopher wishes to bring forth the <term>metaphysical<note>Dealing with the first principles of things, including abstract concepts such as being, knowing, and time.</note></term> in its sublimity, the <margin>20</margin> <term>physical<note>The study of nature and the material world.</note></term> in its weightiness, or the <term>ethical<note>The study of moral principles.</note></term> in its morality, they search through inquiry so that, by judgment, they may contemplate, observe, and prescribe laws by their declarations. Whether as a clamorous orator speaking and proposing matters placed under consultation, or as a <term>judge<note>original: "praetor"</note></term> for the sake of more maturely examining and judging, they do so only <margin>15 P</margin>

# THE HUNTING MATTER.
---
## I. MEMBER.

<margin>10</margin> Across the same field of the hunt, not just one, but several types of hunting matter run about. Of these, however, there are two primary heads: namely, the <term>dialectical proposition<note>original: "propositio dialectica." A statement put forward for debate that is based on probability rather than absolute certainty.</note></term> and the <term>dialectical problem<note>original: "dialecticum problema." A question or topic of inquiry that has two contradictory sides, serving as the starting point for a debate.</note></term>. They define a dialectical proposition as a probable inquiry which is confirmed by the judgment of either all people, or most, <margin>15</margin> or the wise—and among the wise, either by all, or most, or the most eminent. By a dialectical problem, <margin>17 P</margin> however, they understand a contemplation concerning that which has been placed into controversy.

## II. MEMBER.

<margin>20</margin> A dialectical proposition is either, first, probable in itself—such as the one which says that there is the same knowledge of contraries—or second, similar to a probable statement, such as that there is the same sense-perception of contraries, or third, a statement that contradicts a given probable one; for example, if it was probable that one ought to do good to friends, it is [also] probable <note>The sentence breaks off here, continuing the thought that it might also be probable that one should do harm to enemies or do good to all; the logic follows Aristotle's *Topics*.</note>

# THE WATCHTOWER.

-> — <-

### I. Member.

For those wishing to be informed about the truth of things, it is first 
<margin>21 P</margin>
worthwhile to purify the very thing under consideration by, as it were, separating it from all others, so that its nature—what it is and of what kind—may be contemplated more clearly and evidently. 
<margin>5</margin>
For gold is recognized and judged poorly and with difficulty when it exists in a state of physical impurity and chemical mixture. Secondly, once the <term>reason or essence<note>original: "ratio sive essentia." This refers to the core definition that makes a thing what it is.</note></term> of the thing has been perceived without any confusion of <term>ambiguity<note>original: "homonymiae." A logical term for when one word is used to mean different things, leading to confusion.</note></term>, it should be considered according to its <term>absolute being<note>original: "esse absolutum." The existence of a thing viewed in isolation, regardless of its relationship to anything else.</note></term>, insofar as it participates in unity. 
<margin>10</margin>
Thirdly and finally, it should be considered according to its <term>relative being<note>original: "esse respectivum." The existence of a thing as it relates to, compares with, or differs from other things.</note></term>, in which it is seen to consist in a certain duality, so that it may be apprehended without error. 
The next point is that the <term>Pythagoreans<note>Followers of the ancient Greek philosopher Pythagoras, who believed that numbers and mathematical ratios were the fundamental principles of the universe.</note></term> spoke of two principles of things: "Unity" and the "Indeterminate Binary." By the former, they meant the absolute being that all things possess, and by the latter, they intended to signify relative being. 
<margin>15</margin>
Most skillfully, therefore, Aristotle distinguished the work of the <term>hunter<note>Bruno’s metaphor for the philosopher or seeker of knowledge who "hunts" for truth using the "lamp" of method.</note></term> into the discussion of equivocation, the intuition of similarity, and the consideration of difference. 
Through the first, a purification (as it were) is achieved; 
<margin>20</margin>
through the second, we are led as if by the hand to know more of what the thing is in itself; and through the third, we conceive rather of the <term>relationship<note>original: "habitudinem."</note></term> it bears toward other things. For in these steps, first, distinction contributes to truth; second, similarity contributes to unity; and third, difference contributes to duality and plurality.

### II. MEMBER.

Now, as we turn our commentary to <term>absolute being<note>original: "esse absolutum." This refers to the existence of a thing considered in itself, rather than in its relation to other things.</note></term>, we wish to indicate only this: that whatever is conceived is introduced either through an evident "incursion" <note>An "incursion" (incursio) refers to a direct impression on the senses or the mind.</note>, such as 
<margin>5</margin> bitter, sweet, light, and darkness; or through a "transit" from things already evident, which is certainly achieved according to four modes. First, from the presenter to that which is presented, as from an image to the thing portrayed, or from its own extrinsic accidents to the subject itself. Second, from the composite to the part, and universally from that 
<margin>10</margin> in which or with which something exists to the thing itself which is in and with the other—as from a body and its surface we conceive of "length." Third, from the components to the composite, as from the knowledge of the people, the senate, the knights, and the rest, we arrive at the concept of the **Republic**. Fourth, we conceive through augmentation from the smaller to the 
<margin>15</margin> larger, or through decrement from the larger to the smaller; for with little effort we descend from the same starting point to the concept of a giant, who is a large man, and a <term>pygmy<note>original: "pygmaei." Bruno uses the classical reference to a diminutive race to illustrate the concept of relative scale.</note></term>, who is a very small man. In these ways, although a thing may be known through something else, it is not said to be known as it relates to another, but as it is in itself.

As for what pertains to <term>relative being<note>original: "esse respectivum." Existence defined by how a thing stands in relation to, or differs from, other things.</note></term>, we say that a manifold investigation takes place in those things whose being consists in a respect toward something else. This, naturally, occurs either 1. according to similarity; 2. comparison; 3. con-
<margin>25</margin> tradiction; 4. contrariety; or 5. privation and...

### IV. MEMBER.

Behold in how many various ways all things together and individually are distinguished from other things that surround them; to all of these, surely, it is fitting for one who wishes to find many things through differences—the **Searcher**—to look. And truly, among the types enumerated, I can see none that you could reduce to another without loss; for each of them, essentially distinct from all the others, multiplies [the possibilities of knowledge]; therefore.

### MEMBER V.

<margin>5</margin> Therefore, the power to select differences contributes greatly to the richness of <term>invention<note>original: "inventionis." In Renaissance logic, 'invention' refers to the systematic method of discovering new arguments or knowledge.</note></term>. Aristotle testifies that this faculty is most effectively gained through the exercise of distinguishing between things that are very similar; he asserts this can be done in three <margin>10</margin> ways. First, when differences are selected from things contained under one <term>proximate genus<note>original: "propinquo genere." A genus is a general class; a 'proximate' one is the most immediate category above a specific thing.</note></term>; second, when they are captured from those in a more remote genus; third, when they are contained in the most remote—namely the <term>highest categories<note>original: "supremis [generibus]." These are the Ten Categories of Aristotle, the most general classes of being, such as Substance or Quality.</note></term>—provided those things happen to be similar. 

<margin>14</margin> In the first way, this occurs by looking at **fortitude** and **justice**; since their proximate genus is **virtue**, fortitude concerns things to be feared, while justice concerns social interactions. In the second way, where **prudence** (according to the intellectual power) and **temperance** (according to the <margin>26 P</margin> <margin>19</margin> appetitive faculty) look toward a more distant universal commonality. <margin>20</margin> <margin>731 G</margin> In the third way, | where we look on one hand at **sense** in the <term>category of relation<note>original: "praedicamento relationis." Sense is categorized as a relation because it requires both a perceiver and an object.</note></term>, and on the other hand at **science** in the <term>category of quality<note>original: "praedicamento qualitatis." Knowledge or "science" was considered a "habit" or quality of the mind.</note></term>. 

Yet a great similarity is perceived between these, says Aristotle. But perhaps he understands "proportion" in place of "similarity"; for there is indeed a <term>proportion<note>original: "proportio." Here Bruno refers to an analogy: A is to B as C is to D.</note></term>, because just as <margin>25</margin> **sense** relates to the **sensible**, so **science** relates to the **knowable** (or the intellect to the intelligible); yet sense is never truly similar to science, nor to the intellect.

## MEMBER VI.

Furthermore, so that no labor or time is wrongly spent, one must carefully observe that differences are not to be sought for all things, nor in all things. For while it is permissible <margin>5</margin> to inquire into the differences of other things (so that we may distinguish one from another), seeking the "differences of differences" would be no less absurd than seeking the "substance of substances," the "quality of quality," or the "magnitude of magnitude." Nevertheless, nothing prevents one from distinguishing, dividing, and discerning <margin>10</margin> within these categories themselves. It should also be noted that we do not speak of a quality as a "difference of quality," just as we do not speak of a "substance of substance" or a "motion of motion." For the differences of **color** are nothing but qualities; yet they are called **substantial** <term>differences<note>original: "differentiae." In logic, a specific difference is the characteristic that distinguishes a species from others in the same genus (e.g., "rationality" is the difference that distinguishes humans within the genus of animals).</note></term> because it is according to <margin>15</margin> them that substance is divided—not into the differences themselves, but into <term>species<note>A sub-category of a genus.</note></term>, and it is these species that indicate the types of substance.

Numbers also (as Plotinus <note>Plotinus (c. 204–270 AD) was the founder of Neoplatonism. He argued that numbers have their own essential reality and are not merely the result of addition.</note> says) are not "differences of numbers." For <margin>27 P</margin> five does not differ from three "by two"; rather, by a group of three, two are surpassed by five. <note>original: "non enim quinque a tribus per duo differunt, sed trinario duo a quinque superantur." Bruno is making a metaphysical point: a number's identity is an essential unit, not just a mathematical remainder.</note> There are <margin>20</margin> also some things that clearly differ by their own nature, such as **virtue** and **vice**; some that clearly differ through something else, such as a **stone** and a **plant** differing by way of **life**; and certain things are so related that they are mutually species and differences to one another. For thus, **heavy** and **light** are species of "impetus" <note>original: "appulsus." In the physics of the time, this refers to the natural tendency of an object to move toward a specific place.</note>, which are constituted by "the movable toward the center" and <margin>25</margin> "the movable away from the center." Conversely, "the movable away from the center" and "the movable toward the center" are species of the "transferable," which are constituted by the differences of **gravity** and **levity**.

<summary>Bruno warns against the logical fallacy of infinite regress, explaining that while categories like substance and quality help us define things, they themselves cannot be subdivided infinitely. He uses examples from Neoplatonic mathematics and Aristotelian physics to show how differences define species.</summary>

# THE SPEAR.

---

## MEMBER I.

Since many <term>ambiguities<note>original: "aequivocationes." In logic, an equivocation occurs when a single word is used with two or more different meanings, leading to confusion.</note></term> lie hidden under the dense and thick briars of a forested universality (which are the dens of fleeting wild beasts), it is advised that we apply that scrutiny which certainly consists in a certain distinguishing reason. This reason is informed sometimes by the essence of the thing under a complete definition, or under its <term>genus<note>A broad category or "family" of things.</note></term>, or under its specific <term>difference<note>The specific characteristic that distinguishes a species from others in the same genus.</note></term>; at other times, however, it is informed by those very things which surround it—whether they are things that receive it, or are similar, or are compared to it.
<margin>10</margin>
By many means, therefore, through the "shaking out" and distinction of the members of an ambiguity, we manage to uncover the hidden dens of the beasts and bring them out into the open sun.
<margin>28 P</margin>
For there are very many methods by which, testing with the **spear of discernment**, we examine whether that which is said to be common to many things is spread by the voice alone <note>original: "sola voce." Referring to words that sound the same (homonyms) but have no shared meaning.</note> or also by the same shared meaning.

First, by considering the **opposites** of those things for which a name is used: if we see that those opposites do not share one common name, then the term we started with will be judged ambiguous.

Second, by considering the **disposition** of those things for which the name is used, to see whether that disposition is diverse under the same name.

Third, if there is an opposite not for both, but only for one of those things for which the name is used.

Fourth, if an <term>immediate<note>A direct opposition without a "middle ground," like "odd" and "even."</term> contrariety is found in what the opposite name signifies, whereas in the proposed thing the contrariety is <term>mediated<note>An opposition that allows for middle states, like "black" and "white," which have "gray" in between.</note></term>, or vice versa.

<margin>25</margin>
Fifth, if between one thing and its opposite there is only one middle term, but between the other thing and its own opposite, several are found.

<meta>This page continues Bruno's systematic list of logical tests to detect equivocation. Having covered the first fifteen methods previously, he now details methods sixteen through twenty-one. He focuses on how words like "beautiful," "sharp," "eclipse," and "healthy" can have shifting meanings depending on their logical category or the specific object they describe.</meta>

# ON THE HUNTING LAMP

...is opposed to the form; there is that which lacks form, that which has a bad form, and that which is the form itself. Seventeenth, from the distinction of things according to the form of predication <note>The logical act of asserting a property about a subject.</note> under the same universal: "beautiful" <note>original: "pulchrum"</note> is spoken of as a "whatness" <term>in quid: describing the essential nature or "what-it-is" of a thing</term> if it is taken as a species of quality, but it is spoken of as a "what-kind" <term>in quale: describing a characteristic or "how-it-is"</term> if it is taken as a specific difference. Similarly, "rational" is spoken of as a "what-kind" when used as an adjective, but as a "whatness" when used as a noun. Eighteenth, from the fact that different things can be asserted under different genera <note>The broad categories or "families" of classification.</note>; for example, "white" <note>original: "candidum"</note> is here a species of color, there a distinction of voice, and elsewhere a property of snow or milk. Nineteenth, from the expression of one or both things (which are called by the same name) according to "more" or "less," yet not in comparison to one another. For although both a voice and a knife are called "sharp" <note>original: "acutum"</note>, one would not say the voice is "sharper" than the knife, nor the knife "sharper" than the voice. Twentieth, from considering the nature of their definitions; as when "eclipse" is said of the moon and of the sun. When inspected, we see that an eclipse of the moon is a falling into the shadow-cone of the earth, while an eclipse of the sun is the interposition of the moon between us and the sun. Therefore, "failure" or "eclipse" is common in name, but not in its underlying definition. Twenty-first, from their analogical participation according to "prior" and "posterior" <note>A logical order where one meaning is primary and others are derived from it.</note>, where <margin>736 G</margin> "healthy" <note>original: "sanum"</note> is said to belong to the same definition | according to a certain order of participation: first of the | <margin>32' P</margin> animal, second of the limb, third of medicine, fourth of food, fifth of a sign, and sixth of a good doctor. "Healthy" is also used equivocally regarding a doctrine and all of these. Hence, the same name can be both equivocal <note>Having different, unrelated meanings.</note> and analogical <note>Having different but related meanings.</note> according to different respects. No less can the same word sometimes be univocal <note>Having one single, consistent meaning.</note> and equivocal; for "man" is a univocal term when predicated of specific individuals, but it is an equivocal name when it signifies at one time a living man, at another a dead man, and at another a man made of stone <note>i.e., a statue.</note>.

<meta>This page continues Bruno's technical manual on logic and the "Hunting Lamp." The previous page concluded the list of twenty-one methods for detecting ambiguity (equivocation) in language. This page moves into broader reflections on how to apply these distinctions and the different roles played by the Sophist, the Dialectician, and the Scientific Demonstrator in the search for truth.</meta>

# GIORDANO BRUNO

## SECTION II.

However, those brandishing this distinguishing tool <note>original: "hastam discretivam"—literally a "distinguishing spear," a metaphor for the sharp logical tools used to pierce through linguistic confusion</note> must be careful everywhere: we must not rashly judge something to be equivocal <note>having multiple meanings</note> when it is in truth univocal <note>having a single, consistent meaning</note>. This happens when we assign a common definition to things that actually share a specific nature, or when we measure the meaning of a name beyond its proper limits based on some other common reasoning, thereby assuming an equivocation exists where we should believe it to be far removed.

## SECTION III.

<margin>33 P</margin>
Truly, the present series of investigations can bring no small benefit for constructing and destroying arguments, for proving and disproving, and for discerning between true and apparent categories and species. The sophist <note>in this context, a "wise-cracker" or someone who uses clever but fallacious arguments to deceive</note> labors to tempt, pressure, and confound; he strives to argue for ambiguity where a true category exists, and in turn tries to sell ambiguous terms as if they were solid categories. The dialectician <note>a logical practitioner who uses dialogue and debate to test opinions</note>, however, acts to distinguish, examine, and prove. Indeed, the dialectician is comparable to one who can use the same drug <term>pharmaco: a Greek-derived term for a substance that can be either a medicine or a poison</term> to heal or to poison; the demonstrator <note>one who provides certain, scientific proof based on first principles</note> is like a doctor who only heals; but the sophist is like one who knows nothing except how to be a poisoner.

## SECTION IV.

The usefulness of recognizing similarity and difference extends to many things. <margin>737 G</margin> First, it is useful for performing induction <note>the process of drawing a general conclusion from specific instances</note>, which is prompted by the understanding of these similarities...

...is followed, it receives firmness and is enriched. <margin>10</margin> how shall we distinguish:

<margin>15</margin> 4. How shall we know whether things that appear the same or different are, in the truth of the matter, different or the same?

<margin>20</margin> name, one person defends one thing and the other attacks another?
6. How will it be possible to see the virtues and passions <note>original: "passiones"—in this logical context, these are the properties or characteristics that belong to a subject</note>, which consist in the foundation of that diversity or similarity?
7. How shall we guard against the tricks by which sophists <note>original: "sophistae"—those who use clever but fallacious arguments to deceive</note> are more effective at deceiving?

An entrance and exit lies open to each of the four fields. At this point, the first place requires us to ask whether any of the following apply to none of the species: what is called an **accident** <term>accident: a non-essential quality, such as being "clothed" or "sitting"</term>, **genus** <term>genus: a general category, like "animal"</term>, **property** <term>property: a quality unique to a species, such as "the ability to laugh" in humans</term>, **definition**, **difference** <term>difference: the specific trait that distinguishes one species from another within a genus</term>, or **description**.

The second place asks whether it applies to none, to all, or to some of those things which 
<margin>5</margin> consist within the same species or genus. Regarding the truth of the matter, we must observe that not everything found in a genus is also found in a species; however, those things denied to a whole genus are likewise understood to be excluded from every species. 
<margin>10</margin> Furthermore, those things cannot fit a genus if they are proven to belong to none of its species. Beyond these points—which, according to logical intent, are specific to genus and species insofar as they *are* genera and species—it is necessary that in a physical sense <note>original: "physice"—referring to the actual nature of things rather than just logical categories</note>, if a genus is predicated <note>predicated: stated or asserted about a subject</note> of something, some species must also be predicated of it. Whatever is affirmed of a specific species or group of species, 
<margin>15</margin> we may safely confirm of the genus in a particular way | **739 G** <note>This refers to page 739 of the Glandorp edition</note>. Just as whatever is denied of a specific species or group of species is understood to be denied of the genus in a particular way; for whatever exists or is affected, is or is affected according to some species. 
<margin>20</margin> Because whatever moves is moved according to a specific species of motion, just as we would not lie if we affirmed that something which exists or is affected by a certain species (or species) exists or is affected absolutely. | **36 P** <note>This refers to page 36 of the Prague edition</note>

The third place asks whether the statement is repugnant <note>repugnant: logically inconsistent or contradictory</note> to the definition of the subject—namely, whether it is foreign to the species that serves as the subject of the problem.

The fourth asks whether the connection with such a subject or species is 
<margin>25</margin> repugnant to the definition of the accident, or genus, or property, or difference, or to the definition or description itself.

The fifth asks whether a contrary or generally opposite term can be shown to either belong to this subject or be attributed to these subjects.

### SECTION III. <note>original: *III. MEMBRVM*</note>

And now, having passed over the part of the hall adjacent to the margin of the accident <term>accidens: in logic, a non-essential quality (like color) that can change without the object becoming something else</term>, we encounter the places belonging to the three remaining parts; for the Enclosure B, consisting of three sides, suggests this.

The first of these requires consideration as to whether, with respect to those things which differ in species or genus, that which is called a genus, or property <term>proprium: a characteristic that belongs to all members of a species and only that species, but is not part of its definition (like "the ability to laugh" for humans)</term>, or definition is likewise held.

The second, whether for one of those things which refer to the same genus, property, and definition, it is not a genus, property, or definition; for I would wrongly call "black" the genus or property of an Ethiopian, or a part of his definition, since it cannot be said of the Scythians <note>Bruno uses the ancient Greeks' classic examples of human diversity: Ethiopians (from the south) and Scythians (from the north) are both humans, but their accidental traits like skin color differ.</note>, who are of the same species.

The third, whether one has mistaken the difference <term>differentia: the specific trait that distinguishes one species from another within the same genus</term> for a genus, or a genus for a difference, or a property for a genus, or the genus itself for a property, or the definition in place of a property, or the property in place of a definition; for it is foolish to have accepted a common accident in place of the others, such as for a genus, difference, etc.

The fourth, whether it can be shown to be not the genus, not the property, and not the definition, but something similar to what is proposed. Thus, people are accustomed to using contiguity <term>contiguitas: the state of being in contact or touching</term> for the determination of continuity <term>continuitas: an unbroken and consistent connection where the parts share a common boundary</term>, and continuity for contiguity, | <margin>41 P</margin> since these refer to a certain mode of mutual relationship; for contiguity is indeed a certain kind of, or in some way, continuity, and the latter is similarly the former. But truly in certain cases these do not reciprocate...

<margin>743 G</margin> whether the genus, property, or definition is stated metaphorically; although it is sometimes permissible to use these, it should not be done like Plato, who defined man as an "inverted plant." For what is proper to poets must not be usurped by philosophers, whose duty it is to reveal hidden things. It was permissible, therefore, for Homer to define death as "the end for which we were born," <note>original footnote: Homer refers to the line "it has the end for which it was born," a phrase often attributed to him but likely cited from Aristotle's *Physics*</note> but not for another who strives to define it according to the nature of the thing itself. **Seventh**, whether in all things it holds the same way in action, act, and effect as it does in virtue <term>virtus: an inherent power or quality</term>, potential, and faculty; and undoubtedly likewise in acting and being acted upon, in being corrupted and being dissolved. For just as one is potentially able to see, and thus is "seeing" when he actually sees, so to build is to act, and the building process is the action. **Eighth**, whether the genus, property, and definition are taken from the nature of the subject or by chance, or whether the subject is understood to be affected by chance in those things that are naturally determining. **Ninth**, whether the predicates, or the subject, or both are corruptible <note>corruptible: subject to decay, change, or ceasing to exist</note>. 

<margin>42 P</margin> **Tenth**, whether these are not simple, nor to be taken simply, but according to their mode of composition. **Eleventh**, whether a genus, property, or definition is taken from one category for a subject that belongs to a different category, as was done by the one who said the soul was a "certain number." <note>Bruno refers to the Pythagorean or Platonic definition of the soul as a self-moving number</note>. **Twelfth**, whether, if one of these predicates is destroyed, it is not inconsistent for the species to remain. **Thirteenth**...

### ON THE HUNTING LAMP.

<margin>5</margin> ...whether a proposed species admits anything contrary to its own genus and definition. **Fourteenth**, whether the subordinate species communicates anything that is entirely impossible for those things that serve under this specific genus and definition; for instance, how can we say the soul <note>original: *anima*</note> is a species of number, or admit the definitions and properties of number to it, if the soul communicates life, which no number is able to communicate? **Fifteenth**, whether it holds the same way in negation; for if the delightful is that which is good, then that which is not good is not delightful. 
<margin>10</margin> But be careful in certain specific properties, because if "one who philosophizes" <note>original: *philosophativum*</note> 
<margin>744 G</margin> is a human, it does not therefore follow that "one who does not philosophize" is not a human—while it remains true that "that which is not a human" is not a philosopher. **Sixteenth**, whether a contrary applies to a contrary, or contraries to a contrary; for it happened to Thrasymachus <note>A character in Plato’s *Republic* who argues that "might makes right."</note> in the works of Plato to assert that injustice is "good counsel" and justice is "bad counsel." **Seventeenth**, whether, since the species is a relative term <term>relative: a term whose meaning depends on a relationship to something else, like "double" or "parent"</term>, that which is signified through the genus and definition is not relative, or vice-versa. 
<margin>43 P</margin> But take care lest you be deceived in place of the truth; for virtue, which is a species of goodness, is referred to something <note>original: *ad aliquid*, a technical term for relative categories</note>, while "the good" and "the honorable," which are genera <term>genera: the plural of genus, the broader category</term>, are not referred to anything else at all. No less, although knowledge (which is a genus) is referred to something else, grammar and rhetoric (which are its species) are not relatives; but it is pleasing, in imitation of Aristotle, to have numbered this place (on behalf of the Sophists) <note>Refers to Aristotle's *Sophistical Refutations*</note> along with the others.
<margin>25</margin> **Eighteenth**, whether the species does not refer to the same thing according to itself and according to its assigned genus, property, or definition. For so Aristotle says: where "the double" (which is a species of "the multiple") is called the double of a half, then "the multiple" must be called the multiple of a half.

...is said: of which we say the cause is, because the species <note>original: *species*</note> is referred to not according to the reason <note>original: *rationem* — the underlying logic or defining principle</note> of its genus <note>original: *genus* — the broader category</note> and its property and definition, which follows that genus, but according to its own proper reason. The same holds true in reverse, where knowledge <note>original: *scientia*</note> is referred to the thing known <note>original: *scibile*</note>, not indeed according to the reason by which the species is a habit <note>original: *habitus* — a stable disposition or state of being</note> or the genus of grammar, but according to the proper reason by which it is the knowledge of something. **Nineteenth**, whether a term named through analogy and a derivative term behave in the same way as a term naming through primary analogy: for just as the property and definition of a "multiple" is shared with the "double," so is the "submultiple" shared with the "half." **Twentieth**, whether the genus or property or definition is found in the same subject as the species: for there is none of these that is verified except with, in, or concerning the species. Here also one must generally beware, along with accidents <term>accidents: qualities that a thing can lose without ceasing to be what it is, like being "tan" or "sitting down"</term>, lest what is present "in a certain respect" be said to be present or to exist "simply" <note>original: *simpliciter* — meaning absolutely or without qualification</note>, or vice versa. **Twenty-second**, whether he has declared that which is a genus, definition, or property according to potentiality <note>original: *potentiam*</note> belongs to a species which is according to act <note>original: *actum*</note>; for I would hardly call one who is *able* to teach false doctrines a sophist, or one who is *able* to snatch things stealthily a thief, but rather the one who actually teaches false doctrines and the one who actually steals.
