->### ON THE HUNTING LAMP<-

...similarly, on the other hand, those things will not be correctly understood according to the activity <note>original: *actum* — the actual doing of something</note> if that activity is taken from the perspective of potentiality <note>original: *potentiam* — the capacity to do something as opposed to the performance of it</note>. 

**Twenty-third**, whether a definition that describes a state of being <note>original: *habitus* — a stable disposition or quality, like "knowledge" or "virtue"</note> or signifies such a state is mistakenly used as the general category <note>original: *genus*</note> of the activity itself. This was the error of the one who said that the <margin>5</margin> "dietary regimen of the recovering" is medicine; in truth, a regimen is not a specific type <note>original: *species*</note> of medicine, but is medicine itself. 

**Twenty-fourth**, whether an activity or a feeling <note>original: *affectum*</note> is positioned as the general category of the state of being itself, or if the definition of that state is drawn from an activity or an effect. (An example is the person who said a fever is a "harm to activity," when in fact <margin>10</margin> a fever is actually a certain *effect* of an activity). Similarly, consider whether the potential capacity <margin>45 P</margin> <note>Page 45 of the Plantin edition</note> of the state is accepted as the category, or if the state is defined by it—for instance, if one wishes "gentleness" <note>original: *mansuetudinem*</note> to be the "restraint of anger," and calls "courage" <note>original: *fortitudinem*</note> the "restraint of fear" and the "abstaining from flight." For it is one thing to be brave and gentle, but quite another <margin>15</margin> to be merely "restrained." A gentle person is one who is not gripped by anger at all; a restrained person is one who suppresses the anger that has gripped him; and a brave person is one who conquers anger <note>original: *iram vincit*. Note: some versions of the text, such as the G edition, suggest "conquers fear" (*metum vincit*)</note>. 

**Twenty-fifth**, whether a consequence is positioned as the general category, or whether the definition of a preceding thing is based on what follows it, or vice-versa. An example is one who calls the category of anger "sadness," or <margin>20</margin> the category of sadness "anger," where sadness follows from anger, or where <margin>746 G</margin> <note>Page 746 of the G edition</note> occasionally sadness gives birth to anger. Furthermore, these final logical rules <note>original: *loca* — literally "places," the traditional term for patterns of argument in logic</note> serve to discuss what is unique to a subject <note>original: *proprium* — a property that belongs to all members of a species and only to them, like "capacity for speech" in humans</note> by using the opposite reasoning. For example, it is not "one who is laughing" but "one capable of laughing" <note>original: *risibile*</note> that is the unique property of a human; likewise, it is not being a "philosopher" but being "capable of philosophizing" <note>original: *philosophatile*</note>. <margin>25</margin> Nor is such a property simultaneous with the nature of the species or prior to it; rather, unique properties everywhere follow the specific difference <note>original: *differentiam* — the essential trait that defines a species within its category</note>. An "accident" <note>original: *accidens* — a quality that can change without the thing losing its identity, like being tall or short</note> is defined as that which immediately follows the established species.

## FOURTH SECTION.

The third partition <note>marked as 'C' in Bruno's mnemonic system</note>, encompassing two sides and granting access through twin gates to twin ranks of fields, belongs to the property <note>original: *proprii* — a "proprium" is a characteristic that belongs only to a particular species, like "the ability to laugh" belongs only to humans</note>, where the places common to the definition itself and to the property are reported, arranged in order. Of these, <margin>46 P</margin> <note>Page 46 of the Plantin edition</note> <margin>5</margin> the **first** requires that we consider whether it [the property] comes to the underlying nature <note>original: *subiectae naturae*</note> through itself, or by accident, or always, or sometimes, or absolutely, or relatively and comparatively, or to every instance, or to some instance, or even to the one alone, or merely to that alone. The **second**: whether that which was in, is in, and will be in [the subject], could <margin>10</margin> not have been in, cannot be, or will not be able to be. The **third**: whether the definition or the property brought forward does not equal the subject species—for instance, if we see such terms <unclear>for</unclear> exceed [the species], or on the contrary, if the property and definition encompass more than the proposed species: since these must <margin>15</margin> both be convertible <note>original: *convertibilia* — logically interchangeable, where if A is B, then B must be A</note> with the subject. The **sixth**: whether the property draws out the definition, as it were, or conversely, the definition draws out the property. The **seventh**: whether a definition or property falls <margin>25</margin> only upon one thing, when several properties or definitions of a subject could be combined. The **eighth**: whether you can show any of those things by a single given species, where such a property or <margin>747 G</margin> <note>Page 747 of the Gessner edition</note> <unclear>common thing</unclear> might not be possible. 8.  Because the term used equally requires determination, seeing as it is placed in the same division;
9.  Because it precedes [the subject] neither in the order of nature nor in the order of our knowledge;

This occurs, for example, if one were to state a substance—of which "man" is a species—as if it were the property or definition of an "animal"; or 12. <margin>748 G</margin> <note>Rule 11, sub-point 12</note> because the term employed does not precede the subject either in its nature or in our cognition of it; likewise, the understanding of the term is joined to the understanding of the other thing being declared, and the state of ignorance regarding one follows from the state of ignorance regarding the other. The **twelfth** rule: whether the proposed definition or property admits of redundancy <note>original: *superfluitatem* — literally "superfluity" or "overflow"</note>. This will happen either: 
1. Because one attaches a difference <term>difference<span>In logic, the "differentia" is the specific characteristic that distinguishes a species from others within the same genus (e.g., "rational" distinguishes humans within the genus "animal")</span></term> to the genus that is of such a kind that it lacks the power to separate the thing from any other thing; 
2. Or because, although it may be a property and narrows the subject within its own proper boundaries, the part that is added could nonetheless be removed and the essence or property would still remain clearly stated; 
3. Or because some part of the description or definition is not true of all the instances contained under the term being defined; 
4. Or because a particular instance of that thing is attached to the universal; 
5. Or because the same thing is noted by a synonym under another name; 
6. Or because a trifling repetition <note>original: *nugatorie* — "triflingly" or "frivolously"</note> of the same word is made.

The **thirteenth** rule: whether the presentation of the definition or property is defective <margin>49 P</margin> <note>original: *manca* — literally "maimed" or "crippled"</note> or diminished. This will occur either: 
1. Because, even with the terms provided, the subject species has not been driven from foreign boundaries into its own, clearly because the definition is not stated about that species alone—from this, it is understood that a "difference" has been overlooked; 
2. Or because, while it may refer to something else either by its own nature or by reason of its genus, its correlative <note>The corresponding term in a relationship (e.g., "parent" is the correlative of "child")</note> is not indicated; 
3. Or because, while it exists for the sake of a specific end <note>original: *finem* — the "telos" or purpose</note>, it is not revealed through that end, but the end is either kept silent, or in its place is substituted that which belongs to it or the path leading toward it.

# THE FIELD OF ACCIDENT.

## I. THE FIRST PART.

Now, for one proceeding from the courtyard through the gate of the enclosure into the field of accident, there occurs first on the right a list of those reasons by which something is judged to be an accident <term>accident<span>In Aristotelian logic, an "accident" is an attribute which may or may not belong to a subject, without the subject's essence being destroyed (e.g., "being tan" is an accident of a "human").</span></term>.
<margin>5</margin> First, namely, because it is neither genus nor species, nor property nor difference, and yet it is predicated <term>predicated<span>To be stated or asserted about a subject.</span></term> of something.
<margin>749 G</margin> Second, because it is separable from the substance <note>The underlying reality or "thing itself" that supports attributes.</note>, and yet it cannot exist without substance; for it consists through that substance which retains it, to which [the accident] no ground of self-subsistence can belong.
<margin>10</margin> Third, because although it is in the substance itself, it is nonetheless later in time <note>In the order of existence, the thing (substance) must exist before it can have qualities (accidents).</note>. Fourth, because it has a subject other than its own nature. Fifth, because although it possesses a "new being," it is not for that reason said to be "generated" or "created" on its own, but rather "con-generated" <note>original: *congenerari* — it comes into existence alongside or within a substance.</note>; and that which is con-generated is by no means said to "be" or "exist" by itself, but is said to "be in" <note>original: *inesse*</note> and "consist."
<margin>15</margin> Sixth, because it is in the substance not as a part is in a whole. Seventh, because although it is as if it were "somewhere," it is not however like a thing placed in a location. Eighth, because it is in a category <term>category<span>One of the ten classes of being (such as quantity, quality, or relation) which are distinct from the category of Substance.</span></term> other than substance, acting as a species or a subordinate genus within that category.
<margin>20</margin> Ninth, because it belongs to no species of substance. Tenth, because it admits of "more" and "less" <note>For example, a person can be more or less "brave" (accident), but not more or less "human" (substance).</note>.
<margin>50 P</margin> Eleventh, because there is something contrary to it. Twelfth, because the genus which is stated quidditatively <term>quidditatively<span>Relating to the "quiddity" or "whatness"—the essential definition of a thing.</span></term> of it is itself an accident. Thirteenth, because the things of which it is itself stated quidditatively are themselves accidents. Fourteenth, because a substance is denominated <note>i.e., named or described. For instance, a man is "denominated" as "white" because of the accident of "whiteness."</note> from...

is said only by origin. 

Fifteenth, because it is predicated of substance denominatively <term>denominatively<span>In logic, this refers to a name derived from another, such as "white" being derived from "whiteness." It suggests the attribute is not the thing itself, but something the thing "has."</span></term>. 

Sixteenth, because it is predicated as a quality <term>in quale<span>A technical phrase meaning to describe "what kind" of thing something is, rather than "what" the thing is in its core essence.</span></term>, and it is spoken of not as an essence nor as something essential.

Nineteenth, because it follows the subject as being *in* it, not as being *from* it <note>The accident exists within the subject, but the subject is not "made of" the accident.</note>.

Twenty-first, because it is an accident in respect to something else; for such a thing cannot be a substance, because that which truly *is* happens to no one <note>Bruno is arguing that a true "Substance" is independent; if something "happens" to a subject, it must be an accident.</note>. 

Twenty-second, because it does not move from subject to subject, nor from place to place; and when it is no longer where it was, it has already vanished, since the numerically same <term>numerically same<span>A philosopher's way of saying "the exact same individual instance." For example, the specific "redness" of one apple cannot move to another apple; if the apple rots, that specific redness vanishes.</span></term> thing cannot exist without that in which it is; for it is not independent <note>original: *sui est iuris* — "of its own right."</note>. 

Twenty-third, because it does not approach the subject nor migrate from the subject, but results from the subject and must necessarily perish within it. 

<margin>750 G</margin> Twenty-fourth, because it is reached only by the senses and the imagination, and it does not exist above the level of sense and imagination. 

Twenty-fifth, because it is not matter, not form, not a composite, not a "this" that can be predicated, nor a separate substance. 

Twenty-sixth, because it is not itself the subject of anything, but is rather enslaved <note>original: *mancipatum* — a legal term for something transferred as property.</note> to some subject. 

Twenty-seventh, because it is a disposition of something, or a habit, or a figure, or something resulting from a complexion <term>complexion<span>In Renaissance science, a "complexion" is the specific balance or mixture of the four humors/elements within a body.</span></term>.

Third, if it is contrary to that which exists through itself. 

Fourth, if it is opposed to the natural.

->### CONCERNING THE HUNTING LAMP <note>Original: *De Lampade Venatoria*. This refers to a "lamp" or light used to "hunt" for logical truths and categories.</note><-

...to be examined, through which you may test whether that which is proposed as a **genus** <term>genus<span>The broad category or family to which a thing belongs, such as "Animal."</span></term> is truly so according to the sense of logic. The first of these rules requires one to consider whether it is said not as "what a thing is" <term>what a thing is<span>Original Latin: *in quid*. This refers to the essence or definition of a thing.</span></term>, but as "what kind of thing it is" <term>what kind of thing it is<span>Original Latin: *in quale*. This refers to a quality or description rather than a core essence.</span></term>. For who would call "white" the genus of snow? While white is predicated of snow, lime, wool, and <margin>5</margin> milk, through that term we can only declare *what kind* they all are, not *what* they are. Likewise, "capable of walking," since it describes a qualified animal, is not a genus. The second rule: whether it is said not univocally <term>univocally<span>Using a word in exactly the same sense for different things.</span></term>, but denominatively; for whiteness is not called "snow," but "white." The third: whether the genus and the species are said of equal things; <margin>10</margin> for how could **being**, **the one**, **something**, **the good**, and similar terms be a genus to one another? <note>These are "transcendentals"—concepts so broad they apply to everything and therefore cannot be divided into genus and species.</note> The fourth: whether the species is asserted of more things than the genus; for who would say it is credible for the genus to be "true"? Here it is also fitting to see whether the genus is removed when the species is removed; for it is necessary that the species be removed when the genus is removed, but not <margin>15</margin> the other way around. The fifth: whether someone thinks the genus is a species of a "difference" <term>difference<span>The specific trait that distinguishes one species from another within the same genus (e.g., "rationality" is the difference that makes a human a specific type of animal).</span></term>, as if one were to say "capable of laughter" or "rational mortal" is the genus of man. The sixth: whether they put forward a species or something outside the genus as a genus of a difference, as those who say that "immortal" is what God or the divine is. The seventh: whether a difference is put forward as if it were a genus, <margin>20</margin> <margin>55 P</margin> as if "even or odd" were said to be what "number" is. | The eighth: whether only one species lies hidden under one genus—indeed, whether that which is called a genus is only one species; for a genus is said of several species. To this belongs the error of one who accepts "line" as the genus of "length," since outside and beyond the line, <margin>25</margin> length does not happen to consist or exist. The ninth: whether something is contrary to the genus, but nothing is contrary to the species which is said of it. The tenth: whether some species is contrary to the genus; for things should not be contrary to the genus, but contrary within the genus.

...concerning the species **essentially** <term>quidditative<span>A philosophical term meaning 'relating to the essence' or the 'what-ness' (quidditas) of a thing.</span></term>; for just as we can say "man is a rational animal," so we can also perpetually say "man is an animal." But if one wishes to call wind "moved air," air is present there not as a genus, but as the subject to which a genus is attributed—just as saying snow is "solidified water,"
<margin>5</margin>or mud is "earth stuck together by water." Yet mud is not, for that reason, "earth," nor is snow "water." Nor is wine—as **Empedocles** <note>Empedocles was a pre-Socratic philosopher who famously proposed that the world was composed of four elements: earth, air, fire, and water. He believed wine was a form of water that had undergone a chemical-like change within the vine.</note> said—"water rotted in wood." This is because something cannot be a genus if it cannot also be stated of the species in an absolute sense. Therefore, if it is not true to say "wine is water,"

# OF GIORDANO BRUNO <note>original header: "IORDANI BRVNI"</note>

...there is a certain difference which is predicated of a species, yet it does not admit the definition of a property; for never can a genus or a difference, in which a thing participates, be a property of the subject species.

**Fourth**, whether [the property] comes to a thing <margin>**760 G**</margin> already perfected and established in its complete act; <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, "act" (actus) refers to the full realization or activity of a thing, as opposed to its "potency" or potentiality.</note>
<margin>5</margin> for although a property is naturally and immediately consequent to the substantial form, the "act" of the substantial difference and the property are verified of the subject at the same time. Indeed, according to the logic of its formal being, we know that one depends on the other in a specific order.
<margin>10</margin> Hence, one would be philosophizing poorly to say that "to philosophize," "to navigate," or "to laugh" is a property of man; rather, one should say "capable of philosophizing," "capable of navigating," and "capable of laughter" <note>original: "philosophabile, navigabile, risivum seu risile." Bruno is distinguishing between a fleeting action (the act) and an inherent capacity (the property).</note>.

**Fifth**, whether a property is assigned with a defect because a condition of that property was omitted;
<margin>15</margin> specifically, where one expresses something as a property simply and without modification, when it is only a property "now" and "in this way." For "sitting in a chair" cannot be a property of Socrates, except in a specific place and at a defined time.

**Sixth**, whether such a property is of the sort that is known in no other way than through the senses;
<margin>20</margin> for everything perceived by the senses becomes uncertain once it is removed from the senses; for when it is absent, one will not know if it still exists within the subject. I set aside those things in which one might assume the thing is present by a necessary consequence. <margin>**65 P**</margin>
<margin>25</margin> Therefore, it is poorly said that the property of the sun is to be the "brightest star of those carried above the earth"; for why should a definition most known to the senses be used (namely, that it is carried above the earth), when the senses cannot know if it is still "carried above the earth" once it has set?

**Seventh**, whether he has brought together and massed several properties...

## THE CORNER OF DESCRIPTION.
---
### Section II.

From this very section and the one immediately preceding it, one may derive the principles and conditions of description.
<margin>5</margin>For a description differs from an exact definition in this: a definition distinguishes the subject **species** <term>species: a specific class of things (like "humans") under a broader group</term> from all others under a given **genus** <term>genus: a general category (like "animals")</term> by an essential difference. A description, however, does so through a property that is strictly unique <note>original: "accidente proprie proprio"</note>—one that belongs to every member, only to them, and always to that which is being verified. 
But where a property is indeed unique but does <margin>68 P</margin>
<margin>10</margin>not apply to the whole species—such as being an "astrologer" applies to a specific man—the description of the human will be weaker. It will be weakest of all if it is drawn from traits that do not belong to the subject permanently, even if they belong to it alone. Beyond these, when it happens that a genus—contracted by properties of another kind—is 
<margin>15</margin>predicated of a species, there can be no skillful description at all. There is, however, a **common ground** <note>original: "locus communis"</note> shared by definition and description: if someone lacks arguments against a description or definition as a whole because the thing itself is not obvious, they must act against a known part that does 
<margin>20</margin>not seem to have been correctly presented. For it is clear that if this part is overturned, the whole cannot stand.

<margin>763 G</margin>
## THE FIELD OF DEFINITION.
---

In the field of definition, the first station <note>The "station" or "seat" refers to a specific logical starting point or perspective.</note> requires one to see whether something indefinite, indeterminate, and infinite [has been used] in place of a genus...

<header>GIORDANO BRUNO'S [WORKS]</header>

is applied; for there, we can truly assert that a definition has been provided without its **genus** <term>genus: the broad category a thing belongs to, like "animal" for "human"</term>, if indeed one is permitted to call such a phrasing a definition; such as if someone, wishing to define a **body** <note>original: "corpus"</note>, were to say it is that which has three dimensions. By omitting the genus (says Aristotle), one does not state what the thing is, because the 
<margin>70 P</margin> **essence** <term>essence: the fundamental nature that makes a thing what it is</term> of any | thing is joined with its genus. 

Second: if the thing defined is not fitted to everything it concerns—as with those who define the art of **grammar** as "speaking correctly," whereas they should have added "and writing correctly"; for if either one of these sufficed for a correct definition of grammar, there could be multiple definitions for the same thing, which is inconsistent. 

Third: if, thinking to be complete by adapting it to everything, one couples it with something that is not at all necessary—such as if someone defines **medicine** as the "art of knowing the causes of disease and health," when one could just as well accept either of these, because both signify the same thing as the one, and the one no less than the other; hence, by taking now this term and now that one, one is not providing two or different definitions in any way, but exactly the same one. 

Fourth: if that which is present **by its own nature** <note>original: "per se"</note> in the thing defined is joined to that which is present **incidentally** <note>original: "per accidens"</note> and indirectly—as if someone were to define medicine as the science of inducing health and disease; for one of these, though just as true, does not apply directly. 

Fifth: if it is explanatory; for it is enough that it explains more clearly. 

Sixth: if it has not brought forth the **proximate genus** <term>proximate genus: the most immediate general category (e.g., "bird" for "eagle") rather than a remote one (e.g., "living thing")</term>; for when this is brought forth, all the higher categories are understood to be included, but when those higher ones are all brought forth, this one alone is not. Therefore, either the proximate genus must be applied, 
<margin>764 G</margin> or, if one prefers to have brought forth a more | remote one, let it be done so that all the **differences** <term>difference: the specific trait that distinguishes a species within its genus</term> by which the proximate genus is determined are included.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of logical errors in the "Eighteenth Lamp" concerning definitions. It specifically focuses on the fifth through ninth types of faulty definitions, illustrating why a simple list of components does not constitute the essence of a whole.</meta>

# ON THE HUNTING TORCH
<page-num>70 verso P, 71 P</page-num>

<margin>5</margin>...so that the definition is not attributed to neither part individually; for instance, if one defining **justice** <note>original: "iustitiam"</note> <margin>70' P</margin> says that it is "temperance and fortitude." For if these two are brought forward, and a person possesses only one of the two, it would follow that both people taken together are "just," but individually they are not. This is much like saying two people have a **mina** <term>mina: an ancient unit of weight or currency; here used to show that two people sharing a sum doesn't mean each person possesses that sum</term>, yet neither of them can be said to possess a mina on his own. I set aside the fact that while someone may be brave and temperate, it is still possible for them to be ambitious: hence the same person would be both just and unjust. 

**The Eighth fault** is whether, when one has brought forward the parts, he thinks he has defined the whole. 
<margin>10</margin>It is clear that nothing prevents the parts from existing while the "whole" does not; for a **garment** <note>original: "indumentum"</note> does not exist simply because the cloth and the thread exist. 

**The Ninth fault** applies to one who is cautious of the previous error and says the thing defined is not merely these parts, but "that which consists of them." This definition may be resisted for several reasons:
1. Because the parts are not naturally suited to become one thing from those which were mentioned.
<margin>15</margin>2. Because they do not exist within one primary subject.
3. Because the parts do not perish at the same time as the whole.
4. Because the whole is good or evil, while the parts are neither.
5. Because the whole is a **synonym** <term>synonym: here meaning a word that carries the same essential meaning or weight</term> with one of its parts.
6. Because the **mode of composition** <note>original: "modus compositionis"</note> is not explained; for it does not follow that a house exists
<margin>20</margin>simply by any way in which stones and wood are put together.
7. Because it does not distinguish "being this and that" from "being this thing *out of* those things"; for bread is made *out of* flour and water, but it is not simply flour and water.
8. Because having inspected the ways in which one thing is spoken of with another, it is in no way
<margin>25</margin>established that "this" exists, so that this thing combined with that thing creates "that" result. | It happens, therefore, <margin>71 P</margin> that **fortitude** <note>original: "fortitudinem"</note> is poorly defined by saying it is "audacity with **right reason**" <term>right reason: "recta ratio," a classical concept of acting according to correct moral and logical principles</term>. For what will you say of a man who has the audacity to kill and yet has "right reason" regarding medicinal matters? Is a man who thinks boldly and rightly in medicine therefore "brave"?

# 78 GIORDANO BRUNO

...or ninth, because he did not state what kind of composition it is; for someone who thinks they have defined **flesh** <note>original: "carnem"</note> <margin>765 G</margin> without explaining the manner in which it exists, merely said it is a composition of the four elements. 

**The Tenth fault** is when it happens that two opposites are both found equally in the same thing, yet one defines it through only one of them. For instance, one who defines the **soul** <note>original: "animam"</note> as a "substance capable of knowledge," despite it being no less capable of **ignorance** <note>original: "ignorantiae"</note>. 

**The Eleventh fault** is whether something is not related to its primary subject, especially when the definition pertains to many things. For example, if you define **prudence** <note>original: "prudentiam"</note> as a virtue of a man or of the soul, when its primary subject is actually the **rational power** <term>rational power: "potentia rationalis," the specific capacity for reason within the soul</term> which belongs to the soul. This also applies if the proper subject is not brought forward, such as when **health** <note>original: "valetudo"</note> is called a "symmetry of hot and cold." For we do not call this symmetry "health" in every instance, nor is every weakening of the senses **sleep** <note>original: "somnus"</note>, nor does **pain** <note>original: "dolor"</note> occur in every case where naturally joined parts are separated, nor does **doubt** <note>original: "dubitatio"</note> exist in every instance of opposing arguments. 

**The Twelfth fault** is whether a distinction is not made between the cause and the result, or between the act and that which performs the act. For the **separation of parts** <note>original: "separatio partium"</note> naturally joined is not itself pain, but rather a certain **affection** <term>affection: "affectio," a state of being or a feeling resulting from an external cause</term> that follows from it. 

**The Thirteenth fault** is whether something is added that **weakens** <note>original: "castrat," literally "castrates" or "mutilates," meaning to strip the definition of its universal power</note> <margin>72 P</margin> the definition, as is done when people commonly add to the definition of a **line** <note>original: "lineae"</note> the phrase "whose extremes are two points." 

**The Fourteenth fault** is whether, in establishing the subject, the **form** <note>the essential nature or organizing principle</note> is taken as if it were something arriving later to the subject. This occurs when the soul is defined as the "act of an organic body potentially having life." In truth, the soul does not simply arrive at a pre-existing organic body; rather, the soul itself prepares, makes, and organizes the body at the same time as it **vivifies** <note>brings to life</note> it. For that which is "animated" is properly the part of the animal that receives the soul—namely the body—which is called **inanimate** <note>original: "inanimatum"</note> when without the soul. Therefore, an animal is not truly...

## THE CORNER OF DIFFERENCE.

---

### II. PART.

<margin>5</margin> In the matter of the **difference** <term>difference: (differentia) the specific characteristic that distinguishes one species from another within the same genus</term>, however, where the whole of what constitutes the formal part of a definition seems to consist—namely that by which the **specific act** <note>original: "specificus actus"; the defining activity or essence of a species</note> is designated—one must examine most diligently.

First, by considering whether this is indeed a difference of the **genus** <note>original: "generis"</note> that has been posited. Second, whether it might not be a difference at all, for instance because no opposite to it is perceived in the division. <margin>10</margin> Third, if the genus is not divided by it. Fourth, if, while it divides the genus, it also does not constitute a **species** <note>original: "speciem"</note>. Fifth, if the opposite difference arriving at the genus is not constitutive of any species; for indeed, it will not be permitted to call this one which was posited "specific." <margin>15</margin> Sixth, if the genus is divided through it as if by a negation, or if a negation is opposed to it. This place is suspect. Seventh, if it does not signify "of what kind" <note>original: "quale"</note>. Eighth, if it is not present in the thing defined except **by accident** <term>by accident: a property that is not essential to the thing's nature, like being "tall" or "sitting"</term>. Ninth, if this difference is attributed to the genus rather than the species, <margin>20</margin> just as "being without width" seems to **Aristotle** <note>original: "Aristoteli"</note> to be attributed to length as much as to a line. Tenth, if the genus is **predicated** <note>original: "praedicatur"; asserted or stated</note> of the difference itself; for this is not said of anything other than species. Because if we say truly "**the rational is an animal**" <note>original: "rationale est animal"</note>, we do not mean the difference itself which is signified **adjectively** <note>original: "adiective"</note>, <margin>25</margin> but there "rational" is taken **substantively** <note>original: "substantive"</note>, insofar as it signifies the same thing as "man," who is the subject of **rationality** <note>original: "rationalitatis"</note>.

Eleventh, if the difference is not prior in species; for it must follow after that which it divides, and precede that which it constitutes. 

Twelfth, if the difference is found to belong to another genus. 

Thirteenth, if, when it is posited for something **relative** <note>original: "ad aliquid"; a category of being that exists only in relation to something else, like "double" or "knowledge"</note>, the difference itself is not relative; for just as knowledge is relative, so too are the active, the contemplative, and the effective, as <margin>767 G</margin> | Aristotle says.

> "as one who said that an **odd number** is a number having a middle, because having a middle also fits a line, a body, and speech." 

But we say that this difference, under the genus of number, is most powerful and admits of no criticism. However, it would be a "vague" difference if "number" were taken there according to an **equivocal** <note>original: "aequivocam"; using the same word with different meanings</note> reasoning—mixing proper and metaphorical meanings according to a manifold genus. Therefore, this passage should not be lightly criticized or accepted for the sake of truth.

...the same, so that you may destroy or confirm the identity of the things posited; <margin>75 P</margin> for courage will be the same thing as justice if you find no difference between the just man and the brave man. Likewise in accompanying opposites: **active** and **passive power**, acting itself <margin>5</margin> and being acted upon. 

Second, whether they do not differ according to degrees of comparison <note>i.e., if one thing can be "more" or "less" than the other, they cannot be identical</note>. 

Third, if both are the same as the same thing. 

Fourth, if the same thing is the same for both. 

Fifth, if the things that happen to one also happen to the other. 

Sixth, if those things to which one occurs, the other also occurs. 

Seventh, if the **genus** is the same for both, or the **species** is the same for both. 

Eighth, if one is intensified or diminished, while the other is not, or neither is. <margin>10</margin> 

Ninth, if both opposites applied to the same thing do not produce the same whole. 

Tenth, if when the same thing is removed from both, they do not remain the same. 

Eleventh, if one can exist without the other. 

Twelfth, if the name of one and the **definition** <note>original: "oratio"; here meaning the formal statement of essence</note> of the other do not denote the same thing. 

Thirteenth, if the opposite is compared with the opposite, and the proposed thing <margin>15</margin> | with the proposed thing. <margin>76 G</margin> 

Fourteenth, if contrary differences are **predicated** <term>predicated: in logic, to "predicate" is to assert a quality or characteristic about a subject</term> of contrary things.

It is manifest to everyone that these **Topics** <term>Topics: derived from the Greek *topoi* (places), these are logical "locations" or strategies used to find arguments and proofs</term> offer mutual assistance to the "topics of definition." <margin>20</margin> Nor is it difficult to apply them to the **property** <term>property: a characteristic that is unique to a species (like "laughter" to humans) but does not define its essential nature</term>, to the description, and wherever we intend to employ **convertible predication** <note>a logical relationship where the subject and predicate are equal and interchangeable</note>. 

But in all these matters, one must consider that wherever there is **plurality**, true **identity** cannot exist; for through true identity, things cease to be "many." <margin>25</margin> Therefore, wherever there is distinction and plurality, it is necessary to understand a difference either in genus, or in species, or in number. And wherever there is a unique number and a unique reasoning <note>original: "ratio"</note> and <margin>76 P</margin> distinction, there cannot be identity and (by necessary consequence) natural equality—whatever the logicians might say...

<page-num>82</page-num>
<header>GIORDANO BRUNO</header>

...by common thematic and metaphysical principles, which are shared among species by a kind of widespread equality and identity. However, this occurs in such a way that all things, in their mutual and reciprocal relationship to the Universal One <note>Bruno refers to the "Monad" or the single substance that constitutes the universe</note>, are equal and identical.
<margin>5</margin>Yet, it does not follow that two things that are numerically distinct can ever be identical or equal according to their own specific properties, any more than two things can simply be one. Indeed, things can only be called exactly equal when they are one; but when they are one, they are no longer "equal," because a thing is not said to be "equal" to itself.
<margin>10</margin>Therefore, where there is distinction and number, there can be neither identity nor equality.

<header># GIORDANO BRUNO</header>

[The universe] is the work of God, nature, and reason. Within the analogy connecting these three, nature wonderfully reflects divine action, while human genius in turn emulates the workings of nature—as if even striving toward higher things. <margin>5</margin> Who does not see how nature accomplishes so many things with so few elements? <note>Bruno refers to the four classical elements: Earth, Air, Fire, and Water. His argument is that complexity arises from the arrangement of simple parts.</note> Truly, everyone knows this is possible because she arranges, orders, composes, moves, and applies those same four elements in various ways. Under various signs, shaped and figured, she brings them forth from the depths of potentiality to the heights of actual existence.

But, by the immortal God, <margin>10</margin> what can be easier for a human than counting? First, that there is one, two, three, four; second, that one is not two, two is not three, three is not four; third, that one and two are three, and one and three are four. To do this is to do everything; to speak this is to speak <margin>(:) 3<sup>r</sup></margin> <margin>15</margin> everything. To imagine, signify, and retain this allows one to grasp all objects, to understand what is grasped, and to remember what is understood. This total light is more present, clear, and available to our intelligence than the light of the sun can be to our physical eyes. The sun's light rises and sets, <margin>20</margin> and is not always there when we look for it. But this other light is no less present to us than we are to ourselves; it is so present to our mind that it is the mind itself. 

Would you like me to say, meanwhile, why so few people know and grasp this? Why (I ask) is that which is so close to us thought by us to be as distant as the farthest <margin>25</margin> heaven? It is because the eye sees other things, but does not see itself. But what is that "eye" that sees other things in such a way that it also sees itself? It is He who sees all things within Himself, and who is the same as all things. <note>This "Eye" refers to the Divine Intellect or God, in whom the act of knowing and the thing known are identical.</note> We would be like that sublime Reason if we could perceive the substance of our own nature; <margin>30</margin> just as if our eye could see itself, our mind would embrace its own essence. Then...

<meta>This page continues Bruno's dedicatory epistle. Having previously argued that nature produces infinite complexity from simple elements (the four elements) and that human thought follows a similar pattern through simple numbers, he now explores the psychological necessity of using mental images. # ON THE COMPOSITION OF IMAGES - PREFACE

If it were possible to understand all things, it would not even be difficult to do all things. However, the nature of composite and physical bodies does not permit this; for the substance of such things is bound up in motion and quantity, even if in its own essence it is neither moving nor quantitative. From this, just as we cannot see ourselves—that is, our inner depth <margin>(:) 3v</margin> and our indivisible essence—but can only see certain external accidents of our surface (specifically our color and shape) and the reflection of the eye itself in a mirror; so too our intellect cannot see itself in itself, nor see all things in themselves. Instead, it sees through an external appearance, a likeness, an image, a shape, or a sign.

This is what Aristotle related, which had been expressed earlier by the ancients, and is grasped by only a few of the moderns: 'our understanding' <note>original: *intelligere nostrum*</note> (that is, the operations of our intellect) 'is either imagination or is not without imagination.' And again: 'we do not understand unless we contemplate mental images.' <note>Bruno is referencing Aristotle’s *De Anima* (On the Soul) 431a, a cornerstone of medieval and Renaissance psychology which posits that the mind requires *phantasmata* (mental images) to process thought.</note> This is because we do not comprehend through a simple, static unity, but through composition, comparison, and a plurality of terms—mediated by discourse <note>In this context, <term>discursus</term> refers to "discursive reason," the step-by-step process of moving from one idea to another, rather than instant divine intuition.</note> and reflection.

If our genius is of such a nature, then its works must surely be of the same kind. Thus, whether the mind is searching, discovering, judging, arranging, or remembering, it must not wander away from the mirror, nor should it act without images. Here, if by nature a polished and flat mirror is placed before us, and if through art the light of logical rules <note>original: *lux canonum*, referring to the "light of canons" or fundamental principles of his system.</note> thrives and shines upon the horizon of our reasoning, we will immediately be directed toward that highest happiness in various kinds of action. This is the happiness <margin>(:) 4r</margin> most appropriate to a human being, precisely as a human being, which arises from the clear and distinct images of things coming into view according to our granted faculty.

Therefore, to complete this doctrine, I have compiled three...

...books. In the first of these are contained those general matters which concern the diverse modes of signifying; likewise, the various conditions by which subjects are prepared and arranged, and how images are impressed and painted, are explained. In the "art of memory," these refer to mental spaces or rooms used to store information.</note> and fields <margin>5</margin> of various kinds, and then we provide those that have been built. ### CHAPTER ONE.

->Concerning light, the ray, and the mirror.<-

Being is understood to be distributed into three heads: the metaphysical, the physical, and the logical, in a universal sense; just as there <margin>10</margin> are three principles of all things—God, Nature, and Art; and there are three effects—divine, natural, and artificial.

Every agent that acts by purpose, and not by some necessity, must first conceive the "species" <note>original: *speciem*. In this context, Bruno refers to the mental form, blueprint, or essential image of a thing before it is actually made.</note> of the thing to be produced. Indeed, this species, when it exists before natural things, is called an **Idea**. In natural <margin>15</margin> things, it is called a **Form** or a **Vestige** <note>original: *vestigium*. Literally a "footprint" or "trace," suggesting that physical objects are merely the tracks left behind by divine ideas.</note> of the ideas. In things that come after nature <note>original: *postnaturalibus*. This refers to human thoughts, concepts, and artistic creations that arise from observing the natural world.</note>, it is called a **Reason** or **Intention**—which is divided into first and second intentions—and which I have often been accustomed to call the **Shadow of Ideas**.

Ideas are the cause of things *before* the things exist. The vestiges of ideas <margin>20</margin> are the things themselves, or those qualities within the things. The shadows of ideas are derived from the things themselves, or exist *after* the things; these are said to exist with <margin>2</margin> much less "reason" <note>Meaning their degree of reality or ontological status.</note> than the things themselves which proceed from the womb of nature—just as those things have less reality than the Mind, the Idea, and the Principle—

<summary>Bruno establishes the foundational triadic structure of his philosophy, categorizing reality into Ideas (divine), Vestiges (natural), and Shadows (human/artistic), which sets the stage for his system of mnemonic images.</summary>

# GIORDANO BRUNO ON THE COMPOSITION OF IMAGES, BOOK I.

...effective, supernatural, substance-giving, and super-essential principle.

Therefore, beings are distinguished into those that are—that is, "things"—and into those that belong to the things that are—namely, "signs" or "indications." <margin>5</margin> This distinction is almost the same as the one commonly circulated: that between **substance** and **accident**. <note>original: *substantiam et accidens*. In traditional philosophy, a "substance" is what a thing is in itself (like a person), while an "accident" is a quality it happens to have (like being tall or sitting down).</note>

In our present purpose, we are by no means establishing a method concerning the things themselves, but concerning the *signifiers* of things. In these signs, the power of producing all things will easily <margin>10</margin> be found to reside by those who contemplate, even moderately, the voice and characters of nature—which cries out from every side and describes the species of things. For it seems that matter does not contribute as much to the specification of a thing to be produced as do the **idea** and the **form**. In that first principle [matter], all <margin>15</margin> things converge and are one; but in this [form] and through this, all things are distributed into their genera, species, and finally their individual numbers. This is clear from the fact that the very same nourishment in a dog becomes the substance and seed of a dog, in a man it becomes that of a man, and in an ape that of an ape, <margin>20</margin> because of the "idea" present—which we find is not separate from things, but most closely joined to the things themselves.

In this way, we specify, invert, and adapt everything that has the character of primary, intermediate, or proximate matter within the act of the **inventive** or **memorative faculty** <note>The "inventive" faculty refers to the ability to find new ideas or arguments, while the "memorative" faculty is the capacity to store and recall them.</note> and its application, according to <margin>25</margin> the condition of the thing to be signified. We do this so that all things may be elicited from all things, all things may be signified by all things, and we may contemplate all things in all things. To sum it up in a single word: through application, "all things" behave as "one," and the "one," through its **informability**, <note>original: *informabilitatem*. This refers to the capacity of a single underlying "mental matter" to be shaped into any possible image or concept.</note> behaves as "all things"; <margin>30</margin> just as will be better and more aptly introduced through the practice of the following art.

96 GIORDANO BRUNO

Starting again, therefore, as if from the beginning, let us speak concerning **matter** and **species**. We have already understood that there is one supernatural Being that is infinite—one which is "intensively" the whole everywhere and totally present within the immense. <note>original: "intensive totum ubique." Bruno argues that God is "intensively" infinite because He is fully present at every point, whereas the universe is "extensively" infinite because it is spread out across space.</note> We have also placed before our eyes the one universe, which is likewise "extensively" infinite, and which is clearly visible in its physical form through various parts and locations. Furthermore, we have looked at the species of substance and those accidents that are actually found within substance. Now, there follows the order of the **rational world**. This rational world is formed in the likeness of the natural world, of which it is the **shadow**; the natural world, in turn, is the **image** of the divine world, of which it is the **trace**. <note>original: "umbra... imago... vestigium." This is a central theme in Bruno's philosophy: God leaves a "trace" (vestigium) in nature; nature is an "image" (imago) of God; and our thoughts/memory are "shadows" (umbra) of that nature.</note>

### CHAPTER TWO.

->Concerning those things which relate to the mirror and are within the mirror.<-

We propose that the subject of our present consideration is the universe according to its third meaning: as a kind of **living mirror** in which the image of natural things and the shadow of divine things reside.

Truly, this mirror conceives the **idea** as the cause of things, just as the mental image of a thing to be made informs the mind of the craftsman. It conceives the **form** as the thing itself—namely, the "species." For the entire substance of a thing is defined by this form, even though, in a physical sense, it cannot exist without matter. This is the case if we remain within the "Peripatetic courtyard"; <note>original: "atrio Peripatetico." This refers to the school of Aristotle. Peripatetics generally viewed matter as passive and form as the active principle.</note> however, it is different if we side with the "physicists" <note>Bruno often uses "physicists" to refer to pre-Socratic philosophers or those who believe matter is an active, vital force.</note> who understand matter to be the substance of all things. In their view, matter draws forms out from its own bosom and vital core, just as a mother brings forth, gives birth to, conceives, and hides her own offspring through various cycles. Finally, this mirror conceives the **image** as an effect of the thing itself, emanating in a sense from the thing's surface and informing the cognitive power first...

## CHAPTER THREE.

->Definitions of various notations.<-

As we continue to work within this third category <note>The rational world of human thought and memory.</note>, it is appropriate to further define the distinct meanings of other terms. A **mark** <note>original: *nota*.</note> <margin>14</margin> is said to be anything that demonstrates something in any way—whether by a first or second, near or remote, immediate or mediated reason. <margin>15</margin>

A **character** <note>original: *character*.</note> is that which signifies something through a specific drawing of lines or arrangement of points, such as the letters of the alphabet <note>original: *elementa*.</note>. <margin>19</margin>

A **sign** <note>original: *signum*.</note> is, in a sense, the general category <note>original: *genus*.</note> for everything that signifies, whether it functions as an idea, a trace, a shadow, or otherwise. <margin>20</margin>

A **seal** <note>original: *sigillum*, which is a diminutive of the word "sign."</note> signifies a more prominent part of a sign, or a sign taken in a more condensed manner; for example, we might represent a person or a person’s actions by showing only their head or their hand. <margin>25</margin>

A **token** <note>original: *indicium*.</note>, like the sign and the seal, is that whose function is not so much to represent or signify as it is to show... <margin>28</margin>

...to point, just as a pointer does not signify or denote the thing it points to by itself, but only invites or directs the gaze or attention toward it.

A **figure** <note>original: *figura*. In this context, it refers to a geometric shape or outline.</note> differs from all the preceding terms because figures are the traces and shadows of ideas; <margin>5</margin> while those ideas relate to both the internal and external aspects of things, a figure relates only to the external.

A **note**, **character**, **sign**, **seal**, and **indication** <note>original: *nota, character, signum, sigillum et indicium*. These are the various marks used in memory systems and logic.</note> can be referred to as lines or points or anything that does not enclose a space. A **figure**, however, is that which must enclose a space. <margin>10</margin>

**Likeness** <note>original: *similitudo*.</note> differs from all the aforementioned terms because it does not necessarily belong to the same species as they do. For instance, a man is signified by letters and characters as signs, indications, and notes, but not as a "likeness." A likeness would instead be a painting <margin>15</margin> or a statue, or the mental form <note>original: *species*. Here, the conceptual "type" or image of a thing held in the mind.</note> received through the senses and stored in the imagination.

**Proportion** <note>original: *proportio*.</note> differs from likeness because likeness is always understood to exist between two terms—such as "just as A is a letter, so B is," or "a mule is similar to a horse." Proportion, however, is always <margin>20</margin> understood to exist between four or more terms, or at least three. For example: just as *alpha* <note>original: *alpha*. The first letter of the Greek alphabet.</note> is among the Greeks, so is *A* among the Latins. Here there are four terms: 1. alpha, 2. Greek, 3. A, 4. Latin. Proportion is visible between at least three terms, such as: just as two relates to four, so eight relates to sixteen <margin>25</margin> (here there are four terms: 2, 4, 8, and 16); or, just as two relates to four, so four relates to eight, where there are three terms: two, four, and eight.

Finally, an **image** <note>original: *imago*.</note> differs from a likeness because it encompasses a certain greater energy, emphasis, and universality. Indeed, it is a more significant thing to exist "according to the image" than "according to the likeness." <margin>30</margin>

## CHAPTER FOUR.

->Every mark must be brought back to the atrium of sense and the tribunal of sight.<-

In this art <note>referring to the "Art of Memory" or mnemonics</note>, all things are usually grouped under the general name of **image**, <margin>10</margin> whether they are called notes, signs, indications, or perhaps more conveniently <margin>7</margin> and more accurately <note>original: *propius*. Corrected from the OCR's *proprius*.</note> by some other name; the fact that this practice has its own logic will be clear to those who weigh the matter more carefully. For all things, in whatever way they signify and represent, are traced back and reduced to a **form** <note>original: *species*. In Bruno's psychology, this refers to the "sensible species" or the mental image transmitted from the object to the mind.</note> <margin>15</margin> that can be grasped by the senses. All the various types of sensible forms are finally condensed into **visible forms**, which are surely the most vivid and effective of all; for sight is the most spiritual <note>original: *spiritualissimus*. In the Renaissance context, "spiritual" refers to the subtle, refined nature of the sense of sight, which requires less physical contact than touch or taste.</note> of all the senses. This will easily appear when we examine the degrees by which the senses relate to their own objects. For **Touch**, using both internal <margin>20</margin> and external organs, perceives things that are either clinging to the surface or penetrating the body; **Taste** perceives only those things clinging to it; **Smell** perceives the vapors diffused from a body placed further away; **Hearing** perceives things from a much greater distance; but **Sight** most readily grasps things that are the most remote of all. Therefore, we recall things <margin>25</margin> grasped by this sense to the mind more easily, and we retain them more effectively than those of the other senses. Indeed, it is through the objects of sight that we represent the objects of the other senses, as well as the objects of any desiring or knowing faculties—just as we describe and reveal everything through the use of visible letters.

## CHAPTER FIVE.

### On the physical, mathematical, and logical importance of images, according to all the various meanings of these modes.

Images, **seals**, and **characters** <note>original: *sigilla et characteres*. In Bruno’s system, these are not just drawings, but potent mnemonic and magical symbols used to organize the mind and tap into universal powers.</note> contribute to our ability to act, to perceive, and to signify, and they do so physically, <margin>5</margin> mathematically, and logically. For it is the way of nature to draw out a defined <term>species</term> <note>original: *speciem*. In this context, it refers to a specific form or type of being.</note> from indefinite matter by means of an ever-present or indwelling <term>idea</term> and **form**. When I say "indefinite <margin>10</margin> matter," I am not referring to "prime matter" <note>The most basic, formless substance of the universe in Aristotelian philosophy.</note> in this context, but "proximate matter"—such as common nourishment, which is converted into the substance and seed of a specific species. <margin>8</margin>| Furthermore, in a mathematical sense, **likenesses**, **images**, and **characters** lead us to produce and acquire many things, since it has been observed that there is a **triple world**: the <term>archetypal</term> <note>The divine realm of pure ideas.</note>, the physical, and the <term>shadowy</term> <note>original: *umbratilem*. This refers to the world of the human mind and memory, which contains "shadows" or reflections of the higher truths.</note>. From the first world, a descent is granted through the middle to the third; and from the third, an ascent is granted through the middle back to the first. It is just as we descend from the sun to the sight of the light of the moon (which is shared with the stars and the air), and from this to "shadowy" light, such as that seen in a mirror— <margin>20</margin> notwithstanding the fact that light can also be cast directly from the sun into a mirror, and reflected from the mirror back toward the sun in a direct and immediate path.

In the same way, our mind and our senses procure, acquire, and receive certain <term>forms</term> and **favors** <note>original: *favores*. These are the celestial influences or "gifts" that Bruno believes can be drawn down from the heavens through the use of specific symbols.</note> directly from the supernal <note>highest or heavenly</note> world, while they receive others through the <margin>25</margin> medium of natural and sensible things. All these things, whether they occur in one way or the other, we acquire and achieve only by means of certain signs, archetypes, gestures, and—as they say—**sacraments** <note>original: *sacramenta*. Bruno uses this term in its ancient sense of "sacred mysteries" or signs that bridge the human and the divine.</note>.

Therefore **forms**, **likenesses**, and **seals** are vehicles and, as it were, certain bonds, by which the favors of higher things...

**VI. From an analogy to the thing analogized.** Just as we receive the signified motion from the movement of <margin>5</margin> lower things as if from the effects of higher and invisible things, and from the movement of higher things as if from the causes of lower things; I mean to say, we grasp intelligible things <note>Concepts understood by the intellect alone.</note> from sensible substances <note>Physical objects perceived by the senses.</note>.

**VII. From the concrete to the abstract.** Just as we conceive a quality from a qualified thing <note>original: "ex quali qualitatem"</note>, <margin>10</margin> such as "whiteness" from the "white"; and conversely, the concrete from the abstract, such as the "white" from "whiteness."

**VIII. From a relative to its correlative.** Just as we understand "slave" from the mention of "master," or "master" from the existence of a "slave." By the virtue of this relation or comparison, <margin>15</margin> we can depict a giant with a small pebble—whenever a man is associated with the size of a single fly, while several men stand by the bulk of many ants <note>Bruno explains that size is relative; a "giant" is defined by being compared to something smaller, allowing the mind to scale images accordingly.</note>.

**IX. From the same or similar effects,** we hold the reasoning for the same or similar causes.

<margin>20</margin> **X. From antecedents.** Just as we predict rain from clouds rising from the south <note>original: "ab austro"</note> and from hens turning themselves in the dust.

**XI. From concomitants <note>Things that happen at the same time.</note>,** such as a flame indicating a kindled fire.

<margin>25</margin> **XII. From consequences,** such as wet earth indicating rain.

**XIII. From adjacencies.** Just as we perceive the needle, the pen, and the fly in the cobbler, the writer, and the corpse [respectively] as things that more effectively stir our senses; and we behold the arrow in the archer.

<margin>30</margin> **XIV. From a sensible composite to an insensible part.** Just as we infer the soul from the animal.

**XXII. From a perceptible action to an imperceptible effect**, just as we recognize adultery from an adulterer with an adulteress, or homicide from one man <margin>25</margin> killing another.

**XXIII. From the part to the whole**, just as we recognize a chariot from a wheel, or a "people" from four or five men gathered together.

**XXIV. From the whole to the part**, just as we recognize an infirmity of the eyes from a blind man.

### CHAPTER X. <margin>19</margin>

->On the images of words, or of voices and expressions.<-

<margin>5</margin> Regarding the images of voices and words, it escapes no one that just as words and voices possess no inherent shape, they are also not explained by the specific, descriptive forms of physical things. Strictly speaking, words are categorized as "marks" or "signs" rather than "images." Nevertheless, we apply the term "image" here <margin>10</margin> not based on the nature of the *things being signified*, but rather on the condition of the *signifiers themselves*. <note>Bruno is distinguishing between an image of a "dog" (the thing signified) and an image used to remember the letters or sound of the word "dog" (the signifier).</note> We cannot easily explain the parts of writing and the expressions themselves through imaginary means using the same symbols we draw on paper <margin>15</margin> unless we adopt more vivid forms of physical objects—the kinds of images that exist in nature or art and are visible to the eye. Therefore, these are called "images" in relation to the things from which they are derived, rather than what they are intended to mean in a sentence. Be that as it may, these <margin>20</margin> pre-conceived and designated forms must always be of a type that can serve as signs, standing in as representations of words whether they are taken simply or in combination.

To complete this system of writing, some have devised <margin>25</margin> certain tools and instruments, or even the forms of natural things, which seemed to more closely resemble the shapes of letters: for example, using a **sphere** for the letter **O**, a **ladder** or a **pair of compasses** for **A**, a **column** for **I**, and something **suspended between two forks** for **M**. <note>This is a classic mnemonic technique where the alphabet is "visualized" as physical objects to help the practitioner "read" their memory palace like a book.</note>

## CHAPTER XII.

->On light as the vehicle of images.<-

Light, according to the opinion of those who contemplate more deeply, is first of all a certain substance; indeed, 
<margin>5</margin> Moses introduced it as the very first substance of those things | which are in nature **23**
when he called it "first-born." There, while distinguishing the <term>species: here, the specific forms or types of created things</term> of creatures (which are understood not as belonging to the category of <term>accidents: non-essential qualities like color or size</term>, but of substance), he accepted it not only as a substance, 
but even as the first substance, from whose existence the other types of substance 
<margin>10</margin> are conceived as if they were accidents. For first, both in that book of Moses and in the *Pymander* of Hermes <note>original: *Mercurii Pymandro*; the *Poimandres* is the first book of the *Corpus Hermeticum*, a collection of Greco-Egyptian wisdom texts that Bruno held in high regard</note>, after the massive shadow and the darkness of privation had been placed below, God said: "Let there be light" <note>original: *fiat lux*</note>.

From there, from the meeting of light and darkness—acting as form and 
<margin>15</margin> matter—a vast number of species emerged, consisting of various things in their composition according to various degrees and measures, in which more light or more shadow is perceived. This light is indeed a substance invisible in itself, diffused through the immense universe, 
<margin>20</margin> and implanted in all its parts; which, through the mixing of darkness and a certain association and composition, passes into <term>sensible: perceptible by the physical senses</term> light. Thus, some people rashly fail to distinguish between the "first-born" light and the sun—between the simple 
substance, that is, and that composite one; between the work, I say, 
<margin>25</margin> of the first and the fourth day <note>In the Book of Genesis, Light is created on the first day, but the Sun and Moon are only created on the fourth day. Bruno uses this to argue that Light is a fundamental spiritual substance, not just a physical phenomenon</note>.

With this light, which is a certain spiritual substance, the soul is endowed, even without the sun shining, or fire, or any external object shaping the power of our senses;

not only our own light, but also the universal light diffusing itself through the immense space. Furthermore, it is very clear that <margin>15</margin> when the mind is at rest from the activity of the external senses—as happens in dreams—the forms of visible things shine forth so brightly that the dreamer sometimes does not think he is dreaming at all. He is shaped by an internal light, perhaps even more <margin>20</margin> truly than by an external one.

which is a certain indivisible substance here, one which conceives the figures and characters of many things, even of great things, all at once. Just as we conceive an entire forest of things in the center of the pupil in a single glance, and we contract and judge the <margin>5</margin> massive size of each thing from an indivisible <term>specillo: literally a "little mirror" or lens; here referring to the focal point of the eye</term>, so too must we judge that internal and, in a sense, more spiritual power of the soul. Thus, it is simultaneously <margin>10</margin> the light, the illuminated object, and the act of the sensible thing and its form. It differs from external sight, which is shaped by an outside light, because the internal spirit is at once both the light itself and the one who sees. This is proportional to how the sun's light is distinguished from the moon's light; for the latter is visible as if <margin>25</margin> <margin>15</margin> from the outside, while the former is visible as if from its own nature. Finally, the sight of the eye differs from the sight of the internal spirit just as a seeing mirror differs from a non-seeing mirror. The latter merely represents things, but the internal mirror is illuminated and shaped by itself; it is simultaneously the light and the mirror, and in it the sensible object and the sensible subject are one. <margin>20</margin> This is a certain world and, in a way, an inexhaustible <note>original: *sinus*; literally a fold in a garment, often used to mean a womb, a harbor, or a deep interior space</note> bosom of forms and species. It contains not only the species of things conceived from the outside according to their actual size and number, but also, by the power of the imagination, it adds size to size and number to number. <margin>25</margin> And again, just as nature composes and grows innumerable species from a few elements, so too by the work of this internal agent, the forms of natural species are not only stored in that most vast bosom, but they can also be multiplied for the production of innumerable images <margin>30</margin> to be conceived in any proportion.

## CHAPTER XIV.

### On the producer of images.

From these things, it is clear that this power is the producer of images, or that through which the soul acts as the producer of images. To <margin>10</margin> this end, let us bring forward the opinion of Synesius the Platonist <note>Synesius of Cyrene (c. 373–414 AD), a philosopher-bishop who wrote "On Dreams," arguing that the imagination is the medium for divine revelation</note>, who discusses the power of the imagination and the "phantastic spirit" <term>phantastic spirit: the subtle, vaporous substance that was thought to bridge the gap between the physical body and the immaterial soul</term> in this way: in the waking state, man is his own teacher, but <margin>26</margin> in sleep God himself makes the dreamer a partaker of Himself |; we adopt this view to preserve the dignity of the life of the imagination. For <margin>15</margin> if to behold God himself through Himself is a blessed gift, then certainly to perceive through the imagination is the function of a more ancient and personal inspection. For this is the "sense of senses," because the phantastic spirit itself is the most common sensory organ <term>sensorium commune: the "common sense," a theoretical faculty where all five external senses are unified into a single experience</term> and the primary "body" of the soul. <margin>20</margin> This spirit remains hidden and acts within, occupying the chief part of the living being and acting, as it were, as its citadel (for nature constructed the whole architecture of the head around it). Hearing and sight, however, are not senses themselves, but rather instruments of sense serving the "common sense." They act like doorkeepers and porters of the living being, <margin>25</margin> indicating to the master the sensible things <term>sensibilia: things that can be perceived by the senses</term> that occur outside (by which the external sensory organs are struck). Meanwhile, the innermost sense is whole in all its parts; for it hears with its whole spirit and sees with its whole spirit, from which it distributes different tasks to different organs, and just as from a center to the circumference...

## CHAPTER XV.
### On the storehouse of species and its gates.

He digests the species <note>original: "species"; here referring to the mental images or forms of things perceived by the senses</note> which he collects, embraces, and composes, in such a way that he might draw out or abstract certain "thinkable" things from <margin>10</margin> them, and brings them into the storehouse of the retentive faculty (unless he himself is that retentive faculty), where he introduces, sends in, inserts, and secures them. The keys, doorkeepers, or gates of this storehouse are the various types of affects <term>affects: the emotions, passions, or states of mind that move the soul</term>, which are defined by the irascible <note>original: "irascibili"; the part of the soul associated with anger, courage, and defense</note> and concupiscible <note>original: "concupiscibili"; the part of the soul associated with desire, appetite, and love</note> powers: <margin>15</margin> love and hate, <margin>27</margin> | fear and hope, joy and sadness, and the various kinds of wonder, which we have explained more extensively in our book *On the Shadows of Ideas* <note>original: "De umbris idearum"; Bruno's 1582 work on memory and Neoplatonism</note>. From this, the reason becomes clear why some things—though meditated upon many times or placed before the eyes of cognition—are kept far from the dwelling of this storehouse <margin>20</margin> or the sacred hall of Mnemosyne <note>Mnemosyne: the Greek goddess of Memory and mother of the Muses</note>, while others slip in and are welcomed through an open gate, as if on a downhill and easy path, even if they are unwanted.

# ON THE COMPOSITION OF IMAGES, I.

...[one] is easily affected <gloss>1 perhaps "affected"</gloss>, when he perceives a visible thing through a reflected and double image. Likewise, direct sight is greatly and most clearly superior to oblique sight; that is, a visual ray cast perpendicularly to the visible object is superior to a visual ray cast non-perpendicularly.
<margin>5</margin>

Similarly, simple sight grasps the truth of each thing through its primary likeness, from which the visible image <note>original: "species visibilis"; the formal likeness or "mask" that travels from the object to the eye</note> travels to the eye in a straight path. Again, direct sight is stronger than oblique; thus, in the act of imagining <note>original: "phantasiandi"; the process of forming mental images in the "phantasia" or imagination</note>, it is worthwhile to practice an intuition of the locations,
<margin>10</margin> the receptacles of images, and the image itself as if from a position directly and diametrically opposite. This is done so that the visible object is grasped by the cognitive faculty <note>original: "potentia cognoscitrice"; the mind's ability to know and process sensory data</note> not obliquely, but directly, and the visible image may proceed, as it were, along its own easy path and be drawn in
<margin>15</margin> by the power of the visual ray.

Furthermore, just as in external vision a certain medium of intervening space is necessary between the sight and the visible thing—since a sensible object placed directly upon any sense is not perceived, and one too remote is thinned out <margin>29</margin> and
<margin>20</margin> extinguished by the long distance—so too should the "imaginable" image <note>original: "phantasiabilis species"; a mental form available to the imagination</note> be understood as neither set too far away from the eye of the imagination nor moved too close; for it is necessary that the visible thing be not touching or immediate to the sight.

The objects that move the sight—both internal and
<margin>25</margin> external, whether individually or with many or all of them concurring together—are, first of all, light (which is visible in itself and through which other things become visible); then colors, which are the proper objects of sight; after these, magnitude or multitude, figure, and motion, which are the
<margin>30</margin> common sensibles <term>common sensibles: qualities like size, shape, or motion that can be perceived by more than one sense (e.g., both sight and touch)</term>, and from which the likeness of things...

### CHAPTER I.

<margin>5</margin>As has been shown in the preceding sections, the images and forms <note>original: "species"; in Bruno’s thought, these are the mental likenesses or "intentions" that represent objects in the mind</note> which are the subject of our present focus and study, consist of and are found entirely within matter, which they give form to. Because anything forged from these twin principles <note>form and matter</note> can be neither understood nor imagined without a
<margin>10</margin>place. Therefore, just as in the order of establishing things (whether they have a beginning or not), there must first be a certain space and a receptacle <note>original: "receptaculum"; a container or vessel</note> in which they may be received and held; thereafter, there must be a certain boundary, limit, and end for each thing, by which one may be distinguished from another and
<margin>15</margin>exist in divided regions. Soon, there must also be a difference of figures, through which variety of appearance nature triumphs and rejoices, bringing all things to pass as if unfolding shapes from the center of matter, and then coloring them as if upon its shaped surface. In this universal consideration, as we proceed in a definite and certain order,
<margin>20</margin>it will first be necessary to mention the places of these forms.
