JORDANUS BRUNUS

<margin>31</margin> is distinguished, so in our current proposition, proceeding from a certain order—as if from nature designating and art explaining things discovered and investigated—we first recognize a certain one, immense and unconditioned <note>original: "interminatum"; referring to Bruno’s belief in an infinite universe without a physical outer boundary</note> object, then space and a receptacle <note>original: "receptaculum"; a container or vessel for matter</note>, then the body within that receptacle and space, then the multitude of species <note>original: "specierum"; here meaning both physical forms and the mental images that represent them</note> coalescing from such matter. 
Furthermore, in the infinite, out of things innumerable, we recognize one object of our finite sensory power: the space we call the sky. The common people apprehend this as something bounded by the rotation of the daily motion and the appearance of the visible 
<margin>10</margin> stars; we leave to them those distinctions of the heavens and their numbers, and the distribution of each into various spheres, as well as the scale and boundaries of the elemental region <note>Bruno is rejecting the traditional medieval view of the universe as a "ladder" of elements (earth, water, air, fire) contained within solid celestial spheres</note>, and the universal parts of this globe—made of earth and water as the two predominating elements—shaped in such a great composition. We descend to the particular and common 
<margin>15</margin> places in which the operation of the external sense, as the handmaid of the internal sense, assists their cooperation. To this end, a distinction of thirty common places <note>original: "triginta communium locorum"; these are the "memory rooms" or mental structures Bruno uses to organize knowledge</note> must come to our aid, lest we be troubled by their deficiency or their multiplication—as if 
<margin>20</margin> we were limping on too few legs or preoccupied by more than is proper.

## CHAPTER V. <margin>34</margin>

->The division of places, whose common areas adopt a five-fold relationship according to the eastern, western, southern, northern, and central entrances.<-

Here, by **common places** <term>loca communia; the general rooms or "containers" in a memory palace</term>, we mean a single coordination of particular places—for example, a single temple, the courtyard of a temple, a single cloister, or the interior of a single basilica or large dining room. You should understand this space as being divided into the aforementioned angles, the spaces between those angles, and the various distinctions within those spaces. 

By **substantive particular places** <term>loca particularia substantiva; the fixed architectural points of the room</term>, we mean the angle itself, the right or left side of that angle, the middle of the side-space, or any other specific point. These are regarded as the parts, joints, or members of a "common place." 

By an **adjective place** <term>locus adiectivus; the movable "content" placed within the architectural "substance"</term>, we mean something—either animate or inanimate—which, depending on the occasion, behaves in different ways, is moved, or acts as a mover. This is done so that it may give life to the image or form and make it a living, growing thing <note>Bruno views memory images not as static pictures, but as "vital" agents that help the mind "see" the information.</note>. Now it remains for us to assign adjective places of this kind to the centers and angles of each hall.

<margin>20</margin> ## CHAPTER VI. <margin>35</margin>

->You will vary the "adjective places" of the Hall of the Altar with five forms, based on the five-fold position of the bystander.<-

## CHAPTER VII.

### Concerning the possible addition for the completion of the thirty.

Let the figure of the location be arranged so that its members may be sufficient for equality and conformity with those things which are further applied according to our method (for we observe the <term>trigenary</term> <note>original: *trigenarium*; a system based on the number thirty, which Bruno uses to organize his memory "atria" and "wheels."</note> number in all things). Thus, in the proposed <term>atrium</term> <note>original: *atrio*; a memory chamber or "hall" within a mental palace.</note>, let a double diagonal be drawn from each corner to its opposite. In the middle of the intervals—which are equally distant from the center and the four corners—let four seats and their additions be understood; however, in the center, assign a right-hand seat and a left-hand seat to the two additions.

<image-desc>A rectangular geometric diagram defined by solid lines. At each of the four corners is a five-pointed star. In the center of each side of the rectangle (top, bottom, left, and right), there is a cluster of three five-pointed stars. Within the interior of the rectangle, four stars are arranged in a diamond pattern surrounding the center. At the absolute center point of the diagram, two stars are positioned horizontally side-by-side.</image-desc>

<margin>62</margin>
The rest of the elements are to be understood as they appear in the designation and order of the preceding atrium.

¶ Here you should also bear in mind that certain names, which are occasionally repeated, do not carry the same significance of figures or images... <note>The text here breaks off, suggesting that the same word or name might represent different mnemonic triggers depending on the specific "room" or "seat" in which it is placed.</note>

## CHAPTER VIII.
### On the order of the species.

Once the <term>common places</term> <note>original: *loca communia*; the standard, fixed locations in a memory palace.</note> have been defined for you, as well as the particular receptacles—both those that are <term>substantive</term> and those that are <term>adjective</term> <note>Bruno distinguishes between "substantive" images (the main subject or base) and "adjective" images (attributes or modifiers added to the base).</note>—a series of efficient forms may be <margin>10</margin> established in the same or in another order. Some of these are <term>adjacent</term>, some are <term>adcinent</term>, and others are <term>concinent</term> <note>Bruno uses musical metaphors here: *adcinent* (singing to/accompanying) and *concinent* (singing together/harmonizing). These refer to how different phonetic or symbolic components of an image combine.</note>. For the <term>adcinents</term>, twelve <term>cubicles</term> <note>original: *cubilia*; literally "couches" or "beds," referring to smaller stations within a memory room.</note> are sufficient; for the <term>concinents</term>, however, thirty atria are required.

The cubicles of the <term>adcinents</term>—specifically where a sounding <note>A vowel.</note> precedes a consonant—are these: 1. The Bacchante, 2. The Guard, 3. The Woodcutter, 4. The Smith, 5. ## CHAPTER X.

-> Thirty chambers for the harmonious consonants. <-

The chambers of the harmonious consonants <note>original: *Concinentium atria*; in the Art of Memory, an *atrium* is a mental room or "station" where information is stored. "Harmonious consonants" refers to consonants that "sound together" with vowels.</note> (specifically where a consonant precedes a vowel <note>original: *sonantem*; literally "a sounding thing," here referring to the vowel that follows the consonant</note>) are organized in this order: the center of the chamber
<margin>5</margin> retains its own form, from which the naming and definition of the chamber are derived.
The four corners represent the four sounding elements: 1. of the East,
2. of the West, 3. of the South, 4. of the North; the center
indeed represents the fifth <note>This refers to the "Quintessence" or the central point that unites the four physical elements/directions.</note>. Furthermore, a triangular space should be designated both around the center and around the
corners, where the corner
<margin>10</margin> further from the center is called the "upper," while of the two closer corners, one is considered the "right" and the other the "left."
One of these triangles should be understood as enclosing the other, which is placed within it at an equal distance, so that both the seats <note>original: *sedes*; the specific spots within the memory palace where an image is "seated."</note> and the images may be
doubled.

<margin>15</margin> -> CATALOG OF CUBICLES. <note>original: *CATALOGVS CVBILIVM*; a "cubicle" or "bed" is a sub-division within the memory chamber for a specific letter or sound cluster.</note> <-

| B. BL (or PL). BR. | M. |

<term>sonantia</term>: Sounding things; refers to vowels which give "voice" to the consonants.

### FIGURE OF THE LESSER CHAMBERS,

->*where [in] A is the triangle of the earth, E is the triangle of the east, I is the triangle of the south, O of the west, V of the north.*<-

<image-desc>A complex geometric diagram composed of nested circles, squares, and triangles. In the very center is a small triangle containing the letter 'A', surrounded by the letters M, N, R, L, S, and T. This central element is enclosed by a circle, which is further contained within a square. From the four sides of this square, large triangles project outwards, their tips touching a larger outer circle. These outer triangles are labeled with letters: the left triangle contains 'R L V M', the right triangle contains 'I L R N', and the top and bottom triangles contain 'R' at their apexes with other letters distributed within. Numerous smaller instances of the letters R, L, S, T, M, and N are placed at the vertices and midpoints of the various intersecting shapes.</image-desc>

<margin>70</margin>
According to this form, the particular chambers <note>original: *cubilia*; literally 'beds' or 'couches,' used here as technical terminology for the smaller subdivisions of the memory palace</note> are fashioned: four squares in the corners and a fifth, doubled one in the center.

## CHAPTER XI.

->Images visible in the center of the lesser chambers.<-

For not only this kind of use, but for manifold use and
<margin>15</margin> contemplation, thirty images have been established and defined, so that in the center there is:
I. In the atrium <note>A hall or chamber in the memory palace</note> of **Goodness**: a priest dressed in linen garments, censing the altar with a thurible <note>a vessel for burning incense</note>.
II. In the atrium of **Blasphemy** (near the atrium of Pleasure): in the
<margin>20</margin> center, a priest in red garments sprinkling the altar with the blood of a victim.
III. In the atrium of the **Prize**: a goal-post <note>original: *meta*; the conical turning-post used in Roman chariot races to mark the end of a circuit</note> and above it a collar and a white cloak with a gilded fringe.
IV. In the atrium of the **Cause**: a boy embracing a girl who is
<margin>24</margin> dark-skinned and beautiful <note>original: *nigram et formosam*; this is a classical allusion to the Song of Solomon</note>.
V. In the atrium of **Clarity** (near the atrium of Glory): a matron
<margin>26</margin> holding water in her right hand and a mirror in her left <gloss>having</gloss>.

# CHAPTER XII.

## Explanation of sensible images, primarily those arriving by the action of others.

In addition to the locations of the images mentioned above, you have again:
¶ First, in the center, **one who abstracts or sets free** <note>original: *abstrahentem seu absolventem*</note>; to the 
<margin>5</margin> East, a **drunkard**; to the West, an **ibis**; to the South, an **obstacle**; <margin>73</margin> to the North, a **sign of ubiquity** <note>a symbol representing the state of being everywhere at once</note>.
¶ Second, in another atrium: in the center, an **accuser**; to the East, a **preacher** <note>original: *ecclesiastem*; refers to a public speaker or the biblical author of Ecclesiastes</note>; to the West, an **image of Icarus** <note>the mythological figure who flew too close to the sun</note>; to the South, a **slayer**; to the North, a **pitcher-bearer**.
<margin>10</margin> ¶ III. In the center, an **opponent**; to the East, a **glutton**; to the West, an **idolater**; to the South, an **image of one who hates**; to the North, **something wet**.
¶ IV. In the center, **one who is afflicted**; to the East, **one who effects** <note>one who brings something about or produces an action</note>; to the West, a **void**; to the South, **one who is dutiful** <note>original: *officiosum*; one who performs their duty or service</note>.
<margin>15</margin> ¶ V. In the center, a **nourisher**, or a **binder**, or an **image of height**; to the East, **one who elevates**, or **one who slips away**, or an **almsgiver**; to the West, an **illuminator**; to the South, a **potter** <note>original: *ollarium*; one who works with jars or pots</note> or **one who smells**; to the North, an **avenger**, or an **avenger** <note>The original text repeats *ultorem*; the editor suggests this might have been *ulteriorem*, meaning "one who is further off"</note>, or a **final thing**.
<margin>20</margin> ¶ VI. In the center, **one who embraces**, or an **image of amplitude** <note>broadness or vastness</note>; to the East, an **image of eminence** or **one who sends forth**; to the West, **one who fills**; to the South, **one who prophesies** or **one who omits**; to the North, **one who humbles**.
¶ VII. In the center, a **herald**; to the East, **one who enumerates**;
<margin>25</margin> to the West, **one who inserts**; to the South, **one who burdens**; to the North, **one who unites** or **one who anoints**.

# CHAPTER XIII.

<margin>20</margin>->Secondly, regarding other harmonious arrangements.<-

In the first of the smaller chambers, where the image of **Goodness** <note>original: *Bonitatis*</note> represents things perceived by the senses, again in the triangle of the center imagine a **baptizer** or a **porter** <note>original: *baiulantem*; one who carries a heavy burden</note> with six assistants in the corners cooperating in their proper order, 
<margin>25</margin>according to the six signs of the porters who behave in different ways; to the east, **one blessing** or a **warrior**, whom six sensory forms or circumstances of blessing surround in the corners of the triangles, whether in their tools, their actions, or both; to the west, a **drinker** or a **bookseller** <note>original: *bibliopolam*</note> with various actions and 
<margin>30</margin>the tools of his trade; to the south, a **cattle-dealer**, a **shepherd**, or an **ox-driver**.

Here, Bruno moves from the mineral kingdom into the animal kingdom with the "Field of Juno and Diana." In Bruno's system, Juno often represents the air and the richness of the physical world, while Diana represents the moon and the wilder aspects of nature. This table serves as a memory grid where animals—ranging from the common to the mythological—are used as "images" to store and retrieve complex philosophical concepts.</meta>

<meta>This page continues Bruno's mnemonic system of "Fields." While the previous page (Field 82) focused on the "Field of Juno and Diana," categorizing animals of the wild and the air, this page (Field 83) introduces the "Field of the Lares." In Roman religion, the Lares were deities who protected the household and the cultivated land. Consequently, this grid organizes concepts related to human industry, agriculture, craftsmanship, and the domestic economy—the foundational elements of a settled civilization.</meta>

## CHAPTER XIV.

### On the securing of images through a chain.

To conveniently retain those images of the "adjective places," <note>original: *adiectivorum locorum*; Bruno uses "adjectives" to describe secondary or auxiliary images that are attached to a primary memory "place" to increase storage capacity.</note> one must provide for them through the power of concatenation. <note>The "chaining" or linking method of memory.</note> After <margin>5</margin> the altar itself, with its additions, is placed in the middle of the hall of the altar: in the eastern corner, a plow is suspended by a chain, <note>original: *catena*</note> with a water vessel on the other side; in the western corner, a tree rises from a terrestrial globe, upon which a banquet is hung; in the southern corner, there is an anchor upon a chariot <margin>10</margin> that has a palm branch in its right [side]; in the northern corner, in a prison upon a chair, is a jar; <note>original: *cadus*; a large vessel for wine or oil.</note> to the east, a breastplate <note>original: *thorax*</note> is washed by an amphora; to the west, a sword is tempered by fire in a furnace; to the south, in a stable, there are steaming crops; to the north, in the middle of a skiff, is a chest <note>original: *scrinium*; a case for books or papers.</note> which serves as the foundation of a throne; understand that it must be done <margin>15</margin> in this way for the remaining items.
¶ You will be able to profitably and easily increase the number of such additions up to your established limit; for if you add one to each term, these halls will be able to serve you no less than the fields, since thirty-two additions will abound for you around the altar. From this, you may hold not only <margin>20</margin> thirty images of the first compositions around a single [location], but also—by virtue of position and order—very suitable receptacles will be laid out for the forms of other presentable things.

## CHAPTER XV.

### On the conditions of the parts to be observed in houses, courtyards, and fields.

The conditions of the receptacles <note>The mental "places" or "slots" where memory images are stored.</note> according to common practice and observed by all in the Temple of Mnemosyne <note>The Greek goddess of memory and mother of the Muses; Bruno uses her temple as a metaphor for the system of memory.</note>, we have explained as follows:
<margin>5</margin> The internal sensory faculty <note>The imagination or "inner sense" that processes images from the physical eyes.</note> holds the likenesses of these things grasped within its breast—those which sight has drawn away from the things themselves with a clearly stable form.
¶ Locations of vast embrace are never fit for small objects, nor do those that are too small receive larger ones. <note>Bruno stresses that the mental "room" must be proportional to the image placed inside it.</note>
<margin>10</margin> A figure vanishes when dispersed in a seat that is too wide; and if the body is tiny, it escapes the scrutiny of the eyes.
Let them [the places] be such that they might hold a man who, brandishing a drawn sword, touches nothing through the width and height. <note>This is a classic rule from the ancient Roman text *Ad Herennium*: a memory place should be roughly the size of a human being with arms extended to ensure it is neither too cramped nor too cavernous.</note>
¶ The wise man rejects what is inaccessible and removed from the hands of
<margin>15</margin> one walking about; let not the heights of a roof receive you, nor the peaks of a tower placed before you, nor a window standing far off, nor a smoking chimney in the distance. <note>Images placed too high or too far away in the mind's eye are difficult to "see" and retrieve.</note>
¶ Despise that which is wooded and covered in varied darkness, consisting of many parts, where things running together entangle themselves in a varied
<margin>20</margin> sight; for who plows a black field and wishes to write a script upon it? <note>original: *exarat*; literally "to plow up." Bruno compares a cluttered or dark mental space to trying to write on a field that has already been turned over and blackened.</note>
¶ In the same way, flee dark places; for just as they cause the eyes of the external senses to be twisted by an uncertain appearance, think that this is much more possible here [in the mind], where the impressions remain pressed by a faint shadow.
<margin>25</margin> ¶ Nor will places turned toward the sun with too much light be effective; for indeed, just as a form absorbed in a vast depth will vanish, so does excessive brightness hurt the eyes. <margin>93</margin>

<summary>In this chapter, Bruno outlines the ideal "lighting" and "spatial" requirements for mental memory places, advising that they should be human-sized, moderately lit, and free from clutter or extreme distances. He emphasizes that the mind's eye requires the same clarity and proportion as physical sight to effectively store and retrieve information.</summary>

This composition is achieved in three ways: first, by remaining within a single sequence; second, by wandering through different sequences of the same kind; or third, by taking the most suitable parts of forms from their own specific places. The matter itself is better introduced through actual practice than through other theoretical instructions.
<margin>5</margin> 

->First example of composition.<-

Regarding the first method (namely, staying within a single sequence), we construct the image for **Art** <note>original: *Artem*. Bruno is describing how to build a complex mental image to represent a specific word or concept.</note> sometimes from the parts of an altar: such as when a torso—which coalesces in a consuming fire—is washed in a basin by water flowing out from a prison, specifically coming from the right side of the eastern corner, the right of the northern corner, <margin>10</margin> the right of the east from the east, and the left of the west. Sometimes we build it from parts of the prison, where there will be a man with snared hands <note>The Latin *manus* (hands) is corrected in some versions to *manes* (shades/ghosts), suggesting a "snared ghost."</note> holding a psalter to his right, and to his left a parrot whose beak is gouging out an old woman's eye. Or sometimes we build it from parts of the crown, as when a camel emerges carrying treasure toward a pool from the underworld, and within the underworld <margin>15</margin> toward the baths. A similar logic applies to all other images.

->Second example of composition.<-

Regarding the second method—namely, wandering through different sequences of the same kind—such as moving from the altar to the basilica, or the fountain, or the mirror, or by proceeding from any of these and others to yet more to take them into the composition. Here, <margin>20</margin> either a vowel <term>original: *sonans*. Or, a consonant precedes a vowel; in that case, the composition is either simple—as when a figure consists of twin elements <margin>25</margin> —and thus the image of the atrium alone will suffice, along with five...

->The third example of composition.<-

Regarding the third method—namely, by wandering through various orders of different kinds—you have 12 chambers of "ac-sounding" <note>original: *accinentium*. In Bruno's mnemonic system, these are specific phonetic combinations where one sound "sings alongside" another.</note> elements, in

<margin>10</margin> corner of the tempering one, with the addition of that which is in the left corner of the interior triangle.
There is also a more universal method by which the species <note>original: *species*. <margin>15</margin> cond with an agent, the third with an action, the fourth with a specific form [species], the fifth with a cooperator or assistant, the sixth with the assistant's action, and the seventh with the specific form [species] of that action. Two, three, or all of these parts [members] may be used according to the requirements of the subject.

### On the fifth complement of forms. <note>original: *species*. In Bruno's system, "species" or forms are the mental archetypes or images used to represent information.</note>

¶ Finally, once you have the center of the chamber [atrium] <term>atrium: a "room" or "hall" within the mental memory palace</term> formed
<margin>5</margin>with its corners and the distinctions of its sides standing by through their respective side-points—namely to the right and to the left—there is a place for concatenation <note>original: *concatenatio*. This refers to "chaining" or linking images together in a sequence.</note>, so that one may look upon the images of all things in their proper orders. For all things are reduced back to "heads" <note>original: *capita*. Bruno uses a body metaphor: a main concept is the "head," while details are the "limbs."</note> placed within the 
<margin>10</margin>previously established chambers; subsequently, the "bodies" and the different "members" <note>original: *membra*. These represent the sub-points or narrative details following a main topic.</note> belonging to those same heads are opened up under different conditions and additions. We have explained the form of this concatenation in the book *On the Thirty Seals*. <note>A reference to Bruno's 1583 work, *Explicatio triginta sigillorum*, which details his mnemonic techniques.</note> 
And it will appear quite convenient if, in the unfolding of a single fable,
<margin>15</margin>or a history, or a monster, or a building—where the distinct actions and figures have been marked and ordered by the signs of the elements—we apply the strength and stability of concatenation. But this requires explanation, namely [thinking of it] as if in a forest 
<margin>20</margin>spreading out from a single tree in the middle.

## CHAPTER XIX.

It remains for us to describe the form of composition. Let each individual image contain and definitely represent three things: I. The **AGENT**, II. The **INSTRUMENT** (either attached to the agent or standing nearby), III. The **OPERATION**, so that in this way, the agent represents the same thing as their tools and action. <note>This is a foundational principle of Bruno's "Memory Palace" technique: creating a vivid, active scene to represent data.</note>

## CHAPTER XX.

->The Platonic view on the dual sense as the shaper of the intellect and harmony.<-

<margin>5</margin> It is generally from hearing and sight together that we receive the greatest distinction of species <note>original: *specierum*. In Bruno’s philosophy, these are the mental forms or "intentions" that represent external reality in the mind.</note>. <margin>102</margin> Through the work of the external senses and the internal imagination—involving both passive impressions and active processing—visible and audible objects are to be contemplated by the soul. From one perspective, this leads toward the likeness of divine harmony; from another, toward the image of the beauty of the gods. <margin>10</margin> These are to be looked upon as if in a certain shadow or mirror, as the soul progresses... <note>Bruno is suggesting that sensory data (sight and sound) are not just physical experiences, but reflections of a higher, divine order that the "art of memory" helps us organize.</note>

<summary>This page concludes a mnemonic coding table and begins a philosophical exploration of how sight and hearing serve as the primary gateways for the intellect to grasp divine harmony. Bruno argues that mental images act as "mirrors" or "shadows" of a higher reality.</summary>

...move and lead us. By these two senses <note>Sight and hearing.</note> we capture those species <note>original: *species*. In Bruno’s thought, these are the mental forms or "intentions" that represent external reality in the mind.</note> through which we are affected by alienation and frenzy <note>original: *furore*. This refers to the "divine madness" or inspired states described by Plato, which lift the soul toward higher truths.</note>. By means of this frenzy, we may fly—and not in error—toward conceiving the species of the intelligible world. Through the ears, a sense deeper within us is 
<margin>5</margin>excited to apprehend divine music with a sharper effort and power. Indeed, compelled by the effective light of truth, we understand music as threefold, according to the order of things: the first and primary music is in the Mind of God; the second is in the order and movement of things; the third is in that 
<margin>10</margin>formation which our soul drinks in from those objects. This occurs by virtue of that harmony which the soul previously enjoyed and possessed before it was enclosed in the chains of the body, according to the teaching of the Pythagoreans and Platonists. Hence, light and common musicians dwell upon the sounds of 
<margin>15</margin>living and instrumental voices; whereas serious musicians, with a firmer judgment and the flow of inward reason, are famously inspired by a certain divine breath <note>original: *afflatu*.</note> and receive in their minds the infused food of heavenly ambrosia. For the latter, the harmony of things is better instilled through the eyes; for the former, indeed, it is introduced through the ears by a lighter fate. Elsewhere 
<margin>20</margin>I have spoken of a certain marvelous kinship that exists between true poets—who belong to the same category as musicians—true painters, and true philosophers. Since true philosophy is music, or rather poetry and painting; true painting is both music and philosophy; and true poetry or music is a certain divine 
<margin>25</margin>wisdom <note>original: *sophia*.</note> and painting.
* Elsewhere it was said that a certain painter <note>Bruno likely refers to the "internal painter," or the faculty of the human mind that creates images.</note> is the shaper of infinite images, constructing them through the power of fantasy <term>fantasy: *phantastica potentia*. In Renaissance psychology, this is the faculty that combines sensory images into new and complex mental forms.</term> <margin>103</margin> by combining what is seen and heard in manifold ways. Indeed, the fantasy that is regulated by the governance of reason is easily recognized; for its expression on the 
<margin>30</margin>surface of the senses perpetually demonstrates the order and more fitting arrangement of the things of the world with their members...

connection. But we also taught, in the explanation of the *Thirty Seals* <note>original: *Triginta sigillorum*. This refers to Bruno’s 1583 work, *Explicatio triginta sigillorum*, which introduced his mnemonic system where "seals" act as cognitive tools to organize knowledge.</note>, an art that makes all things from all things; keeping in mind that even without formal art, cleverer minds know how to twist empty words toward organized meanings. <margin>5</margin> observe a confused seed-bed of words falling from the mouths of fanatics and adapt them to current successes and false histories. In this way, the fanatics are regarded as prophets, while the observers are held to be the "interpreters" of those prophets. Thus Cerinthus <note>original: *Cherinthus*. A 1st-century Gnostic teacher often portrayed by early Church historians as a deceptive heretic.</note> promoted a young woman he had disgraced as a Sibyl <note>A legendary prophetess of the ancient world.</note>; indeed, he pushed her to such 
<margin>10</margin> audacity that she would babble whatever came into her mouth before the people, not only without trembling, but even with a certain emphatic gravity. **"JUST SPEAK,"** (he said) **"AND YOU WILL PROPHESY."** As soon as she spoke, he would take up her words with a wrinkled brow, as if astonished, and with a raised eyebrow he would exclaim: 
<margin>15</margin> "O great oracle! O marvelous mystery <note>original: *mysterium*. The OCR *nysterium* is a typo.</note> of the divine voice!" Immediately after, that same shape-shifting master-swindler <note>original: *archisycophanta*.</note> would adapt everything to current events and the customs of the people. Nothing was more calculated to let him triumph longer—mocking the people for his own gain—among the other sects of bloodsuckers. 
<margin>20</margin> This kind of fashioning is artificially sophisticated <note>In the sense of "sophistry"—clever but fallacious reasoning.</note>, but this sort of currency is not spent in the kingdom of philosophy. Yet undisciplined minds will attribute the same deception to the images of wisdom and truly divine oracles, in cases where the eyes of owls cannot endure the light of the sun <note>A classic philosophical metaphor: just as an owl is blinded by daylight, the unrefined human intellect is often blinded by the highest truths.</note>. And although we do not write in such a way that 
<margin>25</margin> we wish to be—or even could be—understood by everyone in every detail, nonetheless there is no one whom we cannot greatly help or please in some measure (if they approach with attentive faith and faithful attention), according to the capacity of whatever discipline they are practiced in.

### Images of Saturn.

First, there arises one who is winged and helmeted, and his helmet is covered with a dark veil, around which a serpent holds its tail in its mouth <note>The Ouroboros, a symbol of eternity and the cyclical nature of time, often associated with Saturn/Cronus</note>; he is

Many wax candles are lit around him.

¶ Care, I believe, is ever-diligent, goading the heart; 
<margin>5</margin> She is watchful, anxious, bitter, restless, wretched, standing guard, 
Goading the mind with a biting and sharp rigor, 
Torturing envious breasts with a silent heat, 
Just as a fire applied makes wax melt away, 
So these hearts melt, laid open by continuous cares. 
<margin>10</margin> Striking herself, she vexes herself, and she breaks 
The times of rest; she refuses the counsel of sleep and peace. 
She burns while acting, and glows the more as she

She neglects countless others; yet she wants everything, 
<margin>15</margin> Nor does she withdraw her mind from that which she has separated by her action.

### **The Image of Fear.**

¶ Then a shadow, having swift wings upon its feet, with a feminine face, almost blind, thunderstruck, and speechless, drawing itself **113** <note>This bold number likely refers to a specific image or theorem in Bruno's mnemonic system.</note> into a narrow space, turning itself rapidly here and there;
<margin>5</margin> from her mouth issued a cold cloud covering the body of the wretched girl. Dripping with cold sweat, as if her use of reason had been stripped away, she was disturbed; with a pale face, she wove her fingers into her stiffened hair. Standing by her were Weakening, Deception, Trembling, Horror, Preoccupation, Frost, and many others from the court of Care. 
<margin>10</margin> To these were added doubtful Harshness, foul Stupidity, complicit Silence, anxious Suspense, Shaking of the breast, Numbness of the heart, Palpitation of the vitals, and the sick Disturbance of the whole body.

   I would believe this to be trembling and wavering Fear,
   Fearing with a suspended expression and thunderstruck eyes;
<margin>15</margin> Carrying the traces of his steps with suspended feet,
   Unhappy <note>original: "Infelix"; the variant "Infaelix" is noted at the bottom of the original page</note> and sparing of himself, he flees all things, nor does he
   Trust himself to himself, nor does he cling safely to others.
   He speaks broken words, and hides sighs in the depths of his
   Breast.
<margin>20</margin> Anxious and at the same time sluggish, he clings to himself in agitation;
   While he doubts, he makes future dangers certain and confirms them.
   Wavering now to this side and now to that, he finally plunges 
   Into the worse part, since Fear is a bad prophet <note>original: "augur"; a Roman religious official who observed natural signs to predict the future</note>
   And a bad interpreter of things, insanely senseless,
<margin>25</margin> Because the fates help the bold and repel the timid.
   Wavering, looking at all things around himself so astonishedly that
   While he sees all things equally, he is blind to all things;
   Lest he should sometimes know where he, a stranger, might take himself.

->The Image of Doubt.<-

<margin>5</margin> ¶ In the same sequence of images <note>Bruno is describing a "memory theater" where abstract concepts are visualized as specific figures to help the student remember them.</note> is the figure of a man bound by his right arm and leg to one wheel, and by his left leg and arm to <margin>115</margin> another wheel; suspended in the air, he was tortured as he leaned now more toward one side and now more toward the other.

<margin>15</margin> He flies toward his goal and then grows numb as the strength of his spirit is withdrawn;

Fearfully snatching away his strength, joined now here, then there;

<margin>25</margin> He moves his unwilling steps, and yet desires to move his limbs

While he fears things to be feared, he thinks nothing is to be feared.
He rebukes his doubting self from this side and reproaches himself, like one who
<margin>30</margin> Limps toward one side and is inclined toward both.

### The Image of Sadness.

<margin>15</margin> ¶ Out of a whirlwind of black and ashy darkness comes a ghost <note>original: "spectrum"</note> wrapped in a dusky garment, hiding its lowered face beneath the black rust of its brow. It is torn and ragged, goading thin and weary horses that pull its chariot, proceeding very slowly through a willow-filled swamp that lies sluggish with foul mud.
¶ This is the ghost of Sadness, which cooks the sick soul, 
Burning the anxious heart with an eternal flame. 
Excruciating the worried mind and disturbing its rest, 
<margin>20</margin> In a dark hour it afflicts the soul with horrific spirits <note>original: "Laemuribus," referring to the *Lemures*, the restless or malevolent ghosts of the dead in Roman mythology.</note>; 
Even while awake, its dreams are such 
That it seeks in vain for the forgetfulness found in the waters of Lethe <note>The river of forgetfulness in the underworld.</note>. 
The limbs waste away so poorly from constant pain, 
<margin>24</margin> And anxious care thrives, so poorly distressing the breast. 
<margin>25</margin> While the dead ash <note>original: "cassa favilla"</note> drinks up the vital vapors with its light, 
The power of the natural breath is worn down within, 
And the gliding evil hastens the time of one’s passing.

<margin>5</margin> It throws itself into filth, and hope, now despaired of, gives way to pain; grief seeks out grief as its only solace.
<margin>117</margin> The dark figure carries a chest pierced by a hundred arrows. To relieve the evil by weeping is its only granted pleasure. Just as a vine sends drops from its cut trunk, 
<margin>10</margin> so the substance flowing out to avenge its own wound is gradually consumed through tears in a downward motion. At last, having grown accustomed to evils, it avoids friendly comforts, and turns its eyes away from the hated light of day; it loves being an exile, deserted; it hates joy and flees it as if fleeing an enemy race.

->The Image of Famine.<-

Loathsome even to itself, its Cyclopean <note>meaning monstrous or insatiable, like the one-eyed giants of myth</note> rage slowly eats away its own limbs. 
<margin>20</margin> Standing by as its companions are Savagery, Rage, Insanity, Anger, Cruelty, Fury, Sloth, Fasting, Thinness, Squalor, and a Deformity that exasperates and defiles <note>The original OCR reads "fędansque," a common Latin contraction for "foedansque."</note>; and many of those things which are numbered in the same field and the Court of Saturn <note>In Renaissance astrology, the "Court of Saturn" refers to the planet Saturn's influence, which was associated with cold, hunger, poverty, and destruction.</note>. Along with her and others runs Disease—

She runs with the counsel of deaf fury,
And unbridled, she tears apart everything in her way with a lightning-quick mouth.
Stirred up, she runs more roar-filled with a blazing heat,
<margin>15</margin> And she strengthens the hands of the weak with steady might,
And by rapid courage makes the soft ones fierce;
She makes unbridled the one who before was of a relaxed mind.
The cold and sluggish person is inflamed by her fire;
By this, the timid one—stirred by a fury's sting <term>oestro</term> <note>original: "oestro"; literally a gadfly, but used here to mean a stinging, frantic impulse or divine madness</note> among the strong—
<margin>20</margin> Though not daring, carries out arduous monstrosities with soft goads.
The face swells, the veins turn black with foul blood,
And bloody eyes scatter sparks with striking rays of fire;
She grinds her teeth, and stains her mouth with foam;
A burning heart protects the soaked flames.
<margin>25</margin> She denies rest to weary limbs, and for the sake of harming
She seizes whatever weapons grief suggests to her, and
Whatever occurs to her she destines for the duties of a weapon to her ill-sane self;
She truly turns everything into a javelin or a sword,
And her fierce madness <note>original: "rabies"</note> makes all things fly [as missiles].
<margin>30</margin> The Fury <note>original: "Erinnys"; one of the Furies of Greek myth who punish crimes and incite vengeance</note> makes her boil with a torch placed beneath her.

->Statue of Fortune, of the Lots, and of Plutus.<-

## CHAPTER XII.

### Images of the Moon.

The first image of the Moon follows: a most beautiful maiden sitting in a chariot made of ebony, covered for the most part with silver plates; <margin>5</margin> it is drawn by a black bullock together with a white heifer. She herself is dressed sometimes in white, <margin>152</margin> sometimes in black, and sometimes in garments composed of both white and black. She has horns on her forehead; as they wax <note>increase</note>, she puts on black clothing, and as they wane <note>decrease</note>, she takes up white garments.

<margin>10</margin> ¶ The second image: a handsome shepherd <note>Likely Endymion, the mortal lover of the Moon goddess</note> reclining under a beech tree, to whom, as he calls upon her, a naked and white maiden descends, who is an archer and horned.

¶ The third: a half-goat man <note>original: "semicaper"; referring to Pan, who in myth seduced the Moon by offering her choice wool</note> (followed by a ram) approaches, bringing the Goddess the whitest wool.

<margin>15</margin> ¶ The fourth: a maiden in the habit of a huntress acting as a midwife <note>The goddess Diana/Artemis was traditionally invoked during childbirth</note>, accompanied by other maiden attendants, several of whom, unbinding their belts <note>original: "zonam discinctae"; a ritual gesture to symbolize a loosened womb</note>, throw them before her feet.

¶ The fifth: a naked maiden, preceded by a leopard and a lion.

<margin>20</margin> ¶ The sixth, an unusual one: a man crowned with a golden diadem riding a doe, dressed in a green garment variegated with silver ornaments. A boy precedes him, walking between twin geese, holding an arrow in his right hand, while his left is extended empty before his chest. <margin>25</margin> A woman follows him, covered in a white linen cloth <note>original: "sindone"</note> speckled with golden drops. All around is a dripping cloud, beneath which is a moist and thick court, as if from the mouth of fat, shaven, or bald men [dripping] with... <note>The text cuts off mid-word at "san-", likely "sanies" or "sanguine", meaning blood or discharge</note>

## CHAPTER XIII.
### The Images of Venus.

Let us conclude the taste <note>or "pleasure"</note> which is gathered from the contemplation of the seven courts with the contemplation of a divine image. The first image of **Venus** is a young girl emerging from the sea foam, who, upon coming into <margin>10</margin> dry land, wipes away the moisture of the sea with her palms.
¶ Second, the **Hours** <note>original: "Horae"; the goddesses of the seasons and natural order</note> cover that naked girl with garments and crown her head with blooming flowers.
¶ Third, a girl walking, in whose footsteps lilies, roses, and violets spring up. Her attribute is the **cestus** <note>original: "Cestum"; a magic girdle or belt worn by Venus to inspire desire</note>, in which all the <margin>15</margin> enchantments of all fascinations <margin>15</margin>—arising from her face, words, and movements—are believed to reside. A prophetic maiden follows her, carrying a **willow wand** <note>original: "salignam virgam"</note>.

<header>GIORDANO BRUNO</header>

¶ The fourth [image] is a chariot shining softly, which seemed to be fashioned out of electrum <note>original: "ex electro"; a natural alloy of gold and silver, often associated in antiquity with an amber-like brilliance</note>. It was drawn in turns by most beautiful swans, then by peaceful and lovely doves, and then by more lustful sparrows; although, by a certain living and seemingly innate spirit, <margin>5</margin> among all the chariots belonging to the Gods, this one alone is carried along by a certain swift and spontaneous power <note>Bruno suggests this chariot moves by its own internal will or "soul" rather than just the animals pulling it</note>.

¶ The fifth is a most majestic, triumphant queen holding a scepter in her right hand, at the top of which is an image of the Sun. In her left hand, she holds a globe representing the form of the world, engraved with stars, <margin>10</margin> in the transparent center of which the Earth <note>original: "Tellus"</note> is seen enclosed with its own ornaments. Every kind of living thing seems to applaud her, like a divinity most welcome to all. In her chariot, a trophy was to be seen, in which she also testified herself to be the conqueress of the Fates <note>original: "Parcarum victricem"; referring to the three goddesses of destiny. Venus, as the force of love and generation, is presented here as transcending even fate</note>.

<margin>15</margin> ¶ The sixth is a statue of an especially beautiful woman, over whose head was the sky; in her right hand she holds a poppy, and in her left, a pomegranate <note>original: "punicum malum"</note>.

¶ The seventh depicts three heroines <note>original: "viragines"; here referring to the three Graces or the three goddesses in the Judgment of Paris</note>, marked by more than human beauty, standing beside a shepherd who holds a golden apple in his hand.

<margin>20</margin> ¶ The eighth is a youth slain by a boar, who is buried by Venus among lettuces <note>This refers to the myth of Adonis, whose death and rebirth were celebrated in ancient vegetation cults</note>.

¶ The ninth is a naked boy distinguished only by a quiver and a bow, from whose entire body radiant sparks are emitted, affecting his surroundings with a voluntary sweetness. He is so uniform that, <margin>25</margin> according to anyone's temperament, nature, and appearance, he is diverse and "all-formed" <note>original: "omniformis"</note> within his unity. Indeed, we humans are deceived, thinking that he exists only in the single human image in which he presents himself to us. And so, by the strike of a conforming likeness, he pierces all the species of nature at once with his arrows, <margin>30</margin> ignites them with heat, and binds them with chains.

### The Application of Cupid.

¶ Cupid applies himself alongside those who belong to the court of Mercury by rising, awakening, working industriously, by Investigation, Running, Sensing, Solicitude, and Watchfulness; by summoning, inquiring, <margin>5</margin> examining, and directing. From there, he spreads his Nets, Snares, Grappling-irons, and Hooks, acting as a Seeker, a Predator, and a Ravisher in the likeness of a hawk, powerful in beak and claw. From this comes Hunting, Invention, Gain, Obtaining, Profit, the Casting of Lots, Sampling, Attainment, Comparison, Conception, Harvesting, Fishing, <margin>10</margin> Forging, Gathering, Collecting, Deprivation, Scraping together, Cheating, Draining, Hooking, Taking away, Skinning, and Stripping. And there is the Entrance into the court of Mercury: the Thief, the Cutter, the Circumciser <note>original: "Circumcisoris"; likely referring to one who clips or shaves the edges of coins</note>, the Maimer, the Pilferer, the Pickpocket, the night-wandering Harpy, the hiding Lar <note>a Roman household spirit, here used to imply a lurking or secretive presence</note>, and the "Man of Three Letters" <note>original: "trium literarum Hominis"; a classic Latin idiom for a *FUR*, the Latin word for "thief," which contains three letters</note>. <margin>15</margin> Not to mention those who enter the court of the Sun through the "bad gate": the one who has, the one who possesses, and the one who gives.

### VENVS.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of the goddess Venus and Cupid. Venus is seated in a chariot, holding a long arrow or spear. Beside her, a winged Cupid aims a bow. The chariot is drawn by two birds of prey, referred to in the text as "accipitres" (hawks or eagles). The wheels of the chariot are inscribed with zodiac symbols: Scorpio on the left wheel and Libra on the right wheel. The entire scene rests on a decorative horizontal base with floral scrolls.</image-desc>

# ON THE COMPOSITION OF IMAGES, BOOK II.

## CHAPTER XIV.

->Images of the Earth.<-

First, there appears a huge monster, covered in eyes on all sides, and therefore naked, shining with a blue color and a sort of hyacinthine transparency, <margin>5</margin> with eyebrows like flaming gold surrounding the eyes in a circle; the lights <note>referring to the eyes</note> sparkle miraculously from the center of the orb. Although it is of immense size, it seems somewhat shapeless overall. However, that which it carries in its lap is an easily visible gesture: a spherical animal, covered with a skin like a leopard’s, <margin>10</margin> variegated with spots. In some places, its hair rises up like leafy forests; in the rest of the body, it resembles the sea radiating under the sun's splendor.
¶ Second is the majesty of radiant Apollo, to whose lyre-playing various nymphs, bright with a similar beauty, run around in a circle. <margin>15</margin> One of these may be contemplated closely: as she leads the dance, she continuously leads her own circles, revolving into herself with swift rapidity; then, with her other hand held, she revolves around herself in a swift course, retracing almost the same steps; then both <margin>20</margin> move at a slower pace around the central lyre-player, while others from different directions seem to perform the same actions in oblique courses.
¶ Third is a queen distinguished by a height more than human, around whose head towers are arranged in a circle to form a crown <note>This is the "mural crown," the traditional attribute of the goddess Cybele, representing the walls of a city</note>; four lions <margin>25</margin> pull her massive chariot, and at its pole is a maiden beating a drum. She holds a scepter in her right hand, which you would not know how to distinguish whether it is made of crystal or the purest silver, at whose end...

# ON THE COMPOSITION OF IMAGES, BOOK II

Here <note>the mental images</note> are composed with a wonderfully manifold variety through the mediation of
**Assimilation** <note>likening one thing to another</note>, **Proportion**, **Opposition**, **Modification**,
and **Distinction**; for all things can be spoken of in relation to all other things, and this can be done 
fittingly—whether affirmatively or negatively, according to the subject <note>original: "secundum rem"</note> or according to
<margin>5</margin> the manner <note>original: "secundum modum"</note>.

## ON THE COMPOSITION OF IMAGES, BOOK III,

### WHICH IS CONCERNING THE IMAGES OF THE THIRTY SEALS

## CHAPTER I.

->The Fields of Zoroaster<- <note>original: "Campi Zoroastri"; Bruno uses the name of the ancient Persian sage to evoke a mystical or primordial space for organizing knowledge</note>

It remains in this third contemplation to descend further into specific details. We shall begin first with images that are by no means magical—for that is not our purpose here—but rather images that are adapted to our methods, depending on our methods as their governing principles, and which are also representative according to their scale.

<margin>10</margin> ¶ <term>APISTOS</term> <note>a mythical gemstone described in ancient lapidaries</note> features a man dressed in black clothing with red hair. He is adorned with a beard and holds fire steadily in his hand.

<margin>15</margin> ¶ <term>BAROPTENUS</term> <note>a stone said to be black with red and white veins</note> likewise wears black clothing, has a chest stained with blood, holds snow in his hands, and walks upon the waters.

¶ <term>BRONTIA</term> <note>the "thunder-stone," believed to fall from the sky during storms</note> depicts Jupiter <note>original: "Iovem"</note> wielding lightning, or Prometheus <note>the Titan who stole fire from the gods</note>.

¶ **<term>Chelidonia</term>** <note>the "swallow-stone," traditionally said to be found in the bellies of young swallows</note> depicts a youth dressed in purple cloth that is sprinkled with black spots.

¶ **<term>Cinedia</term>** <note>a stone supposedly found in the head of a fish of the same name</note> depicts an older man riding a fish of that name over the waves, holding a diviner’s rod.

<margin>5</margin> ¶ **<term>Chlorites</term>** <note>a green stone</note> depicts the image of Circe <note>the enchantress from the Odyssey</note> in an iron chariot, disemboweling a Scylla bird <note>original: "scyllam avem"; a reference to the mythical sea-monster Scylla, often associated with birds in medieval lapidaries</note>.

¶ **<term>Dracontias</term>** <note>the "dragon-stone," allegedly taken from the brain of a living dragon</note> depicts a figure holding a severed dragon's head in the left hand and a gemstone in the right.

¶ **<term>Evmetris</term>** <note>likely Eumetris, a stone associated with prophetic dreams</note> depicts a girl sleeping with a flint stone placed under her head,
<margin>10</margin> with Mercury <note>the messenger god</note> or Apollo <note>god of prophecy and light</note> standing nearby. She wears a dress dyed a color between green and white.

¶ **<term>Galactites</term>** <note>the "milk-stone," often a variety of chalk or quartz</note> depicts a nursing woman, entirely in white clothing and of a pale complexion. **<term>Gasidane</term>** depicts a pregnant woman crowned with flowers.

<margin>15</margin> ¶ **<term>Glossopetra</term>** <note>literally "tongue-stone," historically fossilized shark teeth</note> depicts Philomela <note>the princess who, in myth, was transformed into a nightingale to escape her pursuer</note> fleeing from Diana <note>goddess of the hunt</note>.

¶ **<term>Gorgonia</term>** <note>coral, believed to have been formed from the blood of Medusa</note> depicts Perseus turning men into stone by the presentation of Medusa's head.

¶ **<term>Heliotropivm</term>** <note>the "bloodstone" or "sun-turner"</note> depicts a boy with red hair, wearing a greenish linen garment, looking at the sun. Clouds surround him.

<margin>20</margin> ¶ **<term>Hephestites</term>** <note>the "fire-stone," named after Hephaestus</note> depicts a fair girl in a black cloak, crowned with a golden circle, extinguishing a flame of fire with water in her right hand, while carrying a mirror in her left.

¶ **<term>Hammonites</term>** <note>the "stone of Ammon," or ammonite fossil, resembling a ram's horn</note> depicts a youth wearing a saffron-colored garment, sleeping under a laurel tree, and possessing the horns of a ram.

<margin>25</margin> ¶ **<term>Hienia</term>** <note>the "hyena-stone," said to be found in the eye of a hyena</note> depicts a youth holding a rod in his right hand and applying the eye of a beast to his mouth. A raven sits upon his head.

¶ **<term>Liparis</term>** depicts a woman who offers a sacrifice <note>original: "adolet," meaning to burn incense or offerings</note>, to whose smoke the forms of wild beasts come running.

### ON THE COMPOSITION OF IMAGES, BOOK III.

In my sense, indeed, it fits everything with words and gestures (however much it may sound varied or foreign) so that it may restore it before its own signs and numbers. When the first verses of the famous Maro <note>original: "Maronis"; referring to the Roman poet Publius Vergilius Maro, known as Virgil.</note> come up, I define the sense to be reported by these signs. Look here: Armed, Man, Singing, First and Pleading, Italian, Fate, Fugitive, Lavinia, Wind, Coastal, Much, From the Earth, Tossed, and Deep <note>These words correspond to the opening of Virgil's *Aeneid*: "Arma virumque cano... fato profugus, Laviniaque venit litora... multum ille et terris iactatus et alto."</note>—these give me:

**MATTER**, because a Phalanx is armed with iron;
**FORM**, for the painter depicts the man on a white tablet.
Because the Marsian <note>A member of an ancient Italian tribe famous for snake-charming and incantations; here used as an image for a singer whose song falls on deaf ears.</note> sings to a deaf mind, **PRIVATION** <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, "Privation" is the absence of a quality that should naturally be present.</note> occurs to me.
In the (Prince) because he commands, I behold the **EFFICIENT CAUSE**.
And the **END** <note>The "Final Cause" or goal of an action.</note> when (one praying) rises and departs.
From here, the (Italian) dancing gives **MOTION**;
(Fates) made void give **TIME**;
and the (Fugitive) gives **PLACE**.
The (Lavinian) woman gives the **VOID**.
The (Shore) which limits gives the **INFINITE**.
Because this (Much) brings forth, it gives the **PRINCIPLE**.
The (Earths) which propagate so much give the **CAUSE**.
The tossed sea and the great element give **FORTUNE AND CHANCE**.
Therefore, you, being skillful, are able to capture these things that are absent from the senses under a sensible image.

¶ But when you connect things to things, take care lest the individual items be referred to uncertain classes, 
<margin>**182**</margin> or that the unnumbered ones fail to recognize their own proper head and place; 
for otherwise, distracted by a double object, the mind wanders astray.

->Proteus in the house of Pallas <note>Pallas Athena, the Greek goddess of wisdom.</note>, where Gorgias is.<-

Thus they demonstrate the eternal world: 
I. **ARMS**, shaken by a powerful hand; 
II. and the **STRENGTH** of the one who preserves; 
III. and that wondrous series of **HARMONY**; 
IV. and the **SONG** of the poet.

<summary>Bruno demonstrates how to use the opening lines of Virgil's Aeneid as a mnemonic scaffold, mapping specific words to the fundamental Aristotelian categories of reality such as Matter, Form, and Cause. He emphasizes the need for a rigorous mental structure to prevent "the mind from wandering" when storing complex information.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Bruno’s ingenious mnemonic exercise from page 287. He uses the opening lines of Virgil’s *Aeneid*—a text every scholar of the Renaissance would know by heart—as a series of "hooks" or "pegs" to hang his complex cosmological theories. By linking the words of the poem (like "First," "Fugitive," and "Shores") to his arguments for an infinite universe, he ensures the philosophy is as unforgettable as the poetry.</meta>

<page-num>288</page-num>

# THE WORKS OF GIORDANO BRUNO

V. And because no such **CIVIL** <note>original: "CIVILE"; referring to the "man" (virum) or citizen in the mnemonic peg.</note> strife threatens, which would utterly disturb the perennial peace.

V. Furthermore, there is a **FIRST** <note>original: "PRIMA"; referring to "Troiae qui primus ab oris."</note> power, exalted without end, by which the thing made flourishes and persists; and nothing resists the produced immensity.

VI. Which also comes **FROM THE MOUTH** <note>original: "AB ORE"; a play on "oris" (shores/borders) from Virgil’s text. Bruno links the "mouth" of the speaker to the "shores" of the world.</note> of him whose words remain, and by a similar lot endure forever.

VII. I deem it worthy, because it is his **KINGDOM** <note>original: "REGNVM"; referring to the "Italian kingdom" in the Aeneid peg.</note>, and there is the evidence of his goodness—a temple and high honor to be thus admired by us in its corporeal form.

VIII. Moreover, the Whole is not subject to **FATE** <note>original: "FATO"; referring to "fato profugus."</note>, although whatever part exists is subject not to its own elements, but to foreign ones.

IX. Nay, even whatever perishes had consisted of **FUGITIVE** <note>original: "PROFVGIS"; referring to the "fugitive" Aeneas.</note> elements, which for that reason glide away to other shores. Furthermore, who shall speak of other shores outside the Whole? Whither shall the Whole or its parts snatch themselves away? For what native thing could flow out from here to the outside, or what foreign thing could flow in from there? It is fitting for contraries <note>In Bruno’s physics, "contraries" (like heat and cold) are the opposing forces that drive all change and life in the universe.</note> to remain perpetually within it, for there is no fullness nor void from elsewhere to oppose it.

X. Finally, if destruction comes, it must come **FROM A REGION** <note>original: "E REGIONE"; a mnemonic link to the "Lavinian" region.</note> outside, and this cannot be, as the nearest things demonstrate. Nor do I fear internal destruction, because nature stands active by the powerful principle of Mind; there is also the ready virtue of matter's potential, and the Ends <note>The "Final Causes" or purposes of things.</note> constrain 

<margin>183</margin>

all things: nor does anything leap outside the order proper to its own 

(**SHORES**) <note>original: "LITTORA"; referring to "Laviniaque venit litora."</note> but just as all rivers tend toward the sea, so all these same things return from the depth of the sea, and they flourish in an eternal circuit. Nothing that you see is annihilated; all things finally resume their own mass. For if the power of contraries should fail, the One <note>The Universe or God as the singular source of all being.</note> would fail for lack of nourishment.

<term>Proteus</term> <note>In mythology, a sea-god who could change into any shape; for Bruno, Proteus represents "prime matter," the underlying substance of the universe that remains the same even as it takes on different forms.</note> is entirely that same underlying matter, transformable into all images and likenesses, by which we can subsequently establish, order, resume, and discuss all things, just as from the same wax we raise up all the figures and images of sensible things, and then signs of all things that can be understood. Now, let us try this on a premise which, in my judgment, seems rather difficult. It has been determined in the mind to argue for the eternity of the world. I must take the "middle terms" <note>In logic, the "middle term" is the bridge that connects the subject and the predicate in a proof.</note> by which this property, **ETERNITY**, may be concluded from the subject, **THE WORLD**. According to custom, I take the "Proteus"—the parts or simple words of a very famous and well-known poem—and transform them into as many middle terms, by which I may gather so many arguments for the form of the proposed object. These words are:

Of **Arms**, and the **man** I sing, who **first** from the **shores** of **Troy**, a **fugitive** by **fate**, came to **Italy** and the **Lavinian shores**, **much tossed** on **land** and the **deep**. <note>original: "Arma, virumque, cano, Troiae, qui primus, ab oris, Italiam, fato, profugus, Lavinaque, venit, Littora, multum, ille terris, iactatus, et alto." First, from "**arms**," signifying power and infinitely enduring instruments, I conclude the world is eternal.

--- Page 305 ---
<meta>This page continues Bruno’s philosophical argument for the eternity of the universe. He is using the famous opening line of Virgil’s *Aeneid*—"Arma virumque cano, Troiae qui primus ab oris Italiam" (Arms and the man I sing, who first from the coasts of Troy to Italy)—as a mnemonic framework. Each word of the poem serves as a "peg" for a specific theological or physical proof that the world, as an effect of an infinite God, must also be infinite and eternal.</meta>

<page-num>290</page-num>
<header>GIORDANO BRUNO</header>

II. From the **man** <note>original: "viro"; referring to the *virum* (man) in Virgil's poem.</note>, an act capable of being infinitely preserved by a powerful agent.
III. From the **song** <note>original: "cantu"; referring to *cano* (I sing).</note>, which reflects the harmony of things and their indissoluble temperament, most fittingly persistent, which consists of constant changes and successions.
IV. From the **city** <note>original: "civitate"; here Bruno likely associates the city of Troy with the "city of the world."</note>, which signifies the "republic of the world" (for nothing is truly opposed to it) regarding its corruption and death; for those things that are opposites *within* the world are not opposites *to* the world itself, because they are merely its parts and members.
V. From **primality** <note>original: "primitate"; referring to *primus* (first).</note>, of the agent who is always acting and preserving; for indeed the <term>first efficient cause</term> <note>The primary source of action or change; in this context, God.</note>, who is the world’s immediate cause, must be an eternal actor. This is because a derivative effect cannot be an "efficient cause" unless it comes from another preceding principle, which would then be more truly the first principle. And if one must stop at a first cause that has no antecedent, it is absolutely necessary that there be nothing succeeding it later; it must always be the cause, for if the derivative effect were removed, the cause would no longer be a "principle." Therefore, the universal effect <note>The universe.</note> necessarily accompanies the universal cause in its duration.
VI. From the **shores** or **mouth** <note>original: "oris"; Bruno puns on the Latin *ora* (shore) from Virgil and *os/oris* (mouth).</note> (on account of the similarity of the sound, though it is also a medium for the thing signified, which we shall not pass over), because the word of the divine mouth—that is, the work of God as the effect of the Almighty—remains eternal. For since it is supremely true and greatly good, it is greatly fitting for it to exist, and greatly unfitting for it not to exist.
VII. From **Italy** <note>original: "Italia"; the destination in Virgil's poem.</note> (which I transfer to mean a kingdom or region), which is the region, place, and temple in which the supernal majesty is praised, worshiped, and honored. God would cease to be a father, a king, a lord, a providence, a governor, and the "Highest Good" <note>original: "optimitas"</note> if this [the world] were not a good temple and kingdom. Therefore, just as He is to be eternally magnified, so too must there be that which eternally magnifies, praises, and tells of His glory.

<meta>This page continues the sequence of philosophical proofs for the eternity and stability of the universe. Bruno uses the individual words of Virgil’s *Aeneid* (specifically the opening lines) as "memory pegs" to anchor complex metaphysical arguments. Having covered the first seven proofs on the previous page, he now moves through the eighth to the fourteenth, focusing on the conservation of matter, the nature of change, and the immutability of the Divine Will.</meta>

<page-num>291</page-num>
<header>ON THE COMPOSITION OF IMAGES, BOOK III</header>

The eighth [proof] is from **fate** <note>original: "fato"; from Virgil’s phrase "fato profugus" (a fugitive by fate)</note>, since there is no necessity above the universe—which is the entire body of nature—but nature itself is that very necessity. For the universe can neither be moved nor altered [as a whole], but motion and alteration (and consequently <margin>5</margin> **fate**) exist *within* the universe; that is, they belong to those things which are part of it and contained in it. Likewise, all <term>corruption</term> <note>In this context, the breaking down or decay of physical objects.</note> is a certain restoration of the elements; however, this does not apply to the universe in the same way it applies to us.

The ninth is from the **refuge** and **displacement** <note>original: "profugio et delocatione"; derived from "profugus" (fugitive)</note> of those things which are dissolved, which is possible for particular things—such as the stars and <margin>10</margin> especially the earth—but for the universe as a whole, there is no place outside into which its parts could gapingly fall.

The tenth is from the **shore** <note>original: "littore"; derived from "litora" (shores)</note>, namely a certain boundary by which things are reflected back to their principles, and the elements are repaired once again to begin a similar composition. Therefore, there is change, but <margin>15</margin> not a true destruction of things. Just as the waves of the sea flow toward the shores, so they also flow back from the shores.

The eleventh is from the **multitude** <note>original: "multitudine"; derived from "multum" (much)</note> of formed things passing by, while their <term>matter</term> <note>The underlying "stuff" that takes on different forms.</note> and true <term>substance</term> <note>The essential reality that remains when appearances change.</note> is a single, permanent thing.

The twelfth is from the **lands** <note>original: "terris"; from "multum ille et terris" (much tossed on lands)</note>, according to that [scriptural] saying: "A generation passes <margin>20</margin> away and a generation arrives, but the earth remains forever" <note>Ecclesiastes 1:4. Bruno uses this to argue that while individual forms change, the material world is eternal.</note>; that is, particular composed things are changed and their shapes are moved, but the species and the substance stand invariable.

The thirteenth is from the **tossing** <note>original: "iactatione"; derived from "iactatus" (tossed about)</note>, by which nothing is seen to fly apart from the body of the earth, because the sea always appears to be as great <margin>25</margin> as it was, and what is subtracted from one place is added to another.

The fourteenth is from the **height** <note>original: "altitudine"; derived from "alto" (on the high sea/deep)</note> of the presiding cause; for there is no higher cause that could alter or make void what that cause itself has willed. Furthermore, this cause cannot [contradict] its own <margin>30</margin> command, as if it were only now becoming wise, or [finding something] better or more eminent, <insert>**186**</insert> or [becoming] submissive or more weakly powerful, so that what it once ordered to be as "good," it might soon judge not to be good. On the contrary, in [the Divine Will]...

<meta>This page continues Bruno’s metaphysical exploration of the universe. On the previous page, he argued for the eternity and stability of the universe as a whole. Here, he distinguishes between the infinite, eternal "Universe" and the individual, "corruptible" worlds (like the Earth and Moon) within it. He continues using the opening words of Virgil’s Aeneid as mnemonic hooks for his philosophical points.</meta>

<page-num>292</page-num>
<page-type>text</page-type>
-># GIORDANO BRUNO<-

Within the whole, the parts are eternal; they vary in their outward appearance, but not in their underlying substance. Indeed, water, vapor, flame, and air are entirely the same thing; air is flame, vapor is water. Nor does one form possess greater <term>power</term> <note>original: "vim"; referring to the inherent force or essence of an element.</note> than another, or a higher condition. For if fire <margin>5</margin> were to dissolve everything, it would eventually cease to be fire due to a lack of anything left to dissolve; thus, that which was dissolved congeals once more, and from this thickening comes the fire again, to be nourished (as far as it can be). Fire, by the very fact that it consumes all things (as if ruling from above everything), in turn restores those very same things as it fails and recedes.

<margin>10</margin> ¶ This same series of terms (taken in a different sense) will show that a "world"—such as the earth and the moon, which we distinguish from the rest of the universe—is <term>corruptible</term> <note>Subject to decay, change, and eventual destruction, unlike the infinite Universe itself.</note> by just as many means.

First, from the **arms** <note>original: "armis"; Virgil's first word, "Arma". Here Bruno uses it to mean the "tools" or "media" of composition.</note>, that is, the variable means from which they are composed.
<margin>15</margin> Second, because of the forces of particular and immediate causes, which are finite, just as the effect, the subject, and the subject’s potential are finite; for the matter, form, and power of the earth is finite, its quality is variable, and its composition can be dissolved.

Third, because of its alterable symmetry and balance, for it no longer produces the same kinds of living creatures as it once did. Or as the song of the prophets says: "I will move heaven and earth," <margin>20</margin> <note>original: "movebo caelum et terram"; a reference to the Book of Haggai 2:6.</note> which means "I will change them"; and "a single day will give both the earth and the sky over to destruction." <note>original: "una dies dabit exitio terramque polumque"; a quote from Lucretius or Ovid regarding the end of the world.</note>

Fourth, because of the dissonance among the members of this "commonwealth" <note>original: "reipublicae"; Bruno views the components of a planet as a functioning political body or system.</note> [of the world].
<margin>25</margin> Fifth, because its efficient, conserving, and forming cause is secondary and dependent, not the primary cause.

Sixth, because it has **shores** <note>original: "oras"; from Virgil’s "litora" (shores/borders). Here meaning boundaries.</note> outside itself, upon which it acknowledges its dependence.

Seventh, because of the shifting of dominion found in the <margin>30</margin> rule of forms; for since the sun is made of the same matter...

<meta>This page continues the technical instructions for Bruno’s mnemonic architecture. Following the discussion of "The Chain," Bruno moves into the "Sixth Seal," known as the "Tree" (Arbor). This system uses the organic structure of a tree—from root to flower—to organize concepts hierarchically, moving from the most basic "elements" at the roots to complex "virtues" and "actions" in the branches and leaves.</meta>

<page-num>296</page-num>
<page-type>text</page-type>
<header>BY GIORDANO BRUNO</header>

¶ If the figured numbers <note>Bruno refers to numbers that have been assigned specific shapes or "images" to make them easier to remember.</note> are arranged according to the light and power of the third seal, not only will their own mirrors—the images of things, senses, and signs—be perfectly established for you, but they will also become perpetual receptacles for things through various orders of chaining.

<margin>5</margin> ¶ Here it occurs to me what must be added to the second seal, specifically if the signs for words ought to be numbers. Let their circle, or the distinction of the fingers, be completed by using both the hands and the feet; this system represents a character of twenty forms and just as many types of matter. <note>original: "digitorum distinctio"; Bruno is likely referring to "finger counting" or "manual alphabets," a common medieval and Renaissance practice where different joints or positions of the fingers represented numbers or letters.</note>

<margin>10</margin> ## CHAPTER VII.
### Seal VI. The Tree.

> Whose roots and trunk represent a chain <note>original: "catena"; following the previous chapter's theme of linked sequences.</note>
> And are soon multiplied into the same series by the branches.
> For just as you grasp individual things there by ascent and descent, <margin>191</margin>
<margin>15</margin> > Here you also turn to the right and to the left,
> So that the bark and the marrow <note>original: "cortex atque medulla"; a metaphor for the external appearance and the internal essence or "hidden meaning" of a thing.</note> may become known to you,
> Inward, outward, forward, and you shall grasp backward:
> The root, the trunk, the branch, the palm, the leaf, the seeds, and the flowers.
> Therefore, perceive the figure rising into a pyramid,
<margin>20</margin> > From which comes growing judgment and a rich intention;
> For whatever you wish to understand from the monuments of others
> Or from your own light, and to be given in true order,
> Whether things already investigated or those cited to be sought,
> We command that they be recalled to the pattern of this plant.
<margin>25</margin> > Here are the roots which are from the first origin—
> I mean the principle, the foundation, the cause, and the element.
> You may refer to the trunk as much as there is of essence and being;

...those definitions are futile and vain due to the disadvantage of his era, but the form which looks to the substance of discovery, understood by a few, is certainly such that I could easily believe it was divinely bestowed upon them.
<margin>5</margin> ¶ Our tree differs from that one <note>referring to Lully's tree</note> because this one is solid, while that one is flat; indeed, just as a pyramid differs from a triangle, or a body from a surface. Therefore, that one presents the path of discovery through height and width, but this one also through manifold depth. And yet, that one is the mother, while this one is the daughter as far as the formal work of discovery is concerned; <margin>10</margin> as for the matter of the **speculative sciences**, there is no reason for us to consult Lully. | But regarding certain other intellectual <margin>193</margin> powers of the soul, this tree is of an entirely different kind, which Lully certainly seems not to have even thought about.

### On the circular and square encyclium <note>From the Greek *enkyklios*, meaning a circular or general education; the root of the word "encyclopedia."</note>.

Under the shadow of our tree let the circular **encyclium** be contained, the figure of which is a circle first divided into two parts, as in **A** and **B**, then each of them into two others, as **A** into **C** and **D**, and again **C** migrates into two, **E** and **F**, <margin>20</margin> and so on; where just as branch **A** grows and is amplified by a continuous two-part section, so too is **B**, whereby the figure will be increased into a circle down to the furthest distinctions. Its proper expression is found in those writings *On the Minimum* <note>Referring to Bruno's 1591 work *De triplici minimo et mensura* (On the Triple Minimum and Measure).</note>, and is titled **THE GARDEN OR THE BANNER OF THE SUN**.

<margin>25</margin> ¶ Thus mother Nature proceeds by the distinction of her own duality;
For there are two primary opposites,
From whose fountain fall the two nearest things: light and darkness,
