Cold and hot, then thick and thin;
From these connected and combined together
Into a cycle, the distinctions of things forever arise.

¶ It differs from the tree <note>Referring to the "Tree of Science" discussed on the previous page.</note> because this figure is flat, enclosed, and round, whereas the former is solid and not defined by a regular or fixed boundary.

¶ Truly, the square **encyclium** <note>From the Greek *enkyklios*, meaning "circular" or "general," the root of the word "encyclopedia." Bruno uses it here to describe a comprehensive system of knowledge mapped into a geometric shape.</note> first takes four boundaries around one; second, it takes four secondary boundaries around each of those; and third, it takes four tertiary boundaries around each of the four secondary ones.

Just as there are four bodies of the moon around the sun,
One of which is called splendid from its crimson rising,
<margin>194</margin> Another from the region where the sun hides its head in the waves,
A third where the sun, being positioned, gathers the narrowed waves,
And the last is at the opposite borders of the **Erymanthian bear** <note>A poetic reference to the North, named after the mountain in Arcadia; it refers to the constellation Ursa Major.</note>;
Then the sister and rival of shining Phoebus <note>The Moon, sister of the Sun (Apollo/Phoebus).</note>
Describes four stars, each in its own order,
Around the mass of light, including the **basiliscus** <note>A name for the star Regulus in the constellation Leo.</note> and the **eye of the bull** <note>The star Aldebaran in the constellation Taurus.</note>;
Meanwhile, they are sub-multiplied by equal signs
So that each is always aptly walled in by as many conforming parts,
As if each has its own fourfold cause.
Soon each of these takes on four systems of reasoning:
The Divine, the physical, the logical, and the one proper to **Mathematics**.
And first is the primary thing, which is the boundary, the rising, and the origin;
Following this is the middle, namely action, motion, and the path;
Then there is the work, acting as the end or goal toward which it tends;
Following this is the conception of things, which forms the mind.
These take up the aforementioned things in their own way, and neither
These nor others lack a thousand further fourfold sets.

# CHAPTER VIII.

### The Seventh Seal. The Dresser. <note>original: *Indutor*. In Bruno's mnemonic system, this refers to the "investor" or "clother"—the process of "dressing" an abstract concept in a specific image or character to make it memorable.</note>

I will grant ten halls distinguished by various orders 
Of places, and also decorated with various figures.
<margin>5</margin> Here I will place men, there the banners of men;
Elsewhere are instruments to be bound by the left hands,
Or perhaps touching the neck, chests, or back,
And in other seats I will soon locate the signs of works. <margin>195</margin>
Thus, by standing near, the site, the place, the possessor, and his
<margin>10</margin> Circumstances I will provide, numbered in a more convenient lot.
From here you take the elements by which all things are constituted,
And being fused with their own numbers, they become present.
It is enough that twenty <note>original: *bis dena*. Likely referring to the 20-letter Latin alphabet Bruno often used for his memory wheels.</note> of each be given,
So that the whole may be formed from simple parts.

<margin>15</margin> ¶ The formation or configuration, if it is made from the primary combinations of elements, will be done with less mental "scattering," <note>original: *distractione*. Bruno uses this to describe the cognitive load or the effort of keeping disparate images in the mind.</note> but it requires a larger (that is, more numerous) apparatus of images; if indeed (as we teach here) it must be made from the primary elements, the scattering is somewhat greater, but it is completed with a smaller <margin>20</margin> apparatus. You will easily be able to collect the terms from the halls, yet in such a way that instead of Calchas, Oedipus, Tiresias, <note>Calchas (the seer of the Iliad), Oedipus (the riddle-solver), and Tiresias (the blind prophet) are used here as "agent" images—standardized characters used to represent specific data points in the memory palace.</note> and others, you receive those known to you by sight and defined under such names and offices.

<summary>Bruno introduces the "Seventh Seal," a mnemonic method involving ten "halls" where users place familiar characters and objects to organize information. ### PATTERN OF THE OPERATION. <note>original: *Typus Negotii*. This refers to the practical application or "working model" of the mnemonic system.</note>

| I | II | III | IV | V |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Apollo | Crowned | With Laurel | Rides | A Lion |
| Venus | Enwrapped | In a Cloud | Adorns | A Goat |
| <margin>5</margin> VI | VII | VIII | IX | X |
| Overturning | The Foundation | Of a Tent | Of a Soldier | Set on Fire |
| Cutting | The Herbs | Of a Garden | Of a Maiden | Plucked Up |

¶ Thus, for twenty deities <note>original: *numinum*. Bruno uses the names of Roman gods as placeholders for specific letters or concepts.</note>, each of which may take on the appearance of nine accidents <note>original: *accidentium*. In logic, an "accident" is a non-essential quality—such as what a figure is wearing or doing—that distinguishes it without changing its essence.</note> according to the described form, <margin>10</margin> you will set out a table for yourself twice as long as it is wide. **196** <note>This "196" refers to the page number in a standard early edition, likely the 1591 Frankfurt printing.</note> These accidents should be such that all can be combined with all others—not, I say, according to the logic of nature, but for the sake of forging a striking image. Indeed, it is worthwhile here that Venus and Apollo <margin>15</margin> can take on the banners, instruments, and works of all the others, along with other circumstances.

For the apparatus and for retaining the meaning of the accidents, twenty places are sufficient, containing as many formed images (in the same manner as the images of Venus and Apollo were formed).

Let this song examine the five famous types of art. <note>original: *quino celebres genere artis*. This refers to the five distinct methods or categories Bruno uses to organize his mnemonic system.</note>

<note>This 3x3 grid acts as a coordinate map for the mind. Vowels (A, E, I, O, V) are placed in the corners and the center, while common consonants (LR, R, M, TN) occupy the sides. This allows a practitioner to create a "mental word" by tracing a path through the grid.</note>

## CHAPTER X.

<margin>15</margin> ### Seal nine. The Farmer.

I want a **Farmer** <note>original: *Agricola*. This is the central image for the ninth mnemonic "Seal."</note> to be above whatever field of memory I choose,
Circled by many tools walled in for multiple uses.
The tasks of the weaver are many, and his tools are many;
Many are those of the smiths, and many of the cobbler. Therefore,
<margin>20</margin> Let a "house" <note>A "house" (*casa*) is a specific sub-location within the memory system.</note> be distinguished by three or four assistants
Of the same or different kind, so that each one
Refers fully to a single form. Let **twenty-one tools**
Signify as many as those consonants I have mentioned,
Which, according to a five-fold lot, return a "voice," <note>The "five-fold lot" refers to the five vowels (A, E, I, O, U). By combining one of the 21 tools (consonants) with a vowel, the practitioner "speaks" a syllable in their mind.</note>
<margin>25</margin> Let the matter also be subjected to as many forms.
Then you may see what he does, and toward what or whom these things are related.
For the **spirit** <note>original: *spiritus*. In this context, it refers to the active, imaginative power of the mind.</note> of this kind captures all things, and
Brings forth whatever you ask for your convenience;
It transforms all things that rush toward it, and it reveals all things.

The fifteen fields you have can serve two "presidents" <note>Leaders or primary images governing a section of the memory system.</note>, up to the number of thirty: if six in the middle, or the right, or another part of the field are taken for two in a double form and reasoning, let them be made suitable. The craftsman, standing or sitting, will then note the following or preceding sound in those things combined from a double element. You can provide for the rest in a similar way here and elsewhere.

## CHAPTER XI.
<margin>201</margin>
->Seal X. The Sky.<-

So that you may be able to describe the boundaries of the flame-bearing deep <note>original: *flammiferi profundi*. A poetic reference to the celestial sphere or the heavens, filled with "fiery" stars.</note>,
this series of forms has been retained by reason
<margin>5</margin> in their proper parts, if by chance you divide the whole
into two large cycles, for which a right
angle is fourfold everywhere, rising from the twin poles;
From there, if the quadrants are also dissolved into twin
parts, this ability will become more concise.
<margin>10</margin> For into as many more parts this is distributed,
so much more secure and ready the work will present itself.
Furthermore, if one horizon is split into six triangular sections,
and the other is split into just as many parts,
and the border gives an end to the bases of the earth, the vertex
<margin>15</margin> (which is the center point) is the common boundary of these.
Then conceive of the **sextants** <term>sextant: a division of a circle into six parts, or sixty degrees</term> in a certain
sensible region, and grasp the figures and numbers
nearer to the side. A single house can contain the whole.

¶ The names of the parts of the sky are: the triangle of the east,
<margin>20</margin> whose point is a center point common also to five other triangles,
at the vertex (which the Arabs call the **zenith** <term>zenith: the imaginary point directly "above" a particular location on the celestial sphere</term>,
and the point opposite to it they call **nadir** <term>nadir: the point directly "below" the observer, opposite the zenith</term>);
let one side be an arc from that same point all the way to the point where the **ecliptic** <term>ecliptic: the apparent path the Sun follows across the sky over the course of a year</term> 
cuts the horizon, the base from that same point to the
<margin>25</margin> point which terminates the sextant of the line of the horizon,
the remaining side I understand to be from this boundary to the vertical point of the zenith. 
In this way, for a particular location, the sky [is divided] for me into twelve <margin>202</margin>

## CHAPTER XII.

->Seal XI. The Orbit of the Sky.<-

The orbit of the sky describes, if you please, eight cycles,
Which are easily distributed into twelve parts,
<margin>10</margin>And just as many signs of heaven they represent in varying order.
From the center, a radius is divided into eight parts,
In which (as the common people do) I describe the seven **planets** <note>In the Renaissance, the "seven planets" included the Sun and the Moon, alongside Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn.</note>
More, or all: shown in an open series,
So that the form shaped from above gives the circuits of the radius,
<margin>15</margin>Perpetually and variously, through these members which are substituted.
When one circuit of the radius has been completed,
Let the first of the **fixed stars** <note>original: *Aplanûm*. From the Greek *aplanes*, referring to the sphere of stars that do not move relative to one another.</note> be the last, and into the highest
Place, carry that which was lower than all others.
And let the radius then revolve by a second lot,
<margin>20</margin>To which a third lot succeeds, and finally a seventh.
After this variation which was made because of one member,
Let the first lot proceed for the neighboring twins.
Soon, with one placed in between, let two accompany each other,
Then let there be a movement with more companions, and so on.
<margin>25</margin>You recall all these figures to the number [of the total],
By which the sought-after species may be signified to you.

# CHAPTER XIII.

## Seal XII. The Interpreter.

I, the Interpreter, shall establish twenty-two rooms,
Which shall contain as many locations <note>original: *cubilia*. While literally "beds" or "couches," in Bruno's mnemonic system, these are specific spots or "seats" within a room where a memory image is placed.</note> fitted in each part,
<margin>5</margin> In which, as various inhabitants are established,
All things that consist of a triple root <note>Likely referring to the linguistic or conceptual "roots" of the information being stored.</note> shall be provided.

->**The 22 Rooms**<-

The rooms are the Pyramid, the Fountain, the Grove, the Colonnade, the Altar,
The Cave, the Sickle, the Well, the Turret, the Table, the Bath,
<margin>10</margin> The Masonry, the Seat, the Furnace, the Watchtower, the Chest, the Column,
The River, the Banner, the Engine of War <note>original: *tormentum*. This could refer to a catapult or a device of torture; in mnemonics, striking or violent images were preferred for better recall.</note>, the Crypt, and the Tomb.

->**The 22 Locations**<-

In these rooms, let the locations be of the same form for you,
A single order shall be preserved for the various starting points,
<margin>15</margin> Namely, that which is the name of the Room <note>The Latin text here reads *Atri* (a misspelling of *Atrii*), as noted in the original margin.</note> is also the first Location.
Accept it just as you see the Tomb following the Crypt:
The Pyramid follows as the third, the Fountain fourth, and so on.
Thus they stand in a varied order and yet in the same one,
<margin>20</margin> To which rooms a known crowd of souls <note>These "souls" (*animae*) are the personified figures who "live" in the memory rooms to represent specific data.</note> are granted:
The Shoemaker, the Fisherman, the Wrestler, the Soldier, the Lover,
The Printer, the Trader, the Weaver, the Cupbearer, the Herdsman,
The Painter, the Sailor, the Gardener, the Barber, the Innkeeper, the Jester,

## CHAPTER XIV.

### A summary of the remaining seals.

<margin>5</margin>Anyone who has gained skill in the <term>seals</term> <note>original: *sigillorum*. In Bruno's system, a "seal" is a complex mental diagram or "key" used to organize and retrieve knowledge.</note> already explained, and who is endowed with even modest intelligence, will be able to arrive at the discovery and unlocking of the remaining ones by one way or another on their own. Therefore, there is no reason for us to occupy ourselves too diligently in explaining the rest.

<margin>206</margin>->The Thirteenth Seal: The Princes.<-

¶ The zodiac has twelve chambers <note>original: *cubilia*. These are divisions of the celestial circle used as "rooms" for memory storage.</note>, each of which is famous for a variety of things, because they contain the members of twelve distinct and ordered halls <note>original: *atriorum*. These are the primary rooms within the memory palace.</note> or fields. By wandering through these, <margin>10</margin> Saturn—acting, suffering, giving, receiving, affected in one way or another—will indicate his nature to you from his various circumstances and accidents, sometimes alone, sometimes proceeding with Jupiter, sometimes with others, either individually or in groups. <note>Bruno is describing a mnemonic technique where planetary gods move through the zodiac signs to represent complex logical or astrological propositions.</note>
<margin>15</margin>

->The Fourteenth Seal: The Wheel of Fortune.<-

¶ There are four players, to each of whom I assign a field with "seeds" <note>original: *seminibus*. Likely referring to bits of information or data points.</note> chosen from the storehouses of the halls or chambers. The first has field A, the second field B, the <margin>20</margin> third C, the fourth D. The first throws <note>original: *proiicit*. This suggests a game of chance or a randomized mnemonic exercise, possibly using dice.</note> the Fool; the Fool will therefore occupy the seat of the first field. The second [throws] the Knight; the Knight will take the first seat of the second field. The third throws the Pope, the fourth throws Death, the Angel, the King. <note>These figures—the Fool, Knight, Pope, Death, Angel, and King—correspond to the imagery found in Renaissance Tarot cards (*tarocchi*), which Bruno often used as ready-made mnemonic characters.</note>

<summary>Bruno transitions to a summary of his remaining mnemonic seals, asserting that the reader should now be capable of self-instruction. He briefly outlines the Thirteenth Seal (based on the Zodiac) and the Fourteenth Seal (a game-like system using Tarot-style figures to organize information).</summary>
<keywords>Art of Memory, mnemonics, Zodiac, Saturn, Jupiter, Wheel of Fortune, Tarot figures, memory palace, planetary influence</keywords>

### Fifteenth: The Die.

¶ The same person is crowned by a king, anointed by a priest, seized by a knight, and destroyed by death. Thus, while remaining in the same footprint <note>original: *vestigio*. This refers to a fixed location in the memory palace.</note>, but affected by these various chances <note>original: *casibus*. A pun on "dice rolls" and "accidents of fate."</note>, he will indicate all things to you.

<margin>5</margin>
### Sixteenth: The Field of Circe.

¶ There are four qualities represented by the letters A, E, I, and O. From these, four combinations are possible within the elements: AI (hot and moist), AO (hot and dry, <note>In the Aristotelian system, this corresponds to the element of Fire.</note>), EI (cold and moist), and EO (cold and dry). For these, there are four <margin>207</margin>
<margin>10</margin>fields. Within these, there are various degrees of these qualities. Consequently, for these degrees, there are various halls <note>original: *atria*. Large mnemonic rooms.</note> in each of the fields, and in the halls, there are various chambers <note>original: *cubilia*. Small, specific storage spots for images.</note> according to their proper order, in which the image of every thing will occur to you. And it is not possible—or at least not easy—for you to imagine that you have seen someone in another place when you have already observed them attentively in one specific location (I mean, through the application of this work). <margin>15</margin>In this same way, I shall provide for the remaining types of things to be counted and referred to their own classes.

### The House of Aesculapius. The 17th Seal.

¶ There is a hall which is commonly called the "vestibule of hell,"
<margin>20</margin>where pale diseases dwell and most easily reveal themselves by their appearances and their ranks. Elsewhere, there are tables, gardens, cases, workshops, and flasks for foods, herbs, vegetables, stones, juices, roots, and both "simples" <note>Medicines made from a single ingredient, usually a plant.</note> and compounds; from these, those guided by the hand of <term>Aesculapius</term> <note>The Greco-Roman god of medicine and healing.</note> may pluck what they need.

->The Nomenclator. XVIII Seal.<-

The state, the occurrence, the instrument, the action, and the circumstances attributed to each thing—derived from the established meanings of the elements and their combinations—will suggest the proper name for external objects. <note>The "Nomenclator" is a system for generating or remembering names based on a thing's inherent properties and its "elements" (the building blocks of Bruno’s mnemonic alphabet).</note>

<margin>5</margin>
->History. XIX Seal.<-

Plutarch <note>Plutarch (c. 46 – 119 AD) was a Greek biographer and essayist famous for his *Parallel Lives*, which paired famous Greeks and Romans.</note> sees princes arranged in their proper order within a single hall of his memory. Leading each one out from there, he advances them through a highly decorated and orderly field, teaching each to perform their parts in sequence. Who does not see how variously different individuals can be affected within those circumstances? <margin>10</margin>

->Law. XX Seal.<-

Will you not likewise organize books under a volume, titles under books, laws under titles, and paragraphs under those laws? <note>Bruno suggests a "nested" mnemonic structure to mirror the hierarchical organization of legal codes.</note>

<margin>208</margin>
->Physics. XXI Seal.<-

<margin>15</margin>
In place of the books of Hippocrates <note>Hippocrates of Kos (c. 460 – 370 BC), the "Father of Medicine."</note>, I hold a specific number of underlying principles <term>hypostases</term> <note>original: *hypostases*. In this context, these are the fundamental substances or "building blocks" of the physical world.</note>. Since these conduct themselves according to the order of their subjects, is there anything they might not easily accomplish?

->The Measurer. XXII Seal.<-

I have signs for simple terms: a six <note>original: *sene*. This may refer to the number six or a specific dice-throw/symbol representing a triangle.</note> denoting a triangle, twins denoting parallel lines, scales denoting equality, and other signs for other matching concepts, which are not many. From these, the elements—which are divided into fifteen orders—are composed.

### XXIII Seal. The Time of the Voice.

The voice that precedes has one house, the one in the middle another, and the one that ends has yet another. <note>In Bruno’s system, a "house" is a mental location or a compartment in a memory wheel used to store sounds or parts of words.</note> Each house has four corners, and each corner has two sides; therein are twelve elements:

<margin>5</margin>
| B | F | M | R |
|---|---|---|---|
| C | G | N | S |
| D | L | P | T |

¶ Through the houses, five antecedents, five medians, and five completers wander to the individual parts of the houses, with their own differences and cases, assisted by the Chain <note>original: *Catena*. This is a specific mnemonic device Bruno uses to link concepts in a sequence.</note>, the Numerator <note>original: *Numerator*. Likely a structure for tracking the quantity or order of items.</note>, and if desired, one or more other seals.

### XXIV Seal. The Father of the Thief.

¶ The father of the thief is the population: <note>Bruno uses the term "population" (*populus*) to refer to a comprehensive set or group of categories.</note> A: quantity, B: quality, C: place, D: position, E: motion, F: time, G: agreement, H: difference, I: contrariety, K: habit, L: privation, M: giving, N: receiving, O: action, P: passion. <note>These categories are largely derived from Aristotle’s "Categories," which were the standard way of classifying all possible predicates of a subject in Renaissance philosophy.</note> Let one element combine with the others and each with all in a twofold way, | and you will have **209** parents of those signs for those things for which you cannot have images. <note>Bruno’s system often involves "calculating" possible combinations of ideas; 209 is the result of the combinatorial logic he is applying to these categories.</note> In quantity, perceive number and magnitude; in quality, the clear and the obscure, and similarly in the others.

### XXV Seal. The Thief.

¶ The thief clearly looks toward ten differences: A: part [and] whole, B: large [and] small, C: simple [and] double, D: high [and] low, E: front [and] back, F: right [and] left, G: internal...

->Seal XXVI. The Accomplice of the Thief.<-

<margin>5</margin> ¶ The accomplice of the thief has at least indicative signs on the head and hands: **A** eyes, **B** eyelids, **C** mouth, **D** right hand, **E** left, **F** forehead, **G** cheek, **H** right ear, **I** left, **K** hair, **L** chin. **M** In the hands he uses the numbering, folding, unfolding, and
<margin>10</margin> placement of fingers. Likewise, in various parts of the face, he uses simple touching, scratching, or rubbing. The mouth coughs, breathes, spits, laughs, widens, contracts, and opens. The eyebrows and eyes have their own movements. The variety of movements in one part combined with the
<margin>15</margin> variety of one or more other parts—whether singular or plural—is certainly capable of fulfilling any number of combinations. Bede <note>Referring to the Venerable Bede (c. 673–735 AD), an English monk who famously described a system of "finger-calculation" and a silent finger-alphabet in his work *On the Reckoning of Time*.</note> published a method that explains all the differences of numbers in the fingers and joints. But our "thief" (with no one from the middle of the crowd being aware except his accomplice) explains all his intentions—and those that are most specific to him—all the more easily.

<margin>20</margin> ->The Rhetorician. Seal XXVII.<-

¶ Armed with twenty-four attributes, the rhetorician enters the court of the twelve princes, so that they may all assist him in the three kinds of work. <note>In classical rhetoric, the "three kinds" (*tria genera*) are judicial (legal), deliberative (political/persuasive), and demonstrative (ceremonial praise or blame).</note> Furthermore, in the judicial kind, his primary prince is Jupiter; in the deliberative, the Sun; in the
<margin>25</margin> demonstrative, Pallas. <note>Pallas refers to Athena/Minerva, the goddess of wisdom.</note> Other seals assist him, and perhaps above the rest, the Farmer. <note>original: *Agricola*. This refers to another specific mnemonic structure in Bruno's system, where the mind is "cultivated" like a field.</note>

### The Priest. The 28th Seal.

¶ The priest <note>original: *presbyter*; here likely representing a central mnemonic figure or archetype</note> grows rich in the field of the generator, the one giving birth, the one exiting, the one lifting, the one judging, the king, the counter, the sufferer, the lyre-player, the wise man, the lover, the prophet, the divine, the tragic actor, the boy, the ox, the eagle, the lion, the Roman, the Jew, the doer, and others. As each of these travels through a hundred "beds" <note>referring to specific locations or stations within a memory palace</note>, there is nothing they cannot fulfill with the support of the Chain <note>original: *Catena*; a mnemonic technique for linking ideas</note> and the Abacus of Thoth <note>original: *Theuti Abaco*; Thoth, the Egyptian god of wisdom, was credited by Bruno with inventing the foundations of the art of memory</note>.

### The Polymath. XXIX.

¶ The Polymath <note>original: *Polyhistor*; a person of great or varied learning</note>—that is, the grammarian—if he can speak suitably in Latin, or for even greater and rarer delights in Greek, is able to deliberate on all matters placed in controversy and dispute, since he is learned. Moreover, he will teach, without failing, the genders of nouns in the space of only two hours, perfectly, using three classes: Sun, Moon, and Heaven; namely, the masculine, feminine, and neuter. The common and universal genders are left at the gates and in the courtyard before the doors. Those wandering through the parts of these classes will find a multitude of their own images (conspicuous in the faces of the things they represent). For the conjugation of verbs, he has four courtyards of complexes and an equal number for exceptions, which are brought to life by their own souls <note>referring to Bruno’s concept of "living" or "animated" mnemonic images</note>, and which the practitioners run through while animated, with the "Chainer" <note>original: *Catenante*</note> or Thoth as their guide. The same art will assist his other needs, so that in three days he can easily accomplish what he otherwise would not dare to promise in a year (even with more strenuous labor).

<summary>Bruno describes the 28th and 29th Seals, which use archetypal figures and "animated" memory structures to organize complex information and rapidly master the rules of Latin and Greek grammar.</summary>
<keywords>Art of Memory, Thoth, mnemonics, grammar, Latin, Greek, archetypes, conjugation, Polymath</keywords>

### The Combiner. The 30th Seal.

¶ And what method of discovery <note>original: *inventionum*; in the Renaissance sense of "finding" or "inventing" new arguments and ideas</note> can there be in this, and in similar and all kinds of things, where the form, the matter, the power, the means, the operation, the effect, and the goal of a single seal <note>original: *sigilli*; for Bruno, a "seal" is a complex mental diagram or memory palace used to lock information into the mind</note> might come together and run through various arrangements <note>original: *coordinatione*; a technical term for the structured alignment of memory images</note> alongside the same, similar, different, and contrary qualities <margin>5</margin> of other seals?

->**THE END.**<-

# ALSTED’S PREFACE

...likewise to receive and return favors. For I do not record my friends in some catalog, as some people do, nor do I enter favors into an account book, but I write—or rather, carve—both the friends and the favors in the deepest retreat of my heart. Receive therefore, my most excellent Lord Wrsotzky, this <margin>**6 F**</margin> slight paper gift <note>original: *levidense*; literally "thinly woven," Alsted uses this to modestly describe his book as a humble or small offering.</note> with that same expression you were accustomed to show me, and look upon the spirit of the giver. For this little book does not contain matters which could in any way be of use to Your Honor, <margin>**116 G**</margin> since you are already engaged in a more serious way of life. <note>Alsted likely refers to Wrsotzky’s transition from student life to the "serious" duties of nobility or public office.</note> However, I persuade myself that it will not be unwelcome to you on this account: that in its first part, it explains the rhetoric of Aristotle—of whom you have always been a singular admirer, as the most perfect philosopher in human memory. Furthermore, in the second part, it offers a compendium on the **abundance of words**, <note>original: *copia verborum*; a classical rhetorical technique involving the ability to vary expression and expand on a subject.</note> which is both elegant and easy, and which is not taught skillfully enough in the schools of our time. This book came into my hands two years ago; <margin>**7 F**</margin> I took care to have it transcribed and I corrected it myself, though in such a way that I changed only a very few things of **Bruno’s** <note>Giordano Bruno (1548–1600), the Italian philosopher and occultist whose works Alsted was editing here.</note> which I suspected were faulty. There is no reason for anyone to seek here either an advanced systematic order <note>original: *ordinem acroamaticum*; referring to the "acroamatic" style of Aristotle, intended for advanced students rather than a general audience.</note> or an elegance of style, for neither of these was the author’s purpose. If I had chosen to make a new treatise out of this material, it would indeed have come out more polished. But I preferred to share the teaching of the author—a man by no means unlearned—with those eager for the oratorical art, rather than compose a new treatise myself. Judge for yourself, most noble man, whether I have done something worthwhile, and advise me in writing. I took care that it be published in the same format as the *Trigae Canonicae*, <note>original: *Trigae Canonicae*; Alsted's "Canonical Triplets," a work on logic and theology.</note> <margin>**8 F**</margin> which I dedicated to the Lord Count, so that these two small books can be bound together. In this way, they may bear witness to the philosophical and Christian union which existed between the three of us (though why do I say "existed"? it exists even now!), which I ask you as a friend to deign to preserve, and you, with words...

## JOHANN HEINRICH ALSTED'S
<margin>10 F<br/>117 G</margin>
# INTRODUCTION
->TO<-
## THE RHETORIC OF GIORDANO BRUNO OF NOLA, THE ITALIAN.

5&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Kind reader, this little book holds more in its depths than it promises on its cover. So that you may see this, accept this brief introduction, which will serve as a guide for you in reading the work itself.
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The rhetorical treatise you see is divided into a preface and the main body of the text. <margin>11 F</margin> The preface | begins immediately, containing the driving causes—some general and some specific. The former concern everyone, while the latter concern Alexander, <note>Likely Alexander von Dohna, a student of Alsted's, whom he is encouraging toward statesmanship.</note> encouraging the pursuit of the study of eloquence—which today, I might almost say, is an exile from the schools.
15&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The main body of the text is subdivided into two parts.
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The first part sets before your eyes the first three duties of the orator: namely, <term>Invention</term> <note>The art of finding valid or seemingly valid arguments (original: *Inventio*).</note>, <term>Disposition</term> <note>The arrangement of those arguments in an effective order (original: *Dispositio*).</note>, and <term>Action</term> <note>The delivery of the speech, including voice and gesture (original: *Actio*).</note>.
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Invention concerns both the theme and the arguments; and it is considered according to the three kinds of "causes" or cases: namely, <term>deliberative</term> <note>Speeches given to persuade or dissuade regarding future actions, often in political assemblies.</note>, <term>demonstrative</term> <note>Speeches of praise or blame for a specific person or thing.</note>, and <term>judicial</term> <note>Speeches of accusation or defense used in courts of law.</note>, which are discussed generally in chapter 1, and specifically in the following chapters.
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The deliberative kind <margin>12 F</margin> has "topics" <note>original: *loca* (literally "places"); these are mental categories or "storehouses" from which an orator draws arguments.</note> from which arguments are sought, both common and particular.

<header>ALSTED’S INTRODUCTION</header>
<page-num>331</page-num>

Commonplaces are the sources from which arguments are drawn, even in the <term>demonstrative</term> <note>Speeches of praise or blame.</note> and <term>judicial</term> <note>Speeches for the courtroom.</note> genres. In chapter 2, these are six <note>original: "sex". While the text says six, it proceeds to list seven categories; a footnote indicates that the "G" edition correctly identifies these as seven.</note> in number: namely, the **Just**, the **Lawful**, the **Useful**, the **Honorable**, the **Pleasant**, the **Easy**, and the **Necessary**. In these matters, the useful often clashes with the honorable—or at least appears to do so—as discussed in chapter 3.

<margin>118 G</margin> The special and proper "places" of the <term>deliberative genre</term> <note>Speeches intended to persuade or dissuade an audience regarding future actions, common in politics.</note> are listed in chapter 4 and explained <term>part by part</term> <note>original Greek: "κατὰ μέρη" (kata merē).</note> in this order:
1. How sacred matters should be urged or discouraged (chapter 5).
2. How civil matters should be urged or discouraged—specifically those | regarding the state, safety, and security of the republic (chapter 6). <margin>13 F</margin>
3. How allies are to be recruited and treaties entered into (chapter 7).
4, 5, & 6. How war should be urged or discouraged, specifically:
- how it is provoked (chapter 8).
- how it is restrained (chapter 9).
- how it is ended (chapter 10).
7. How money is to be raised (chapter 11).

The "places" for the demonstrative genre are found in chapter 15. Here, the types and methods of **amplification** <note>The rhetorical art of expanding an argument to make it more impactful.</note> are presented in chapters 16 and 17. The "places" for the judicial genre are in chapters 18 through 23, which include both intrinsic and extrinsic sources of argument.

<term>Disposition</term> <note>The arrangement of a speech (original: *Dispositio*).</note> is defined in chapter 24, but it is presented and explained in chapters 12, 13, and 14, where the | Introduction, Narration, and Confirmation are treated. <margin>14 F</margin> In this instance, a <term>hysterologia</term> <note>original Greek: "ὑστερολογία". A figure of speech or logical arrangement where the natural order is reversed; Alsted is pointing out that Bruno explains the parts of a speech before formally defining the concept of arrangement itself.</note> was committed by our author. <term>Action</term> <note>The physical delivery of the speech, including voice and gesture (original: *Actio*).</note> is explained in chapters 24 and 25.

The second part of the work treats **Elocution** (Style), the fourth duty of the orator. It is subdivided into two sections: the first concerns the <term>abundance of words</term> <note>original: *copia verborum*.</note>, and the second concerns the <term>abundance of things</term> <note>original: *copia rerum*.</note>. Nevertheless, a transition (chapter 1) and a preparation (chapter 2) are placed at the beginning. The art of the abundance of words is handed down through...

<meta>This page continues Alsted’s systematic breakdown of the rhetorical system of Giordano Bruno (the famous Italian philosopher and memory specialist). On the previous page, Alsted discussed the "places" or categories for finding arguments in different types of speeches. Here, he moves into Bruno's unique "alphabetic" system—a mnemonic and structural method for organizing vocabulary and stylistic variations.</meta>

<header>ON GIORDANO BRUNO’S ART OF ORATORY</header>
<page-num>332</page-num>

...six alphabets, the latter two of which he chooses to call **practical**, while the remaining four are **theoretical**.
<margin>15 F</margin>
The **first alphabet** contains general terms that occur in almost any speech. <margin>5</margin> Therefore, let the letters of the alphabet be written in order in some book destined for the <term>oratorical faculty</term> <note>The art or department of public speaking.</note>, and let the terms expressed by Bruno be placed at the heads of the pages. Various formulas may be referred to these as if they were <term>commonplaces</term> <note>Standard themes or arguments used by orators.</note> and titles. For example, under class **A** might be terms by which something is judged to be or not to be; under <margin>10</margin> <margin>119 G</margin> the letter **E**, terms of **affirmation** should be written, such as "I say," "I think," "I judge," etc., and terms of **negation**, such as "I deny," "I reject," "I disapprove," etc. (Chapter 3).

The **second alphabet** concerns **garments** <note>original: "indumentorum"</note> (Chapter 4). The author calls them "garments" because they do not pertain to the <margin>15</margin> matter of the speech, but only to its external form, just as clothes are not part of the essence of the body, but merely its additions. For example, take this proposition: *God is to be worshipped.* <margin>16 F</margin> This is developed through the letters of that alphabet: through **A**: "Reason dictates that God is to be worshipped"; through **B**: "I do not think there is anyone who would say God is not to be worshipped"; through **C**: "Everyone feels this way," and so on.

<margin>20</margin> The **third alphabet** concerns **modes** <note>original: "modorum"</note>, which are like colors with which the "garments" can and should be dyed and adorned (Chapter 5), where their use is handed down with examples provided. 

These two alphabets, namely the second and the third, are combined in Chapter 6.

<margin>25</margin> The **fourth alphabet** concerns **complication** <note>original: "complicationis"; referring to the complex folding or combining of ideas.</note> (Chapters 7, 8, and 9), where a most elegant method of variation occurs. This single method contains almost the entire first book of Erasmus’s *On the Abundance of Words* <note>original: "De copia verborum", a famous Renaissance textbook on how to say the same thing in many different ways.</note>. We ourselves have made mention of this in our *Scholastic Theater*, our *Academic Counselor*, and our *Three Canonical Units*. <margin>30</margin> <margin>17 F</margin> The matter works like this: when some proposition is offered, or...

---

<note>Critical notes on the Latin text: Line 11: "and" in the F edition; "or" in the G edition. Line 13: "author" in the G edition. Line 22: "or" should be "and/or" according to edition G.</note>

<summary>Alsted explains Bruno's rhetorical "alphabets," which serve as a system for organizing vocabulary, stylistic "garments," and methods for varying a single idea into many forms.</summary>

<margin>5, 10</margin>
Even in the phrasing, the idea must be derived through grammatical, rhetorical, and dialectical terms. These are to be written in a specific <term>square diagram</term> <note>The Latin text uses "tetragono." Bruno often used geometric shapes as mnemonic devices.</note>, the <term>outline</term> <note>original: "diatyposin"</note> of which the author provides in that place, and they are to be expressed by specific letters. These terms are considered either alone or in combination. Alone—for instance, if I should lead this sentence, "God is to be worshiped," through A, B, and C, across both longitude and latitude. In combination—if I mix the letters of longitude with the letters of latitude, such as the letter **A** of longitude with **A**, **B**, **C**, etc., of latitude. By this method, there arises a most fertile harvest of variation, which I often look upon with astonishment.

<margin>18 **F**, 120 **G**, 15, 20</margin>
The **first practical alphabet** is found in Chapter 10, where the author teaches the method of <term>oratorical commonplaces</term> <note>Standard categories or "pigeonholes" used by students to organize quotes, arguments, and examples from their reading.</note> in the following manner. Let a specific alphabet be established that contains titles and oratorical commonplaces, such as **A** for "proposing," **B** for "asserting," and so on, so that it contains specific formulas. Now, whatever occurs in approved authors can and should be referred to these places. For example, if today you read a formula for "asserting" in Cicero, refer it to the class or letter **B**; if tomorrow you find a formula for "praising," refer it to that title marked with its own specific letter.

The **final alphabet** contains <term>accidental terms</term> <note>Terms describing non-essential qualities or circumstances of a subject.</note> in Chapter 11.

<margin>19 **F**, 25, 30</margin>
The **second section of the second part** is presented in Chapter 12 and explained in the following chapters. The <term>demonstrative genre</term> <note>The rhetoric of praise and blame, often used for speeches at ceremonies.</note> is treated in Chapter 13; the <term>deliberative genre</term> <note>The rhetoric of persuasion or dissuasion, typically used in political assemblies to decide on future actions.</note> in Chapter 14; and the <term>judicial genre</term> <note>The rhetoric of accusation and defense, used in courts of law.</note> in Chapter 15 and the final chapter. Here the author sprinkles in a fine piece of advice: for a theme to be handled by an orator, it is treated either **purely** or **mixed**. It is treated "purely" if it is explained from its own base—for instance, if the subject is of the deliberative genre, and only arguments of that genre are brought forward. It is "mixed" if these three genres are blended. For if the matter is of the deliberative genre, the orator may mix in...

<header>THE ART OF SPEAKING, I.</header>

# CHAPTER I.
## On the Threefold Genus of Causes.

In accordance with his custom, <term>Aristotle</term> <note>The ancient Greek philosopher whose "Rhetoric" is the foundational text for this study.</note> <margin>28 F</margin> <column-break/> takes the beginning of his treatment from the enumeration of the types of <term>civil causes</term> <note>original: "causarum civilium"; refers to the various types of subjects or "cases" addressed in public and political life</note>, as these are <margin>5</margin> the only matters within which all material that can be brought into a proposal is contained and revolves. He says there is a threefold genus of civil causes: <term>deliberative</term> <note>political speech focused on future action</note>, <term>demonstrative</term> <note>ceremonial speech focused on praise or blame</note>, and <term>judicial</term> <note>legal speech focused on past justice</note>. We say that the first of these deals with the good and the bad, the advantageous and the disadvantageous; the second <margin>10</margin> deals with the true and the false, the worthy and the unworthy; the third deals with condemnation or justification. Therefore, this threefold genus, when accepted in its broader meaning, includes every subject of consideration—not only civil matters, but also academic or philosophical (generally speaking), or even theological <margin>15</margin> matters.

<margin>126 G</margin> He says that underlying these three types are: persuasion, dissuasion, praise, blame, accusation, defense, and <term>inquiry</term> <note>original: "quaestio"</note> <margin>29 F</margin> <column-break/>. The first two species regard the deliberative genus; the next two regard the demonstrative; the three <margin>20</margin> last regard the judicial. From all of these, the last, which is inquiry, is the mercy, rigor, or justice of the judge, which arises from the accusation and the defense.

# CHAPTER II.
## On those things which pertain to the Deliberative Genus.

<margin>25</margin> Deliberation is a certain kind of consultation concerning three objects: namely, things to be chosen or rejected, things to be spoken or proposed versus those to be kept silent or concealed, and things to be done or avoided.

---

9 *edition* 10 "second" and "third" in Edition G : "2." and "3." in Edition F

<summary>This page introduces Aristotle's classification of rhetoric into three main branches—deliberative, demonstrative, and judicial—and explains how they govern all forms of public, philosophical, and theological discourse. It specifically defines the "deliberative" branch as the art of making choices regarding actions and speech.</summary>

<keywords>Aristotle, rhetoric, deliberative, demonstrative, judicial, persuasion, ethics, justice, civil causes, Jordanus Bruno</keywords>

...or what should be omitted. For every deliberation is concerned with choosing or rejecting, doing or omitting. All these things subsequently look toward seven points: namely 1. the just and the unjust, 2. the lawful and the unlawful, 3. the useful and the <margin>30 F</margin> useless, 4. the honorable and the dishonorable, 5. the pleasant and the unpleasant, 6. the easy and the difficult, 7. the necessary and the free. Persuasion and dissuasion revolve around all these things.

The **just and the unjust** are weighed according to the branches of law. For there is natural law, the law of nations, and the law of custom; <note>original: "ius naturale, ius gentium et ius consuetudinis"</note> indeed, this threefold law is called **Unwritten Law**.

The **lawful** <note>original: "legitimum"; refers here to specific codified law as opposed to general "justice"</note> also encompasses three branches according to a threefold law: divine, human (which is divided into ethics, politics, and <term>economics</term> <note>original: "oeconomicam"; in the 16th century, this referred to the management of a household or private estate, rather than a national economy</note>), and the law of pacts or agreements. According to these branches, **Written Law** is subdivided. Thus, the "lawful" and the "just" differ.

The **useful** is weighed according to four headings. The first concerns preserving present or immediate things; 2. concerns attaining future and absent comforts and goods; 3. concerns <margin>31 F</margin> averting evils that are present or immediate; 4. concerns <margin>127 G</margin> guarding against future and imminent evils and disadvantages.

The **honorable** <note>original: "honestum"; implies moral rectitude and social standing</note> is concerned with: 1. those things that serve to ornament a person, 2. averting <term>calumny</term> <note>false and malicious statements intended to damage someone's reputation</note>, 3. acquiring those things which produce honor, glory, emulation, and imitation—things which, if we lack them, we feel shame, and if we possess them, we glory in them.

The **pleasant** consists of those parts which cause delight, repel sadness, drive out fear, bring about security, and establish a peaceful and tranquil life.

The branches of **ease** <note>original: "facilitatis"; the quality of being easy to do</note> are: 1. standing favor or help, 2. the removal of an impediment, 3. the very <term>inclination</term> <note>original: "pronitas"; a natural tendency or readiness toward an action</note>...

He further breaks down the concepts of utility, honor, pleasure, and ease into practical considerations for a speaker.</summary>

### CHAPTER III.

->Topics to be used when the useful conflicts with the honorable.<-

Furthermore, sometimes two opposing sides may stand against one another because one of them disputes based on the **useful**, and the other on the **honorable**. The arguments for the first <note>the "useful" or expedient</note> are derived from peace, tranquility, security, taxes <note>original: "vectigalibus"; referring to state revenues</note>, money, wealth, honors and dignities, from attaining and increasing or augmenting defenses, and from the avoidance of those things which are contrary to these.

The second side <note>the "honorable"</note>, however, opposes this by presenting ancient law and the examples of our ancestors <note>original: "exempla maiorum"; the Roman concept of ancestral custom as a moral guide</note> who preceded us and who secured this state and honor for us. They also cite the examples for posterity <note>future generations</note> which they might receive from us, lest they themselves similarly ruin us and we <margin>33 F</margin> ruin others; and likewise the utility which proceeds from honor itself. 

In this case, it is necessary to consider the character of the persons, both of those who speak and of those before whom the speech is delivered. And indeed, those who are persuading are either private individuals or public figures, <margin>128 G</margin> such as those established in authority or under power. They may be those who are entreating or commanding and ordering, teaching, demonstrating, persuading or inquiring, questioning, or proposing. In these roles, let each person contemplate themselves as if in a mirror: with what expression, what gesture, what gravity, what humility, what authority or submission, what eagerness or...

<summary>This page defines the "necessary" as those factors beyond human control (God, fate, or force) and explores the rhetorical strategies used when practical utility clashes with moral honor. Bruno argues that appeals to honor should rely on tradition, the legacy left for future generations, and the inherent usefulness of being virtuous.</summary>

### CHAPTER IV.
->Concerning the subjects or objects of consultation.<-

The types of things that come under consultation <note>deliberative oratory where a course of action is debated</note> are: 1. sacred or divine matters; 2. laws or statutes; 3. treaties, or confederations, unions, and associations; 4. the waging of wars or the making of peace.

Likewise, there are those subjects that concern profit, gain, and generally the preservation or increase of wealth. All other matters that can <margin>35 F</margin> come under consultation utilize exactly the same "places" <note>original: "locis"; the *loci communes* or "topics" which are mental pigeonholes used to find arguments</note>. Any person who is not entirely unskilled will be able to adapt these topics to any proposed subjects with ease. For all things are either these very subjects and are handled in that same way, or they are similar to them and will be considered proportionally, or they are related to them, or they are contrary to them and will be handled in the opposite manner.

# CHAPTER V.

->Specific topics concerning those things which serve to persuade or dissuade regarding matters<-
->that commonly come into controversy in sacred affairs.<-

To descend then to specifics, we speak first of those things which concern worship and sacred rites. For those wishing to persuade an audience that sacred rites should be either maintained, increased, or diminished, they must look to certain "seats" <note>original: "sedes"; in classical rhetoric, these are the *loci* or logical "places" where an orator finds their arguments</note> of persuasion.

In the first place, an argument for continuing sacred rites is taken from **the just**, because it is fitting that we observe the custom of our ancestors who established the republic and founded our cities; they indeed judged it appropriate, first of all, that temples be erected to the Gods. 

<margin>36 F</margin> 2. Likewise, from **the honorable**, because a civilized people will be distinguished from the unrefined, the city-dweller from the wild, and the urban from the barbarian, chiefly by the worship and religion they observe. 

3. Also from **the useful**, because the minds of the people, when raised up and turned toward the purity of religion and the mind <note>The "F" edition reads "mind," while the "G" edition suggests "correction of morals"</note>, are more easily and regularly directed toward works of justice and the acts of civil life. 

4. Also from **the pleasant**, because the entire populace is cheered and refreshed by festivals of this kind, by sabbath-restings <note>original: "sabbatismis"; referring to the observance of rest days or religious holidays</note>, and by public spectacles. 

5. Also from **the easy**, because the execution of these things will be provided without any expense or loss, but rather with benefit. 

6. Finally, from **the necessary**, because unless divine authority and the <margin>37 F</margin> force of religion reside in the minds of the people, there can be no authority for the prince or the republic. For a person will easily hold others in contempt if they are driven toward poverty, sickness, misery, enmity, rebellion, and slaughter...

<summary>Giordano Bruno outlines six rhetorical "topics"—the just, the honorable, the useful, the pleasant, the easy, and the necessary—that an orator can use to argue for the preservation of religious customs and sacred rites. He emphasizes that religion is the foundation of social order and civil authority.</summary>

Thirdly, when worship is to be diminished <note>original: "extenuandus"; to be scaled back or simplified</note>, these means are available: 1. based on the condition of times, places, and fortunes, all of which have declined for the worse; 2. because it is not likely that the most perfect and holy God turns His eyes more toward external worship and ceremony than toward internal piety and religion; 3. because it is ridiculous if mortals should attempt or strive for anything beyond their strength; 4. because the celebration and ceremony of festivities lies not only within our will or power, but is subject to a certain judgment of fortune.

## CHAPTER XII.
->On the introduction.<-

Regarding its three-fold nature, the **introduction** <note>original: "exordium"; the opening part of an oration</note> (which is a brief statement of
those matters that are to be pursued in the narration or the discourse)
ought to be very concise and admit three conditions:

because what is to be said concerns them or the state 
greatly, both because the assembly must be held concerning difficult and necessary or terrible matters, and <margin>48 F</margin>
finally because they concern those things which 
lead to the increase or benefit of glory, honor, utility, pleasure, and justice; 3. so that the listeners are rendered **well-disposed** <note>original: "benevoli"; having a friendly or favorable attitude toward the speaker</note>. Now, listeners are either already well-disposed (in that you can already count on their favor), or they are hostile, or they are neither. If they are well-disposed, we waste time (says **Aristotle** <note>Greek philosopher whose "Rhetoric" heavily influenced Bruno</note>) 
in this kind of effort; indeed, we will even seem to follow the course of a pre-planned and rehearsed speech rather than taking account of the occasion and the people involved. It is sufficient, therefore,

The **younger speaker** therefore draws his reasons: 1. from a lack <note>original: "pecunia," though the editor suggests "penuria" (poverty/scarcity). If, in the fourth place, it is because of **insolence**, because we appear as new and recent arrivals, then the reason is readily available, arising from a new cause or an unusual case; for when new causes arise, it is no wonder if new effects emerge.

### CHAPTER XIII.

->On the conditions of the narrative in the same deliberative genre.<-

<margin>54 F</margin>
When a **narrative** <term>narratio: the second part of a classical speech, where the orator sets out the facts of the case</term> is to be established, it is considered according to the rules either in respect to the **matter**, or in respect to the **circumstances** of the matter, or in respect to the **manner**. Therefore, a narrative I. according to the **matter** either commemorates and announces the past, or explains and proposes the present, or predicts and pre-investigates the future. All these must be announced sufficiently, with nothing omitted—or at least nothing that would *appear* to be omitted; 2. extraneous matters must not be mixed in, namely those which are neither the business itself nor pertain to the business; 3. nothing should be changed—or at least nothing that would *appear* to be changed. <margin>55 F</margin>
kinds of brevity: one that teaches, and another that misleads <note>original: "dedocens"; literally "un-teaching" or leading away from understanding</note>. clear for two reasons: first, from the matter itself, if we do not confuse the business and the deeds, but
10 set them forth in the order in which each thing was done and said; 2. if proper words are brought forth, not those that are ambiguous, two-sided <note>original: "amphibolica"; referring to amphiboly, a grammatical ambiguity where a sentence can be interpreted in two ways</note>, or obscure. Finally, the narrative must be **probable** [credible], establishing those things that have the appearance of certainty. But if things that are neither true nor 
likely to be true occur, you should omit them altogether.

### CHAPTER XV.

<margin>5</margin>
->On those matters concerning the demonstrative genre.<-

The demonstrative genre <term>genus demonstrativum: also known as epideictic rhetoric, this is the branch of oratory used to praise or blame someone or something, often used in funeral orations or award ceremonies</term> is concerned with praise and blame, whether of things, intentions, purposes, words, or decrees, or of deeds and actions. In **57 F** these matters, it happens that one either amplifies or extenuates: extenuating 
<margin>10</margin>
great things so that they seem small, and amplifying modest things so that they appear great. The principles of extenuation and amplification proceed from the same root; for that which the affirmation and the positioning of a virtue amplifies and extols, the negation of virtue and the positioning of a vice diminishes and accuses.

<margin>15</margin>
### CHAPTER XVI.

->On the types of amplification.<-

Amplification, which is observed in exalting or demeaning men, is common to the praise and blame of all things; for by the same reasoning we celebrate a city and a 
<margin>20</margin>
republic by its founders, its preservers, and its virtues, just as we celebrate men by their ancestors, their parents, and their deeds. Therefore, the "place" <term>locus: a rhetorical "topic" or mental category used to find and organize arguments</term> for amplification is: 1. from things past—for instance, **58 F** from signs, predictions, and those things which preceded someone’s birth, namely their progenitors, lineage, homeland, and 
<margin>25</margin>
family, in which either all were illustrious (and then it will be permitted to present a catalog of all or many of them), or only certain ones among them **139** (and then one must use that sophistry <note>original: "cavillatione"; here meaning a clever rhetorical maneuver or subtle argument</note> that...)

# THE ART OF ORATORY, I.

It is not fitting to burden the ears of the listeners with a long lineage of ancestors; rather, one should only report those who seem relevant to the matter. If, however, only the first ancestors were famous, mention must be made of them. Furthermore, if the line of ancestors is entirely obscure, <margin>5</margin> you will be able to celebrate the subject's birth for this very reason: that he makes a nobility shine forth which was not granted, prepared, or shared by others, but was won by himself. Likewise, one may say, "he who glories in the deeds of ancestors prides himself on the honor and nobility of others, not his own," or finally, that he is not, as it were, the end <margin>59 F</margin> <column-break/> of his ancestors' glory, <margin>10</margin> but the beginning of those who ought to follow—not one who receives splendor from others, but one who radiates and pours out the brightness of his own dignity upon others. 

2. From present things, which are either goods of the body, goods of fortune, or goods of the soul <note>These are the three standard categories of "goods" in Aristotelian ethics: *bona corporis* (health/beauty), *bona fortunae* (wealth/status), and *bona animi* (virtue/intelligence).</note>. Goods of the body <margin>15</margin> include health, strength, tall stature, beauty, and longevity. Goods of fortune include friends, servants, wealth, favors, honors, and courage against enemies, as well as the fear and submission shown by one's foes. From all of these, as with the goods of the body, we might call a person lucky, fortunate, and blessed rather than <margin>20</margin> praiseworthy and virtuous—unless we take from them the material for praise, because he does not abuse such things but uses them well; he does not become puffed up or insolent, but becomes more prudent, wiser, more familiar, approachable, and generous. The goods of the soul, however, are those which pertain <margin>60 F</margin> <column-break/> to the intellect, <margin>25</margin> such as prudence, wisdom, and universally those things which look toward the perfection of the senses and the natural talent; or on the part of the will or the affections, such as the love of virtues and the hatred of vices.

->A particular account of the modes of amplification.<- <note>"Amplification" in rhetoric is the art of expanding an argument or description to increase its emotional impact or importance.</note>

Furthermore, **amplification** arises from things that come before, things that accompany (of which we have spoken), and things that follow. These include memorials, effects, honors decreed, the longing felt for the person, the grief and mourning caused by their death, and the <margin>15</margin> inconvenience arising from the absence of that man or thing.

2. Amplification also occurs through comparison or collation, where the side of an opponent or the virtues of someone else are compared with the subject's own virtues and deeds—diminishing or obscuring the qualities of others while elevating <margin>20</margin> and illuminating one's own. This, however, should be done with caution.

<meta>This page continues Bruno's systematic treatment of rhetorical structures. While the previous page focused on "amplification" (how to expand a point for emphasis), this page moves into the technical terminology of the "issue" or "status" of a legal or rhetorical case. It defines the components of a judicial argument, transitioning into Chapter 19 which deals with the form of judicial speeches.</meta>

<page-num>360</page-num>
<header>OF GIORDANO BRUNO</header>

<margin>69 F</margin>
1. This is the **issue** <note>original: *status*. In classical rhetoric, this refers to the "stasis" or the central point of contention in a legal case.</note>; this, moreover, is the matter or business being dealt with in the controversy, about which there is doubt, debate, and dispute, and which is proposed for a decision. Of this there are three species: first, **conjecture**, which concerns the question of whether something exists or does not, such as whether Antonius was present or not. The second species is **quiddity** <note>original: *quidditas*. A philosophical term meaning the "what-ness" or the essential nature of a thing.</note> or the "what," such as where it is asked whether Antonius is a legitimate and good-faith possessor, or a usurper or occupier. The third is the species of **quality**, "the sort" <note>original: *τὸ quale*. Bruno uses the Greek term for "the quality" or "the kind."</note>, where it is inquired whether something was done well or poorly, justly or unjustly, usefully or uselessly.

2. After the issue comes the **reason** <note>original: *ratio*.</note>, by which the defender or the defendant protests and blunts the slanders or pretenses of the accuser; indeed, unless this is present, there is no place for a defense.

3) It is the **foundation** <note>original: *firmamentum*. The core argument that strengthens the defender's position.</note>, by which the arguments of the adversary are torn down.

4) It is the **question** or **judgment**, being the boundary and central point of the controversy; namely, where that very thing which was expanded and diffused in the "issue" is contracted within the question or judgment.

5) It is the **debate** <note>original: *disceptatio*.</note>, which consists in the gathering, meeting, and comparison of the two parties, as if in a kind of fight or contest <note>original: *agone*. From the Greek term for an athletic or rhetorical competition.</note>; this is concerned either with the thing or the deed—such as whether he did this or not—or with the intention or the writings.

...common to both the opponent and the defender. Some of these are necessary, while others are probable. **Necessary argumentation** is that which is taken: 1. from the senses, as being self-evident; 2. from common opinion or faith; 3. that which is taken from laws or sacred decrees. **Probable** arguments are of other kinds: some are like necessary ones, which the adversary can hardly or not at all resist; some are "more likely" <note>original: *verisimiliora*</note>, such as if one were to think money was stolen by a poor man rather than a rich one; some are "not inconsistent," such as if one should think it more likely that one of those who were inside the house committed the theft, rather than those who were outside. <margin>71 F</margin> Argumentation is either **ordered** or **disordered**. There are four species of simple and ordered argumentation, namely: **reasoning** (or the syllogism), the **enthymeme**, **induction**, and the **example**.

1. **Reasoning** <note>original: *ratiocinatio*. Here Bruno uses it as a synonym for the formal syllogism.</note> is a perfect and complete species of argumentation, the parts of which are: 1. the **proposition** <note>The major premise or opening statement.</note>, 2. the **subsumption** <note>The minor premise or the specific application of the general rule.</note>, 3. the **proof** or verification, 4. the **conclusion** or inference.

The second species is the **enthymeme**, which is an imperfect form of reasoning; specifically, it is one that suppresses or keeps silent about something and retains it in the mind <note>An enthymeme is a "truncated syllogism" where one premise is omitted because it is assumed to be obvious to the audience.</note>.

The third is **induction**, which gathers a conclusion from many causes, particular signs, and facts.

The fourth species is the **example**, which is an imperfect induction; specifically, it does not gather a conclusion from all particulars, but from several; just as when one action or one individual is used to conclude something about another. <margin>72 F</margin>

However, where the form of argumentation is **disordered**—that is, not according to the dialectical manner or an ordered discourse, but as is suitable for the purpose at hand—it is either 1. reasoning that is explained and adorned, or...

### CHAPTER XX.

->On the internal means or topics of arguments.<-

All arguments are derived from certain "means" or "topics" <note>original: *locis*. Literally "places," these are conceptual categories used to find things to say.</note>. Of these topics, some are internal (intrinsic), others are external (extrinsic). Internal topics are derived from the definition or description of a thing, such as: 'That man does not | grant his right to those he should; why then should we **73 F**
call him just? And why shall we not call him just who is beneficial toward his neighbor and religious toward God?'

2. From the **enumeration of parts**: 'Why shall we call him virtuous in whom you find no sign of prudence, no sign of justice, no sign of temperance?' <note>These are the traditional Cardinal Virtues.</note>

3. From **notation or etymology**: 'Why do we see boys and the inexperienced and those with immature judgment taking a place in such a great council, if the *senate* <note>original: *senatus*</note> is so named from the *seniors* <note>original: *senioribus*, referring to the elders or *senes*.</note>, as being the more experienced and wise?'

4. From **conjugates** <note>original: *coniugatis*. Words derived from the same linguistic root.</note>, such as: 'Since I am a human being <note>original: *homo*</note>, I must live humanely <note>original: *humaniter*</note>, not divinely; since this man is a rustic and a barbarian, he will exhibit nothing but the character of a rustic and barbarian way of life.'

5. From **genus** <note>The general category to which a thing belongs.</note>: 'Truly every virtue | consists in action; **74 F**
why then shall we judge someone to be religious and pious if they remain outside the boundaries of action?'

11. From **relative opposites** <note>original: *relative oppositis*. Pairs that exist only in relation to one another, like "master" and "servant."</note>, such as: ‘Just as it is the duty of a prince to display the appearance of majesty, gravity, and preeminence, so it is in <margin>25</margin> the interest of the subject to reflect the appearance of compliance, obedience, and humility toward the prince.’

### CHAPTER XXI.

->Topics of arguments which are drawn from extrinsic sources.<-

Arguments drawn from external sources—namely, from those things which are derived not from the talent of the orator, but from the nature of the case itself—are as follows:
1. From **rumor**, or from that which most people believe, forebode, or suspect.
2. From **reputation** <note>original: *fama*. In a legal context, this refers to the established public character of the accused.</note>, namely from what is well known about the defendant.
3. From **torture**, namely from those things which he himself or another person was forced to confess.
4. From **documents** <note>original: *tabellis*. Literally "tablets," referring to written evidence, ledgers, or letters.</note> or writings, which are produced in his own hand or by someone else providing testimony.
<margin>79 F / 148 G</margin>
5. From an **oath** <note>original: *iureiurando*.</note>, whether past or present, requested or given, or yet to be requested or given.
<margin>20</margin> 6. From **precedents** <note>original: *praeiudiciis*. Legal "pre-judgments" or prior rulings.</note>, namely either from those things which were judged elsewhere in a similar case, or from those things which pertain to the present case, or from things already proven and judged within the same case.
7. From **witnesses**, whom we ought to mention <note>The editor suggests the original might have intended "to recommend" (*commendare*) rather than "to mention" (*commemorare*).</note> as being properly prepared and instructed; specifically, that they are just, wise, were present at the event, are not inconsistent or naturally prone to deceit, and are not for hire.
8. From **laws**, which either support our case—and here the topic arises from their necessity, utility, etc.—and from...

...the duty of the judges, whose business it is to be the guardians and defenders of the laws. Or, if the laws work expressly against our cause, then, lest any room for concealment be given, the points of argument are drawn either from the fact that the law does not apply to this case in this instance; <margin>5</margin> or because that law was bound and restricted <margin>80 F</margin> to certain times and conditions; or because it was issued contrary to the state of the republic and in a tyrannical or ambitious <note>original: *ambitiose*. Indeed, beyond the common utility <margin>10</margin> and the convenience of human society, there is nothing else to which laws ought to look. If, however, the law is ambiguous, such that it can be bent in either direction, then the meaning of the law must be so confirmed and declared that it works in our favor; the doubt or ambiguity must be concealed, and the law must be used as if it favors us. <margin>15</margin> But if the judge should lean toward the other side, we must use the same art, if we can—namely, by interpreting the words of the law with equity <note>original: *ex aequo*. A legal concept where the "spirit" or fairness of the law is prioritized over a literal, harsh reading.</note> in our own favor; and we must deny the contrary sense as if it were a novel and forced distortion of the law, not without a look of astonishment. <margin>81 F</margin> <margin>20</margin> But if the opposing side is rendered more probable, then you must adapt the case so that the law, as understood, seems to favor you more than your adversary, or at least no less. While this ambiguity and perplexity remains, you should decide to take refuge in other reasons and laws.

The primary areas of defense are those which oppose the accusation in the same order as they were presented. If any points are particularly difficult, the response to them should always be deferred with a certain dexterity or transferred elsewhere; for example: "Why is the response not ready?" <margin>5</margin> You might say that you will satisfy this question after certain preliminary matters | have been put forward and cleared away, as if you were intending to give a weightier response later. By this delay, the opponent's logic is disturbed, and the memory of the person presenting the case is eluded.

1. The category of defense, therefore, generally consists of **clearing the arguments** <note>original: *repurgatione rationum*. This refers to the rhetorical process of "cleaning up" or refuting the opponent's logic through counter-arguments.</note> <margin>10</margin> by using contrary reasons.

2. Arguments brought in from "off the path" <note>original: *e via adductae*. Meaning arguments that are irrelevant, tangential, or lack a direct logical connection to the core issue.</note> are not effective.

3. From the unfairness and deficiency that can be found in the accuser.

4. From the integrity of the accused person against whom the action is taken, <margin>15</margin> as if such an accusation could not possibly fall upon a person of this character.

5. From the conditions <note>meaning the status, character, or reliability</note> of the witnesses.

6. From signs and clues, which are not necessarily the results of the alleged act, or which could be signs of contrary or opposite things, or which could signify <margin>20</margin> many other things; or because, while those signs existed for another reason, someone else may have seized the opportunity and handle for committing the crime, led by the hope | that the fault would be transferred to this person or to me.

7. If the deed has been committed in such a way that <margin>25</margin> it cannot be concealed and you must necessarily confess, do your best, if possible, to refer it to some just principle or cause. If, however, there is no access to a just cause, one must fall back on chance, or on disordered events, which it is right to take into account; and it must be shown that the judges are not unfair...

### CHAPTER XXIII.

->On the order of both sides of the arguments.<-

Among the arguments that arise for defense and for <margin>10</margin> accusation, some are flawed and should be passed over entirely. One argument is the strongest, and this should be placed either at the very beginning or the very end. Other arguments close to this one in strength are to be arranged nearby. Others are of middling strength and should be relegated to the middle of the pack <note>This "Nestorian" order—strongest points at the flanks and weakest in the center—was a standard tactical recommendation in classical rhetoric.</note>.
