It must be understood that it is not the fame of a location—such as the seat, the pulpit, the platform, and similar things—that makes the speech or the speaker famous. Rather, it is the speaker and the speech that make the place famous. Just as in an auditorium, at a banquet, or in other gatherings, the most important and worthy man is not judged by the "first seat," but rather the "first seat" is judged by the most important man <note>original: *primus locus a primo homine*. Bruno argues that the speaker's merit confers dignity upon the stage, not the other way around.</note>.

<margin>10 **151 G** **86 F**</margin>
2. Delivery <note>original: *pronunciatio*. In classical rhetoric, this refers to the actual performance of the speech, including voice and gesture.</note> takes its power from one’s demeanor <note>original: *habitus*. This refers to the speaker's physical carriage and internal disposition.</note>, such that one ought to discuss happy matters more pleasantly than a mournful or sad matter, and so on. In all things, however, the orator must maintain a certain gravity <note>original: *gravitatem*. A sense of dignity and moral weight.</note>, since there is a clear difference between an orator and an actor <note>original: *histrionem*</note>, and between the public forum and the stage.

<margin>15 20</margin>
3. The method of delivery is also drawn from the face, so that each person might consider what suits their own nature and what is appropriate for the subject matter; for one facial movement suits some, while others suit others. An old man must behave one way, a young man another; the handsome man in one way, the deformed in another; the serious man in one way, and a face disposed in any other manner in its own way. Indeed, the variety of facial expression proceeds mostly from the movement of the eyes and eyebrows, the contraction and extension of the forehead, and the formation of the mouth.

<margin>25 **87 F**</margin>
4. The method of delivery is also taken from movement, which is either of the forehead, the eyes, the mouth, or generally of the head and the back, or of the arms and fingers, or the feet. In all movements, however, one must take care that nothing is done in an excessive or immoderate way.

5. In the voice, one must consider both natural and artificial qualities. By nature, we do not all have a voice equally and happily adaptable to everything; rather, some have a deep voice, others a sharp one, some a thin one, others affected in different ways, and others a pleasant voice...

...concerning which there are common treatises. It must be observed that certain measures and <term>feet</term> <note>original: *pedes*. Nor should only the rhythmic feet be observed, but also the variety of the sentence
<margin>5</margin>ending, so that we do not speak tastelessly by perpetually placing the verb at the end of the sentence. Instead, just as in nature, let us remember that in art, variety possesses great power. Furthermore, it must be observed that we should deliver a single
sentence in a single breath; however, if the thought is | rather long, <margin>90 F</margin> we should pause for breath in such a way that the 
<margin>10</margin>structural joints of the members <note>original: *membrorum compages*. Bruno uses an anatomical metaphor to describe the different clauses of a sentence.</note> do not seem to come apart. To these points, the logic of timing must be applied; for it is fitting to deliver certain things more quickly and with a certain flowing <note>original: *cursiva*, literally "running" or cursive.</note> speech, but others more slowly and in a more measured way. The first manner is more suited to both exaggerations and more fervent emotions, while the second is better for teaching,
<margin>15</margin>arguing, and persuading. The latter requires a steady state of speech, while the former requires a climax and an epilogue. Likewise, in the continuation of certain speeches a shorter pause is required, while in others a more prolonged delay is needed. 

The greatest power in delivery | is achieved if we hold the matter about which we are treating, or the business at hand, <margin>153 G</margin>
<margin>20</margin>as if it were present before us. For example, if we speak of the danger of the city, we act as if struck by fear; if we speak of the gravity of a crime, we should imagine its various parts and circumstances as present | within ourselves and, as it were, <margin>91 F</margin> set them before the eyes of the listeners. For this is essentially "making a scene," in which many—and perhaps all—of the aforementioned things
<margin>25</margin>converge, such as the changing of the facial expression, the movement of the body, the voice, and so on.

The last type of delivery, which often seems most relevant to the matter, consists in the thing itself or something similar to it; for instance, when to incite anger or pity, we produce the actual wounds, the blows, a bloody garment, and similar things, 
<margin>30</margin>either through a likeness or in reality.

<summary>Bruno discusses the technical rhythms of speech and the importance of varying sentence endings. He emphasizes the psychological power of "visualization," where an orator imagines a scene so vividly that the audience feels it is happening before their eyes.</summary>

### CHAPTER XXV.

->**On the Emotions.**<-
<note>original: *De affectibus*. In Renaissance rhetoric, "affects" are the passions or emotional states of the mind that a speaker aims to stir or soothe.</note>

Furthermore, along with what was recently said and other matters, one must not overlook what Aristotle notes in his works dedicated to Theodectes <note>Theodectes of Phaselis was a student of Aristotle; Bruno refers here to Aristotle's *Rhetoric*, which was sometimes associated with him.</note> regarding the winning over of the emotions. Therefore, although enough has been indicated regarding the form for arousing them, it is nonetheless 
<margin>5</margin> necessary to know | and observe by what means we are all moved <margin>**92 F**</margin> toward anger and patience, toward love and toward hatred, toward pity and indignation, toward envy and emulation. 
<margin>10</margin> We are, then, moved to anger by the perception of contempt, by detraction, and by calumny. We indeed seem to be held in contempt if things granted to those less worthy are denied to us; if our equals or inferiors despise us or seem to despise us—which is not easy to bear patiently even from our superiors; 
<margin>15</margin> or if we see certain people being ungrateful in return for honors and favors bestowed. For the ungrateful person seems to despise both the service and the one who served. We are moved to anger most of all if the contempt concerns those things in which we desire to be magnified and in which we long to excel. Hence, there are some reasons | why a 
<margin>154 G</margin>
<margin>20</margin> philosopher becomes angry, others for a soldier, and others for others. Detraction <note>original: *detractio*</note> is a category pertaining to the same end, | when those things <margin>**93 F**</margin> which are due to us—such as honor, respect, the reputation for true learning, and the dignity that consists in that virtue in which we excel—are denied us. Calumny <note>original: *calumnia*</note> 
<margin>25</margin> truly differs from detraction because the latter treats our rightful and true virtues as if they were foreign to us, while the former attributes to us vices that are far from us. The things that move us to love are the opposites of these. For we love those who think highly of us, who praise us, who imitate us, who...

<summary>Bruno outlines the rhetorical techniques for arousing specific emotions in an audience, focusing on the triggers of anger such as contempt, detraction, and calumny. He notes that the causes of these emotions vary based on an individual's social role, such as a philosopher versus a soldier.</summary>

...those whom we have instructed, educated, and for whom we have served in the place of teachers <note>original: *praeceptorum vice fuimus*. Bruno is concluding a list of social circles where a loss of face causes the most shame: specifically, before those we have mentored.</note>.

Following Aristotle’s *Rhetoric*, Bruno distinguishes this from envy; while envy is the pain of seeing another’s success, emulation is the virtuous distress of not yet possessing that success oneself.</note>, it is a similar sadness, by which we are indeed not pained because others fare well, but because we ourselves do not fare equally well, or perhaps because such success was more rightly owed to us.

## THE SECOND PART OF RHETORIC ADDED TO THE PRECEDING

->A<-

# GIORDANO BRUNO
### THE NOLAN, ITALIAN.

### ON ELOCUTION OR EMBELLISHMENT: DIVIDED INTO TWO SECTIONS, THE FIRST OF WHICH IS ON THE ABUNDANCE OF WORDS, THE SECOND ON THE ABUNDANCE OF SUBJECT MATTER, <note>original: *Copia verborum* and *Copia rerum*. These are central concepts in Renaissance rhetoric, referring to a speaker's ability to vary their language and content to avoid repetition and maintain interest.</note>

## CHAPTER I.

->Transition and introduction into the second part.<-

Next, we shall see what may be desired beyond the precepts already set forth,
<margin>98 F</margin>
10 and we will complete the second part of rhetoric—which was intended from the very beginning—so that everything handed down until now relates perfectly to the formal part <note>In Bruno’s terminology, the "formal" part of the art refers to the underlying structure, logic, and arrangement of an argument.</note> of the art, while that which is about to be taught relates to its material part.

As it concerns this material, we have five methods for varying, multiplying, and amplifying themes: namely, for varying 1. word choices, 2. figures of speech, 3. forms, 4. the arrangement or combination of the sentence structure, 5. and the <term>sententiae</term> <note>These are "sententiae" or maxims—the core thoughts or moral propositions that form the "matter" of a speech.</note>, which are the immediate material of any given proposition. But we shall present these in such a way that the art of rhetoric may be observed in its lesser part through rules, but in its greater and most perfect part through the examples of the orators themselves.

## CHAPTER II.

->An enumeration of those things which require specific alphabets<-
->for varying the form of expression.<-

<margin>99 F</margin>The following alphabets, which we shall arrange, supply us with an innumerable multitude of words or phrases. We do this not at all in the manner of grammarians and humanists <note>The "humanists" were Renaissance scholars who emphasized the study of classical Greek and Roman literature and the art of elegant expression.</note>, who indiscriminately teach how to inflect whatever occurs in various ways—such as the forms for giving thanks, for entreating,
<margin>157 G</margin>or likewise in how many ways one can say they have come, gone, rejoiced, or been saddened <note>original: *venisse, ivisse, gavisum, tristatum*</note>, etc. All these things are utterly childish. For if any are lacking in natural talent, they will only report extreme poverty from such a great "horn of plenty" <note>original: *cornu copiae*. This is a direct jab at Desiderius Erasmus’s famous work *De Copia*, a textbook on how to expand and vary one's style.</note> by misusing that multitude. But if any should prove talented, they will know well enough by themselves what and how, and in what place and occasion, something should be said and brought forth; so much so that such treatises seem to serve no purpose at all. Nor, for that reason, would they have approved of the study of a certain "prince of humanists" <note>The author hints at Erasmus (1466–1536), whose *De Copia* was the standard textbook for stylistic variety in the 16th century.</note> who wrote about the abundance of words in a way so unnecessary that he certainly seems to have written foolishly, as is his habit. 

Now, therefore, regarding those things which constitute the very part and foundation of the present art—which occur in every discourse and speech as constituent parts—no less than a fixed and defined number of letters can forge an infinite multitude of words. Therefore, having rejected those specific formulas which are not universal and which are suggested by the very subject matter being treated, we shall bring forward universal forms and principles, which are reduced to a certain number to be distinguished below:

First, for those things which pertain to simple expression,

### CHAPTER III.

->General terms arranged by alphabet for the convenience of expansion.<-

There are, as we have said, certain terms that have a place either in every speech or in most of them. Of these:
1. **A.** To be or not to be; for there is no speech that is not resolved into the substantive verb <note>The "substantive verb" refers to the verb "to be" (*esse*). Bruno argues that every statement, at its most basic logical level, is a claim that something is or is not.</note> affirmatively or negatively.
2. **B.** To feel, to opine, to know, to understand, <margin>158 G</margin>
likewise to be ignorant, to imagine, to doubt.
3. **C.** To agree, to disagree; for in every declarative speech it happens that either all, or many, or few, or none agree or disagree.
4. **D.** Concerning choosing and rejecting, or caring <margin>102 F</margin>
and despising, valuing highly or neglecting; this alphabet is applied universally to those things which are handled in deliberation <note>In classical rhetoric, "deliberation" is the genre of oratory used to persuade an audience toward or away from a specific course of action based on its utility or morality.</note>.
5. **E.** Concerning affirmation and negation; for the alphabet of affirming will be: I say, I judge, I state, I think, I confess, I judge, etc. <note>original: *aio, censeo, dico, existimo, fateor, iudico*</note>.
6. **F.** The alphabet of questioning, such as: *whether, perhaps, whether indeed, is it not?* <note>original: *an, forte, nunquid, nonne*</note>.
7. **G.** Of the evident and the hidden: of the evident, such as: *it is clear, it is manifest, it is public*; of the hidden, such as: *it is not clear* <note>original: *non liquet*—a legal term used when a verdict cannot be reached due to lack of evidence.</note>.
8. **H.** Of the easy and the difficult.

### CHAPTER IV.

->An alphabet to be derived from the aforementioned alphabet for an infinite abundance of variation through "garments."<-

### On the use of this alphabet.

There is a single method by which we can certainly and definitively vary a speech, a discourse, or a short book in almost countless ways, so that the same "old song" <note>original: *cantilena*. Referring to a repetitive or tedious refrain.</note> never appears to be repeated.
<margin>5</margin> For example, if a speech consists of thirty statements, these are first governed individually by these letters: A is applied to the first, B governs the second, C the third, and so on. Then [in a second variation] B governs the first, C the second, D the third, etc. After that, C governs the first, D the second, E the third, etc., while A governs the last. Or, to better hide the pattern, one might move by thirds <note>original: *occultando tertiam*. Literally "hiding the third," implying a skip-pattern in the sequence.</note>, such as from A to C, from C to E, from E to G; or by starting with D in the middle. First ascending <margin>**110 F**</margin> | and secondly descending, or first descending and secondly ascending. Similarly, beginning from the last to the first, | or from the second-to-last to the last, so that a continuous <margin>15</margin><margin>**162 G**</margin> circulation is created. In this way, we can vary not just a defined number, but an infinite number of sequences, as is shown in this form where the elements are arranged in a circle (Chapter 16), and thus adapting to however many propositions are necessary.

<margin>20</margin> ### Number 1.*

Furthermore, in the use of this system, it must be observed that these elements should be taken according to the mode of whatever is being proposed, whether affirmatively or...

## CHAPTER VII.
### On the folding and connecting of the final figure.

This figure, which we have subsequently called the "figure of garments" <note>original: *indumentorum*. Bruno uses the metaphor of "garments" to describe the different ways a single idea can be "dressed up" or expressed through different grammatical and rhetorical forms.</note>, can be doubled in the same way as the one mentioned before. We do this not by referring <margin>120 F</margin> general categories to specific ones, but rather by mapping one mode of species to another. For example, we might take the terms that vary the syntax <note>The arrangement of words and phrases to create well-formed sentences.</note> in a straight line according to the order of the alphabet, and the terms that change the figure of speech <note>A word or phrase used in a non-literal sense for rhetorical effect.</note> in a descending line. Then, the individual terms of "height" (the vertical axis) are drawn through the individual terms of "width" (the horizontal axis).

The terms of width <note>The horizontal axis of the grid.</note> are: **A** the direct case <note>original: *rectum*, referring to the Nominative case.</note>, **B** the genitive, **C** the dative, **D** the accusative, **E** the vocative, **F** the ablative, **G** the first person, **H** the second, **I** the third, **K** the singular, **L** the plural, and so on.

The terms of height <note>The vertical axis of the grid.</note> are: **A** etymology, **B** amplification, **C** composition, **D** relation, **E** periphrasis <note>The use of indirect and circumlocutory speech.</note>, **F** hyperbole, **G** diminution, **H** metonymy, **I** synecdoche, as is shown in the present figure, Number 3*.

Let them grant us only this: that we have looked more to the clarity and certainty of the doctrine than to the "brightness" (as is the custom among some) of useless and fruitless examples—which, though they may sound very beautiful, bright, and elegant, are found by those looking closely to be entirely empty inside.

## CHAPTER XII.

->The second part, concerning those things which contribute to the richness of thoughts.<-

After we have explained the method for intensifying and acquiring a wealth of speech <note>original: *copia sermonis*. "Copia" was a central goal of Renaissance rhetoric, meaning the ability to express an idea in many different ways without losing clarity.</note> from that aspect which consists in the richness of vocabulary, it remains to see the way of varying thoughts—first indeed in general, then very specifically, and finally regarding the preparation that consists in an abundance of such things.

Since there are <term>three kinds of causes</term><note>In classical rhetoric, these are the judicial (legal), deliberative (political), and demonstrative (ceremonial oratory of praise and blame).</note>, we must categorize the "places" <note>original: *loca* or *loci*. These are "commonplaces" or mental "seats" where an orator looks to find arguments for a given subject.</note> into three main classes, by which we can shape any proposition according to our capacity.

Therefore, "places" are the fixed seats of arguments or lines of reasoning. Although they may initially and
<margin>**131 F**</margin> primarily reflect a single type, they can nevertheless be skillfully converted into every form of presentation and representation—no differently than from the same piece of wax we can mold now the form of a horse, now a man, and now a tower. If, however, a "place" is brought forward that is not easily convertible, it is a "place" in name only, and not in reality.

...likeness and affinity, or proportion and proportionality, dissimilarity or contrariety; thus, after we have completed one **172 G** discourse of speech in a certain principal matter within one genre and purpose, we can convert one **132 F** purpose into another purpose by adapting the terms and <margin>5</margin> changing the order, so that not even the masters themselves, trained under the same discipline, would be able to detect the same artifice. For there is no part or no "place" <note>original: *locus*. A "place" or "topic" is a mental category used to find arguments.</note> that cannot be the first just as well as the middle or the last. For all things are either similar to man himself, or man is similar to them; or they are dissimilar, or contrary, or related in a similar or contrary manner; <margin>15</margin> and therefore, whatever is said about a man can, according to its capacity, be said about those things. From this, even the heavens have their right and left, and other local differences; a ship and a house have their right and left, arms, feet, belly, etc.; likewise a city, a **133 F** <term>republic</term><note>original: *respublica*. For all things, according to their own logic, have a genus as their principle, a proper character and species, their own definition or nature; <margin>25</margin> they have their own virtues, namely the <term>circumstances</term><note>original: *circumstantias*. The traditional rhetorical attributes: who, what, where, by what means, why, how, and when.</note> by which they conduct themselves well within their genus or species. As we exercise this genus upon man, so it is permitted to exercise it and others upon any things whatsoever: namely, according to a more eminent reasoning in more divine things, and according to a more humble [reasoning in lower things]...

### CHAPTER XIV.
<margin>136 F</margin>
->Regarding the "places" pertaining to the deliberative genre.<-

<margin>5</margin>The "places" <note>original: *loca* (plural of *locus*). In rhetoric, these are "topics" or mental categories used to organize arguments.</note> of the demonstrative genre <note>Rhetoric used for praise or blame.</note>, as was said above, are also common to the other genres. Following these in due order are the "places" of the deliberative genre <note>Rhetoric used to persuade or dissuade someone from a course of action.</note>, since it deals with matters <margin>10</margin> about which one must speak or remain silent, choose or reject, or act or refrain from acting. The general categories for all these are: the lawful, the useful, the honorable, the possible, the necessary, and the pleasant. The specific categories, however, are: orders or origins <note>original: *exortus*. A footnote suggests this might mean "origins."</note>, guiding opportunity or direction, the way, the gate, the entrance, <margin>15</margin> the manner, disposition, ease, solution, the foundation, the prop or support, the driving force, the provocation, influence or the influential factor, difficulty, the work or the worker, labor or weariness, disturbance, flight, rebellion or turning aside, a fall, dissolution, a bond, a knot or obligation, nakedness, emptiness, vanity, error, <margin>20</margin> dejection, reproach, vileness, misery, poverty, | <margin>137 F</margin> abjection, weakness, fragility, loss, harm, legion <note>The original text says *legio*, but a scholar's note suggests it should be *laesio*, meaning "injury."</note>, schism, separation, danger, repentance, business, wastefulness, obscurity, deviousness, [obligation,] and hardness. These are the things to be avoided, naturally ordered toward dissuasion, though they may be used <margin>25</margin> for persuasion "by accident" <note>In logic and rhetoric, "by accident" (*per accidens*) refers to an indirect or secondary effect rather than the primary intent.</note>.

Opposite to these are those things which naturally persuade and only dissuade by accident, such as convenience, profit, necessity, excellence, and expediency, from among those things which pertain to life, which—

<note>original: ...diorum</note>...of studies, the seasoning of troubles, a harbor of rest, tranquility of state, eternal life or its likeness.

These are the <term>genera</term> <note>broad classes or categories</note> and (species) <note>specific types</note> with their principal members, through which we can discuss copiously any thing to be chosen, or whatever matter has been established in the <note>original: constitutione; referring to the formal structure of an argument</note> arrangement. For the sake of remembering these, those who lack other <term>artifice</term> <note>skill or technical method, specifically referring to the "Art of Memory"</note> should construct <term>alphabets</term> <note>a mnemonic technique where letters are assigned to concepts to facilitate mental retrieval</note> for themselves through each heading, so that the <term>places</term> <note>original: loca; the "loci" or mental locations used in mnemonics to store information</note> may occur to them more easily at the proper time.

It is manifest, moreover, how we propose from these means every matter about which we deliberate and which we consider should be pursued in intention, words, and deeds. These are:
<margin>5</margin>
<margin>10</margin> <margin>141 F</margin>
- **First**, those things which are common because of occasion, origin, principle, ease, necessity, and the like, which were listed in the first place.
- **Secondly**, for the purpose of turning away opposites, such as labors, disturbances, flights, and the like, which were listed in the second place.
- **Thirdly**, likewise for pursuing useful things, either because they look toward <margin>15</margin> well-being by themselves or through something else, mediately or immediately, about which we speak in the third place.
- **Fourthly**, or because they relate specifically to the goods of the body, mind, or fortune, about which we speak in the fourth place.
- **Fifthly**, or because they relate to eminence, magnitude, similarity or <margin>20</margin> dissimilarity, conformity or analogy to the best and greatest <note>original: optimum, maximum; a phrase often used for the Divine or the highest good</note>, about which we speak in the fifth place.
- **Sixthly**, or by reason of those things which are extrinsic signs of magnitude and excellence, about which we speak in the sixth place.
- **Seventhly**, or by which names, denominations, and titles they bring or have brought, <margin>25</margin> take away or have taken away, about which we speak in the seventh place <margin>142 F</margin>; or express testimonies...

## CHAPTER XV.
<margin>15</margin> ->On the "places" pertaining to the judicial genre.<- <margin>143 F</margin>

The <term>judicial genre</term> <note>the branch of rhetoric used in courts of law to accuse or defend</note> also possesses certain specific <term>places</term> <note>original: *loca*; these are mental "categories" or "pigeonholes" where an orator finds arguments</note> of its own—and not many of them—distinct from the <term>deliberative</term> <note>political oratory aimed at future action</note> and <term>demonstrative</term> <note>ceremonial oratory aimed at praise or blame</note> genres. However, most are drawn from the same headings and categories because, as stated previously, every <term>accusation</term> <note>original: *accusatio*</note> arises because of
<margin>20</margin> things committed against the law, against <term>justice</term> <note>original: *iustitia*</note> in both a general and specific sense, against what is honorable, against public utility and necessity, or against what is pleasant. Therefore, from those matters that constitute deliberation—intended to be carried out in thought, word, and deed—an accusation arises from things neglected or
<margin>25</margin> violated, and a <term>defense</term> <note>original: *defensio*</note> is mounted by denying them. Thus, for one who does not wish <note>the scholarly apparatus suggests "one who wishes"</note> to intensify the judgment, the same...

<summary>Giordano Bruno completes his list of twelve rhetorical categories for general debate and begins discussing the judicial genre, noting that legal accusations and defenses are primarily based on violations of law, justice, and honor.</summary>

<meta>This page concludes Book II of Bruno’s work on rhetoric. It explains how the three genres of rhetoric—deliberative, demonstrative (epideictic), and judicial (forensic)—are interconnected. The page establishes that arguments for legal defense or accusation are often derived from the categories used for praise and blame.</meta>

<page-num>404</page-num>
<header>GIORDANO BRUNO’S ART OF DELIVERING A SPEECH, BOOK II.</header>

the <term>places</term> <note>original: "loca"; these are "topics" or mental categories used to find arguments</note> are offered which are used in deliberation; the confirmation of these same places from the <term>demonstrative genre</term> <note>the branch of rhetoric used for praise or blame</note> provides a 
<margin>144 F</margin> splendid supply of material. For from these places, which look toward praise, we easily find an occasion for defense; conversely, we find the confirmation for an accusation from their opposites and from those things which, in themselves, seem to look toward <term>vituperation</term> <note>blame or censure</note>. And so, from every side, we can very easily obtain an abundance of matter from those same places enumerated above. To these, the accuser adds those things that are 
10 peculiar to the <term>judicial genre</term> <note>the branch of rhetoric used in a court of law</note>, such as laws, agreements, 
<margin>178 G</margin> <term>tablets</term> <note>original: "tabellas"; refers to legal documents or records</note> or writings, | oaths, and witnesses. The defender, however, uses either these same things, if they favor him, or an extenuation of them. Therefore, it was not by chance that we observed this order from the beginning: that the <term>demonstrative genre</term> should follow the <term>deliberative</term>, while the <term>judicial</term> follows as a third, subordinate to the second, just as the second is subordinate to the first.
